title: Presidential Determination Pursuant to Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as Amended, on Domestic Petroleum Production, Refining, and Logistics Capacity
full_text:
(
printed page 68011)
Presidential Determination No. 2027-01 of October 22, 2026
Presidential Determination Pursuant to Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as Amended, on Domestic Petroleum Production, Refining, and Logistics Capacity
Memorandum for the Secretary of War
On January 20, 2025, I issued
Executive Order 14156
(Declaring a National Energy Emergency), under the National Emergencies Act. That order found that America's inadequate energy production, transportation, refining, and generation capacity constitute an unusual and extraordinary threat to the Nation's economy, national security, and foreign policy. It emphasized that our Nation's current inadequate and intermittent energy supply leaves us vulnerable to hostile foreign actors and poses an imminent and growing threat to the prosperity and national security of the United States.
Consistent with that declaration, I find that ensuring resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is central to United States defense readiness. Petroleum fuels the Nation's Armed Forces, industrial base, and crucial infrastructure. Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption.
Therefore, by the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, including section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended (the “Act”) (
50 U.S.C. 4533
), I hereby determine, pursuant to section 303(a)(5) of the Act, that:
(1) domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity, including exploration and production, gathering and transmission pipelines, storage, and marine terminals, are industrial resources, materials, or critical technology items essential to the national defense;
(2) without Presidential action under section 303 of the Act, United States industry cannot reasonably be expected to provide these capabilities for the needed industrial resource, material, or critical technology item in a timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations; and
(3) purchases, purchase commitments, financial support for the development of production capabilities, or other action pursuant to section 303 of the Act are the most cost-effective, expedient, and practical alternative methods for meeting this need.
I have declared a national emergency under
Executive Order 14156
, and I further determine that action to expand the domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is necessary to avert an industrial resource or critical technology item shortfall that would severely impair national defense capability. Therefore, pursuant to section 303(a)(7) of the Act, I waive the requirements of section 303(a)(1)-(a)(6) of the Act for the purpose of expanding such capability.
(
printed page 68012)
You are authorized and directed to implement this determination, including making necessary purchases, commitments, and financial instruments to enable these projects, and to publish this determination in the
Federal Register
. Any provision of previous memoranda, proclamations, and Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this determination is superseded to the extent of such inconsistency.
THE WHITE HOUSE,
Washington, October 22, 2026

title: Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People
full_text:
(
printed page 68007)
Executive Order 14438
of October 22, 2026
Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:
Section 1
.
Purpose.
The American Dream of homeownership is a vital pillar of our great country. It is the policy of my Administration to reduce regulatory barriers to mortgage origination and costs impeding homeownership; embrace innovative risk and value assessment technologies that incorporate Super Intelligence to drive down mortgage and homeownership costs; and promote competition and innovation throughout the housing and mortgage market.
Sec. 2
.
Proactive Cancellation of Excessive Mortgage Insurance.
(a) The Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency (Director) shall, if he determines that it is in the best interests of the Federal National Mortgage Association and the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation (Enterprises) or the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), and the American public, direct the Enterprises to establish a pilot program, applicable only to mortgages made after the establishment of the pilot program, that periodically reviews single-family mortgage loans they own, guarantee, or securitize, using automated valuation models and other available data to assess current market value, and to identify borrowers who appear to satisfy equity and other requirements for cancellation of mortgage insurance.
(b) The Director shall direct the Enterprises to establish procedures for the pilot program, including financial safety and soundness standards and payment-history requirements, under which mortgage insurance is canceled proactively when an Enterprise determines that:
(i) the borrower satisfies applicable equity requirements based on the property's current market value, as determined through an automated valuation model or other means approved by the Director;
(ii) cancellation is consistent with financial safety and soundness and with the Enterprise's contractual obligations; and
(iii) the borrower satisfies all other applicable statutory, contractual, regulatory, and Enterprise requirements for cancellation.
(c) The Director shall direct the Enterprises to require servicers, to the extent permitted by law and operationally feasible, to notify borrowers promptly when mortgage insurance may be canceled under the pilot program, and to reduce or eliminate unnecessary documentation requests, appraisal costs, and other administrative barriers to cancellation.
Sec. 3
.
Standardizing the Permitting of Homes.
(a) To increase the quality and lower the cost of building a home, there is hereby established the Task Force on Manufactured Housing Innovation (Task Force), which shall be co-chaired by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development and the Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, or their designees, and shall include the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of Commerce, and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, or their designees. The co-chairs may invite the heads of other executive departments and agencies (agencies) to participate, as appropriate.
(b) Within 180 days of the date of this order, the Task Force shall submit to the President, through the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy, recommendations to facilitate the use of modern manufacturing methods in the production of manufactured and other factory-built housing eligible for Federal housing programs, including actions to:
(
printed page 68008)
(i) promote specifications, certifications, inspections, and approvals across Federal housing and housing-finance programs;
(ii) establish reciprocal recognition among agencies of licenses, certifications, approvals, and inspections, where doing so would avoid unnecessary duplication;
(iii) eliminate Federal requirements and duplicative reviews that unnecessarily impede automation, modularization, standardized production, or other advanced manufacturing techniques, or that increase the time or cost of bringing homes to market;
(iv) use Federal financing, insurance, guarantee, purchasing, and other program authorities to encourage innovation and increased production of affordable manufactured and factory-built homes; and
(v) promote competition among manufacturers and other market participants while maintaining appropriate standards for safety, quality, durability, and consumer protection.
(c) The Task Force shall also evaluate whether, and under what existing statutory authorities, Federal grant funding may be conditioned on, or be used to incentivize, State and local adoption of standardized permitting and licensing for manufactured and other factory-built housing, consistent with the best practices issued under section 4(a) of
Executive Order 14394
of March 13, 2026 (Removing Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Home Construction), and shall prepare legislative recommendations to codify the policies set forth in this subsection.
(d) The heads of the agencies represented on the Task Force shall, within their respective authorities, take appropriate action to implement the Task Force's recommendations.
Sec. 4
.
Reducing Excessive Title Insurance, Especially in the Refinancing of Americans Homes.
(a) The Director shall, if he determines that it is in the best interests of the Enterprises or the FHFA, and the American public, and consistent with financial safety and soundness, the Director's authorities as regulator and conservator, and applicable law, direct the Enterprises to expand the title acceptance pilot into an ongoing program, available nationwide through both Enterprises, under which an Enterprise may accept an automated title review or other title-risk assessment approved by the FHFA in lieu of a lender's title insurance policy on eligible refinance transactions.
(b) In expanding the program, the Director shall consider:
(i) extending eligibility to refinance transactions with loan-to-value ratios above the current 80 percent limit where title risk remains low;
(ii) removing geographic limitations and certifying additional title-assessment providers to promote competition;
(iii) waiving appraisals, income re-verification, and other documentation requirements for limited cash-out refinances that reduce the borrower's monthly payment, where the Enterprise's existing data support doing so; and
(iv) reducing or eliminating loan-level price adjustments and other Enterprise fees on such refinances.
(c) The Director shall require that cost savings resulting from the program be passed through to borrowers and that lenders inform borrowers of those savings.
Sec. 5
.
Department of Agriculture and Department of Veterans Affairs Direct Loan Rates.
The Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary of Veterans Affairs shall, consistent with applicable law, including
42 U.S.C. 1490a(a)(1)(B)
and
38 U.S.C. 3762(c)(1)
, and available appropriations, reduce the interest rates charged on single-family home loans made directly by their respective departments.
Sec. 6
.
General Provisions.
(a) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
(
printed page 68009)
(i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or the head thereof; or
(ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
(b) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations.
(c) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any other person.
(d) The costs for publication of this order shall be borne by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.
THE WHITE HOUSE,
October 22, 2026.

title: National Seafood Month, 2026
full_text:
(
printed page 68005)
Proclamation 11075 of October 22, 2026
National Seafood Month, 2026
A Proclamation
Across our Nation's harbors and fishing communities, the unrivaled skill and resolve of American fishermen and seafood producers turn the bounty of our waters into food for our families and enduring economic strength. Food security is national security—we recognize that our fisheries are a vital pillar of American independence. This National Seafood Month, I join the American people in celebrating these hardworking men and women and reaffirm my commitment to helping them compete, prosper, and lead the world in seafood production.
From the fishing ports of early America to today's seafood farms and processing plants, this great industry has rewarded enterprise, sustained family businesses, and helped forge the unmatched spirit of determination that defines our maritime workforce. For generations, our fishermen have braved rough seas and punishing storms, spending long days far from home to earn an honest living and provide for the people they love. Across our land, the incredible American seafood industry harvests nearly 8.5 billion pounds of world-class food annually, sustains more than a million jobs, and fuels more than $173 billion in commerce, bringing wealth and opportunity to communities across our great Nation. And now, as we usher in a new Golden Age of seafood production, we are ensuring our fishing communities remain places where the next generation can raise a family, build a business, and pursue their own share of the American Dream.
Since returning to office, I have taken decisive action to restore American seafood competitiveness and give our fishing communities greater freedom to grow and succeed. Last year, I signed an Executive Order to restore American seafood competitiveness, and my Administration recently launched the Department of Agriculture Office of Seafood. I have also signed three proclamations to restore commercial fishing access to nearly 5,000 square miles in the Atlantic Ocean and to hundreds of thousands of square miles in the Pacific, enabling American vessels to work additional fishing grounds and compete more effectively in the global seafood market. Under my leadership, we delivered the largest single-year quota increase in the history of the United States Atlantic bluefin tuna fishery, secured a massive 1,200 percent quota increase for Atlantic mackerel, and revived the West Coast salmon season to yield the first full commercial fishery in 3 years. My Administration was also proud to allocate $123.6 million in fishery disaster assistance to help communities recover from devastating losses, strengthen shoreside infrastructure, and support job retraining to help workers get back on their feet. We will continue slashing burdensome regulations so our fishermen can reinvest in their fleets, expand their operations, and keep more of what they earn. Through these historic efforts, we are putting American fishermen first and fighting to make our Nation the strongest, most successful seafood producer in the world.
As our Nation celebrates National Seafood Month, we give thanks to the families whose skill and sacrifice have built and sustained this essential American industry for over 250 years. We will stand with them as we build a future of thriving ports, successful businesses, and an American
(
printed page 68006)
seafood industry that is stronger, more competitive, and more prosperous than ever before.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, do hereby proclaim October 2026 as National Seafood Month. I call upon all Americans to express their thanks for the American citizens who sustain this crucial industry, and to mark this month with appropriate events and ceremonies.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this twenty-second day of October, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.

title: Adjusting Imports of Wind Turbines and Their Parts and Components Into the United States
full_text:
Proclamation 11074 of October 22, 2026
Adjusting Imports of Wind Turbines and Their Parts and Components Into the United States
A Proclamation
1. Within the past 90 days, the Secretary of Commerce (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his investigation into the effects of imports of wind turbines and their parts and components on the national security of the United States under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended,
19 U.S.C. 1862
(section 232). Based on the facts considered in that investigation, and taking into account the close relation of the economic welfare of the Nation to our national security and other relevant factors,
see
section 232(d) (
19 U.S.C. 1862(d)
), the Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that wind turbines and their components and subcomponents are being imported into the United States under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States and provided me recommendations for action under section 232 to adjust the imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States.
2. Among other things, the Secretary found that wind energy is an unreliable and intermittent energy source and that the use of wind energy diverts the United States electrical grid from more reliable energy sources. The Secretary also found that products used to generate and use wind energy pose serious national security concerns, including by relying on foreign parts that contain cybersecurity vulnerabilities that could lead to remote control access to wind turbines and cause power disruption; undermining the United States' electrical grid, and potentially causing disruptions to critical infrastructure; interfering with national airspace and air safety; and causing radar interference that can affect air traffic control, weather forecasting, homeland security, and national defense missions. And the Secretary found that imports of wind turbine components and subcomponents have increased over the last decade, and that United States wind energy is reliant on imports of foreign produced wind turbine components and subcomponents.
3. The Secretary found that wind energy is intermittent and burdensome on the United States electrical grid. Wind energy is inherently intermittent, and this unpredictability undermines wind's suitability as a standalone energy source compared to the steady output of fossil fuel or nuclear energy, particularly if used for critical infrastructure. And even though wind energy comprises only a small portion of total utility scale power generated in the United States, grid operators must frequently rely upon fast-ramping fossil fuel backup generators to compensate for wind energy's high net load variability and maintain grid stability. This results in higher operational costs and increased maintenance burdens.
4. The Secretary found that the unpredictability of wind energy makes it less reliable than other energy sources that conversely provide steady output as standalone energy sources. Given wind energy's intermittent reliability, use of wind energy diverts the United States electrical grid from more reliable energy sources. And resources that are used to support wind
(
printed page 68002)
energy and wind energy projects could instead have been used to strengthen more reliable energy sources that are essential to the national and economic security of the United States.
5. The Secretary found that the use of wind energy poses unique national security risks compared to other energy sources. Among other things, wind energy products have serious cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can cause power disruption; interfere with radar, thus significantly affecting air traffic control, weather forecasting, homeland security, and national defense missions; and burden the United States electrical grid, including by diverting the United States electrical grid from more reliable energy sources.
6. More specifically, the Secretary found that wind energy products—particularly foreign imported products—present unique cybersecurity risks that could lead to remote control access to wind turbines and cause power disruption. Inverters are a crucial piece of electrical equipment for using wind energy, as inverters convert the electrical energy generated by wind turbines into a form of energy that can be used by the power grid or local systems. The vast majority of these inverters are produced outside the United States and imported into the United States. But modern networked inverters used in wind farms—particularly those produced and imported from outside the United States—are an exploitable vulnerability that can allow remote access and interference with United States power systems. Attackers could gain remote control over power generation, which presents risks of power disruption or sabotage of installation facilities.
7. The Secretary found that wind turbines can affect ground and air-based radars by creating “clutter,” reducing detection sensitivity, obscuring potential targets, and scattering radio wave returns. For example, clutter from wind projects obscures legitimate moving targets and generates false targets in the vicinity of the wind projects, and some mitigation techniques can lead to missing actual targets. These circumstances thus pose grave national security risks to the United States, particularly in response to threats (e.g., unauthorized aircraft) targeting sensitive United States critical infrastructure. And degraded radar performance from wind turbines can also have negative implications on weather forecasting, air traffic management, and military radar systems.
8. The Secretary found that the United States is reliant on imports of foreign produced wind turbine components and subcomponents and that imports of wind turbine components and subcomponents have increased over the last decade, while domestic manufacturing capacity for certain products, such as blades, has not meaningfully increased.
9. In light of these findings and the other findings in the Secretary's report, the Secretary recommended a range of actions to adjust the imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security.
10. Moreover, in Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting Imports of Steel Into the United States), and Proclamation 10962 of July 30, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Copper Into the United States), I found that aluminum, steel, and copper are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States and took action under section 232 to address the national security threats found in those proclamations. Certain wind turbine components and subcomponents are made of significant amounts of aluminum, steel, or copper and contribute to the national security threat found in Proclamation 9704, Proclamation 9705, and Proclamation 10962. Accordingly, certain wind turbine components and subcomponents are subject to the tariffs imposed in Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; or Proclamation 10962, as amended, to address the national security threats found in those proclamations.
(
printed page 68003)
11. After considering the Secretary's report, the factors in section 232(d) (
19 U.S.C. 1862(d)
), and other relevant factors and information, I concur with the Secretary's finding that wind turbines and their components and subcomponents are being imported into the United States under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States.
12. In my judgment, and in light of the Secretary's report, the factors in section 232(d) (
19 U.S.C. 1862(d)
), and other relevant factors and information, I determine that it is necessary and appropriate to enter into negotiations with foreign trading partners to adjust the imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents to address the national security threat found in this proclamation.
13. I therefore direct the Secretary and the United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) to jointly pursue negotiation of agreements or continue any current negotiations of agreements to address the threatened impairment of the national security with respect to imported wind turbines and their components and subcomponents, with any foreign trading partner the Secretary and the Trade Representative deem appropriate, and to update me on the progress of such negotiations within 180 days of the date of this proclamation. Under current circumstances, this plan of action is necessary and appropriate to address the threatened impairment of the national security found in this proclamation. Depending on the status or outcome of such negotiations, I may consider alternative remedies in the future.
14. Section 232 authorizes the President to take action to adjust the imports of an article and its derivatives that are being imported into the United States in such quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States. Section 232 includes the authority to adopt and carry out a plan of action, with adjustments over time, to address the national security threat. That initial plan of action may include negotiations of agreements along with other actions to adjust imports to address the national security threat, including tariffs. Moreover, if action under section 232 includes the negotiation of an agreement, such as one contemplated in section 232(c)(3)(A)(i) (
19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A)(i)
), the President may also take other actions he deems necessary to adjust imports so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States, including if such an agreement is not entered into within 180 days of the date of this proclamation or is not being carried out or is ineffective.
See
19 U.S.C. 1862(c)(3)(A)
.
15. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (
19 U.S.C. 2483
) (section 604), authorizes the President to embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States the substance of statutes affecting import treatment, and actions thereunder, including the removal, modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of duty or other import restriction.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, including section 232; section 604; and
section 301 of title 3, United States Code
, do hereby proclaim as follows:
(1) The Secretary and the Trade Representative, and any senior executive branch official they deem appropriate, shall jointly pursue or continue pursuing negotiations of agreements to address the national security threat found in this proclamation.
(2) The Secretary and the Trade Representative, in consultation with any other senior executive branch officials they deem appropriate, shall, from time to time, update me on the status or outcome of the negotiations described in this proclamation. The Secretary and the Trade Representative shall provide at least one of these updates within 180 days of the date of this proclamation.
(3) The Secretary shall continue to monitor imports of wind turbines and their components and subcomponents. The Secretary also shall, from
(
printed page 68004)
time to time, in consultation with any senior executive branch officials the Secretary deems appropriate, review the status of such imports with respect to the national security. The Secretary shall inform me of any circumstances that, in the Secretary's opinion, might indicate the need for further action by the President under section 232.
(4) Nothing in this proclamation modifies the tariffs imposed pursuant to Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; and Proclamation 10962, as amended, or any other tariffs imposed pursuant to section 232.
(5) Any provision of previous proclamations and Executive Orders that is inconsistent with this proclamation is superseded to the extent of such inconsistency. If any provision of this proclamation or the application of any provision of this proclamation to any individual or circumstance is held to be invalid, the remainder of this proclamation and the application of its provisions to any other individual or circumstance shall not be affected.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this twenty-second day of October, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.

title: Television Broadcasting Services Elko, Nevada
abstract: This document amends the Table of TV Allotments (table) of the Federal Communications Commission's (Commission) rules by substituting VHF channel 10 for UHF channel 20 at Elko, Nevada in response to a petition for rulemaking filed by Reno (KENV-TV) Licensee, Inc. (Licensee), the licensee of full power television station KENV-DT (KENV-DT or Station), Elko, Nevada. The Media Bureau (Bureau) previously granted a petition for rulemaking submitted by the Licensee to substitute UHF channel 20 for VHF channel 10 at Elko in the table, and subsequently granted a construction permit for its new channel. The Licensee states that it was unable to complete construction of the channel 20 facility by the deadline specified in the Station's construction permit. The Licensee filed the instant petition to amend the table to substitute VHF channel 10 for UHF channel 20 and allow KENV-DT to continue to operate on channel 10 at its licensed parameters and provide uninterrupted service to viewers. The staff engineering analysis finds that the proposal is in compliance with the Commission's principal community coverage and technical requirements, including the interference protection requirements. In support of its channel substitution request, the Licensee filed comments reaffirming its interest and stating that it commits to promptly take any and all steps that may be necessary to effectuate the channel substitution proposed in the petition. An individual commenter, Steven Quinn Singleton, also filed comments, which, for the reasons discussed in the Report and Order referenced below, the Bureau denied.
dates: Effective October 28, 2026.

Overview of This Information Collection
Abstract:
Federal explosives licensees/permittees (FEL/Ps) play a significant role in preserving public safety, including preventing crimes involving explosives, such as domestic or foreign terrorist acts. ATF's regulation at
27 CFR 555.121
provides that FEL/Ps must keep records pertaining to explosive materials in permanent form (
e.g.,
commercial invoices, record books) and in the manner required in
27 CFR part 555, subpart G
. These records are required under
18 U.S.C. 842
(f),(g),(j), (k), 843(f), and 847, and are established in the manner set forth in
27 CFR 555.121
,
555.122
,
555.123
,
555.124
,
555.125
, and
555.127
. As part of their record-keeping requirements, FEL/Ps must take a physical inventory at least once during each year. FEL/Ps must also take special physical inventories when they are: (1) commencing business, (2) changing premises, (3) discontinuing business, or, (4) requested to do so by the ATF Director, Industry Operations. If one of these special inventories occurs, the FEL/P is not required to take an additional inventory that same year. The inventory aids FEL/Ps in accounting for all their explosives material and reconciling cost, sales, and use records with inventory. It also establishes initial figures from which an audit trail can be developed by ATF field officers during a compliance inspection or criminal investigation. Specifically, ATF uses inventory figures to reconcile the physical inventory on hand and the book inventory the FEL/P maintains. These reconciliations are conducted on an ongoing basis, to determine whether any unlawful diversions of explosive materials have occurred, especially those arising through theft by persons not affiliated with the FEL/P.

Overview of This Information Collection
Abstract:
Title XI of the Organized Crime Control Act of 1970 (the Act) and its implementing regulations at
27 CFR part 555
require that persons who want to engage in the business of manufacturing, importing, or dealing in explosives, or using them, must file an application with ATF for an explosives license/permit. This requirement also mandates that the applicant include specific information about responsible persons (RPs) and other employees who are authorized to handle explosives in the course of their duties (employee possessors, EPs). RPs are persons who have the power to direct a federal explosives licensee/permittee's management and policies pertaining to explosive materials. Further,
18 U.S.C. 843(h)
requires ATF to conduct background checks on the applicant and any RPs and EPs, and section 843(a) requires that RPs submit fingerprints and a photograph with the form. These requirements help ensure compliance with the provisions of
18 U.S.C. 842(i)
, which prohibits certain persons from possessing explosive materials. This information collection covers the requirement to submit information on RPs. All persons holding ATF explosives licenses/permits must report to ATF identifying information about their RPs and any subsequent changes to their RPs. ATF's regulations establish that applicants must use ATF Form 5400.27, Explosives Responsible Person Questionnaire (RPQ) for this purpose. Doing so helps ensure that respondents provide all the necessary information to conduct the RP background checks and ensure they are not prohibited from operations involving explosives.

Overview of This Information Collection
Abstract:
18 U.S.C. chapter 40
requires any person engaged in the business of manufacturing, importing, or dealing in explosive materials to first obtain a license.
18 U.S.C. 842(a)(1)
. The statute also requires all persons who wish to obtain explosives, even for limited use, to obtain a federal explosives license or a permit (to use explosives, rather than engage in the business). This also includes all persons who wish to ship, transport, receive, or possess explosive materials.
18 U.S.C. 843
. ATF has prescribed ATF Form 5400.13, Application for Explosives License/Permit, as the means by which persons may apply for a federal explosives license or permit (FEL/P). Each person (individual, partnership, corporation, or association) applying for a FEL/P must submit ATF Form 5400.13. ACTION:
Temporary rule; quota transfer.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces that the State of New York is transferring a portion of their 2026 commercial bluefish quota to the State of North Carolina. This quota adjustment is necessary to comply with the Atlantic Bluefish Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial bluefish quotas for New York and North Carolina.
DATES:
Effective October 27, 2026 through December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Matthew Rigdon, Fishery Management Specialist, (978) 281-9336.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Regulations governing the Atlantic bluefish fishery are found in
50 CFR 648.160
through
648.167
. These regulations require annual specification of a commercial quota that is apportioned among the coastal states from Maine through Florida. The process to set the annual commercial quota and the percent allocated to each state is described in § 648.162, and the final 2026 allocations were published on February 19, 2026 (
91 FR 7896
).
The final rule implementing amendment 1 to the FMP, as published in the
Federal Register
on July 26, 2000 (
65 FR 45844
), provided a mechanism for transferring bluefish commercial quota from one state to another. Two or more states, under mutual agreement and with the concurrence of the NMFS Greater Atlantic Regional Administrator, can request approval to transfer or combine bluefish commercial quota under § 648.162(e). The Regional Administrator is required to consider three criteria in the evaluation of requests for quota transfers or combinations: (1) the transfers would not preclude the overall annual quota from being fully harvested; (2) the transfers address an unforeseen variation or contingency in the fishery; and (3) the transfers are consistent with the objectives of the FMP and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). The Regional Administrator has determined these criteria have been met for the transfers approved in this notification.
New York is transferring 200,000 pounds (lb) (90,718 kilograms (kg)) of Atlantic bluefish to North Carolina through mutual agreement of the states. This transfer was requested to ensure North Carolina would not exceed its 2026 state quota. The revised bluefish quotas for 2026 are: New York, 596,248 lb (270,454 kg); and North Carolina, 1,943,521 lb (881,566 kg).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Wage and Hour Division (WHD) of the Department of Labor (DOL) administers the Employee Polygraph Protection Act of 1988 (EPPA),
29 U.S.C. 2001
et seq.
The EPPA prohibits most private employers from using any lie detector tests either for pre-employment screening or during employment. The Act contains an exemption applicable to federal, state, and local government employers. The EPPA also contains several limited exemptions authorizing polygraph tests under certain conditions, including testing (1) by the federal government of experts, consultants, or employees of Federal contractors engaged in national security intelligence or counterintelligence functions; (2) of employees the employer reasonably suspects of involvement in a workplace incident resulting in economic loss or injury to the employer's business; (3) of some prospective employees of private armored cars, security alarm and security guard firms; and (4) of some current and prospective employees of certain firms authorized to manufacture, distribute, or dispense controlled substances. WHD may assess civil money penalties against employers who violate any EPPA provision. This amount increases annually due to the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act Improvements Act of 2015. For additional substantive information about this ICR, see the related notice published in the
Federal Register
on July 27, 2026 (
91 FR 46970
).
Comments are invited on:
(1) whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Department, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) if the information will be processed and used in a timely manner; (3) the accuracy of the agency's estimates of the burden and cost of the collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (4) ways to enhance the quality, utility and clarity of the information collection; and (5) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology. To help ensure appropriate consideration, comments should reference OMB Control Number 1235-0005.
This information collection is subject to PRA. A Federal agency generally cannot conduct or sponsor a collection of information, and the public is generally not required to respond to an information collection, unless the OMB approves it and displays a currently valid OMB Control Number. In addition, notwithstanding any other provisions of
(
printed page 67862)
law, no person shall generally be subject to penalty for failing to comply with a collection of information that does not display a valid OMB Control Number. See
5 CFR 1320.5(a)
and
1320.6
.
DOL seeks PRA authorization for this information collection for three (3) years. OMB authorization for an ICR cannot be for more than three (3) years without renewal. The DOL notes that information collection requirements submitted to the OMB for existing ICRs receive a month-to-month extension while they undergo review. The Department of Labor seeks approval for the revision of this information collection to ensure effective administration of the laws administered by the WHD.

Rule 17f-1 (

) under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (the “Act”) (
15 U.S.C. 80a
) is entitled: “Custody of securities with members of national securities exchanges.” Rule 17f-1 provides that any registered management investment company (“fund”) that wishes to place its assets in the custody of a national securities exchange member may do so only under a written contract that must be ratified initially and approved annually by a majority of the fund's board of directors. The written contract also must contain certain specified provisions. In addition, the rule requires an independent public accountant to examine the fund's assets in the custody of the exchange member at least three times during the fund's fiscal year. The rule requires the written contract and the certificate of each examination to be transmitted to the Commission. The purpose of the rule is to ensure the safekeeping of fund assets.
Commission staff estimate that each fund makes 1 response and spends an average of 3.5 hours annually in complying with the rule's requirements. Commission staff estimate that on an annual basis it takes: (i) 0.5 hours for the board of directors
[
1
]
to review and ratify the custodial contracts; and (ii) 3 hours for the fund's controller to assist the fund's independent public auditors in verifying the fund's assets. Approximately 4 funds rely on the rule annually, with a total of 4 responses.
[
2
]
Thus, the total annual internal hour burden for rule 17f-1 is approximately 14 hours.
[
3
]
Funds that rely on rule 17f-1 generally use a lawyer to prepare the custodial contract for the board's review and to transmit the contract to the Commission. Commission staff estimate the cost of a lawyer to perform these tasks for a fund each year is $1,548.
[
4
]
Funds also must have an independent public accountant verify the fund's assets three times each year and prepare the certificate of examination. Commission staff estimates the annual cost for an independent public accountant to perform this service is $11,550.
[
5
]
Therefore, the total annual cost burden for a fund that relies on rule 17f-1 would be approximately $13,098.
[
6
]
As noted above, the staff estimates that 4 funds rely on rule 17f-1 each year, for an estimated total annualized external cost burden of $52,392.
[
7
]
The estimate of average burden hours is made solely for the purposes of the Paperwork Reduction Act and is not derived from a comprehensive or even a representative survey or study of the costs of Commission rules. Compliance with the collections of information required by rule 17f-1 is mandatory for funds that place their assets in the custody of a national securities exchange member. AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice of receipt of an application for an exempted fishing permit; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
NMFS announces the receipt of an application for an exempted fishing permit (EFP) to support cooperative research activities funded by the NOAA RESTORE Science Program to verify, characterize, monitor, and model multi-species fish spawning aggregations in Federal waters of the Gulf of America (Gulf). This notice gives the public an opportunity to review the application and provide comments to NMFS regarding the request for an EFP.
DATES:
Written comments must be received no later than November 12, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments on the application, identified by NOAA-NMFS-2026-2806, by either of the following methods:
Electronic Submission:
Submit all electronic public comments via the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal. Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and type NOAA-NMFS-2026-2806 in the Search box. Click the “Comment” icon, complete the required fields, and enter or attach your comments.
Mail:
Submit all written public comments to Frank Helies, Southeast Regional Office, NMFS, 263 13th Avenue South, St. Petersburg, FL 33701.
Instructions:
Comments sent by any other method, to any other address or individual, or received after the end of the comment period may not be considered by NMFS. All comments received are a part of the public record and will generally be posted for public
(
printed page 67822)
viewing on
https://www.regulations.gov
without change. All personal identifying information (
e.g.,
name, address), confidential business information, or otherwise sensitive information submitted voluntarily by the sender will be publicly accessible. NMFS will accept anonymous comments. Enter “N/A” in the required fields if you wish to remain anonymous.
An electronic copy of the application may be obtained from the Southeast Regional Office website at
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/​southeast/​sustainable-fisheries/​cooperative-research-and-management-fish-spawning-aggregations-gulf/​
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Frank Helies, phone: 727-824-5305, email:
frank.helies@noaa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The EFP is requested under the authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act;
16 U.S.C. 1801
et seq.
), and regulations at
50 CFR 600.745(b)
concerning exempted fishing.
NMFS received a request from Sustainable Marine Solutions to obtain an EFP that would exempt research activities funded by the NOAA RESTORE Science Program. The goals of the research are to verify, characterize, monitor, and model multi-species fish spawning aggregations (FSAs) in Federal waters of the Gulf. The applicant requested exemptions from the applicable Federal regulations for project participants to harvest several species of Gulf reef fish and coastal migratory pelagic anytime during a year. If NMFS issues the EFP, the EFP could exempt participants from bag and size limits and area and seasonal closures. The applicant requested that the EFP be valid through December 31, 2030. The EFP request is further summarized below. Specific details, explanations, and reference citations are available in the submitted application (see
ADDRESSES
).
The proposed project would engage federally permitted commercial and recreational charter vessel (for-hire) fishermen to bridge the science-to-policy gap via advisory groups and an inclusive process to identify priority FSAs for characterization, monitoring, and modeling. The would conduct cooperative research trained professional captains on up to 120 sampling trips over 4 years (approximately 30 trips per year). An initial set of sites was identified during a workshop funded by the RESTORE Science Program and additional sites would be identified during meetings with small groups of fishermen during 2026 and 2027 and opportunistically through the life of project using information from a large monitoring database, bathymetric data, and geomorphological and seasonal cues from published and grey literature reports, as well as fishermen's knowledge. The applicant would prioritize those potential FSA sites for verification sampling using criteria developed in collaboration with scientists, managers, and fishermen.
FSAs can be verified using direct evidence (
e.g.,
observed gamete release or gonad dissection) and supported by indirect evidence (
e.g.,
courtship coloration and behavior). The EFP would allow the trained captains to attempt to verify FSAs. Fishermen would conduct limited sampling to verify predicted spawning aggregations largely following protocols outlined in Heyman
et al.
(2017). To ensure data quality, accountability, and project management, captains would undergo training and certification by RESTORE project partners to participate as members of a Study Fleet. Study Fleet participants would operate federally-permitted commercial or recreational for-hire fishing vessels. Participants would be compensated through pre-agreed arrangements.
Sampling trips would be authorized for pre-agreed and limited numbers of pre-determined species at highly specific, pre-agreed times and locations. Target species would include commercially and recreationally important species that are known to aggregate to spawn, including federally-managed triggerfish, groupers, snappers, jacks, mackerel, and cobia. The number of annual samples to be collected at each predicted time and location would be minimal (between 2-5 fish), particularly for large-bodied and slower growing species. In total, the EFP requests permission to collect 233 fishes each year for four years. (See table 1 in the application for details.) Potential study sites include the entire Gulf in depths from 10 to 1,800 feet (1 foot is approximately 0.305 meters) and sampling may occur at any time of the year.
Prior to each sampling trip, Study Fleet participants would complete a pre-trip agreement form with RESTORE scientists and be provided with all necessary equipment for sample and data collection. At specified times and locations, Study Fleet participants would use hook-and-line gear (automatic reel, bandit gear, bottom longline, and rod and reel) to capture targeted species. When captured, each sampled fish would be marked with an identifying tag and photographed to mark time and location of sampling. These samples would be immediately immersed in an ice bath for rapid cooling and euthanasia and then stored on ice. Samples would be returned to the dock as soon as practicable, but no more than 48 hours post capture to ensure sample quality. Study Fleet participants would coordinate their return with RESTORE project partners, who would serve as dockside samplers. Samplers, pre-trained and certified for data collection in this project, would meet Study Fleet participants upon their arrival. Study Fleet collected samples and associated data sheets would be transferred to project scientists and recorded with chain of custody signatures to ensure all samples are accounted for, sample numbers do not exceed agreed-upon numbers or species, and serve as documentation to support fishermen's compensation.
Non-target species caught during sampling would be noted on the data sheet. These fishes would either be released, with a descending device if possible, or retained by Study Fleet participants if retention is permitted under the applicable regulations. All other fishes collected for the study would be donated to charity.
Project scientists would append the field data sheet to include measurements recorded at dockside. These would include time and location of capture, species, sex, morphometrics, and photographs of the entire fish with gonads extracted and close-up photographs of gonads only. Otoliths would be removed for aging and gonad samples would be collected for histology to determine sex and reproductive status as in Brown-Peterson
et al.
(2011). Aging and histological analysis would be conducted under contract with the Marine Resources Monitoring, Assessment and Prediction program, otherwise referred to as MARMAP. NMFS finds the application warrants further consideration based on a preliminary review. In order to allow Study Fleet participants to conduct the requested sampling using commercial and for-hire vessels throughout the Gulf during any time of year, the EFP may include exemptions from size limits specified in
50 CFR 622.37
and
622.380
, bag limits specified in
50 CFR 622.38
and
622.382
, individual fishing quota requirements specified in
50 CFR 622.21
and
622.22
, seasonal and area closures specified in
50 CFR 622.34
and
622.36
, and restrictions on sale and purchase specified in
50 CFR 622.40
and
622.386
. Possible conditions the agency may impose on the permit, if granted,
(
printed page 67823)
include but are not limited to, a prohibition on sampling within marine protected areas, marine sanctuaries, special management zones, or areas where testing might interfere with managed fisheries without additional authorization. Additionally, NMFS may require special protections for Endangered Species Act-listed species and designated critical habitat and may require particular gear markings. A final decision on issuance of the EFP will depend on NMFS' review of public comments received on the application, consultations with the appropriate fishery management agencies of the affected states, the Gulf Fishery Management Council, and the U.S. Coast Guard, and a determination that the activities to be taken under the EFP are consistent with all applicable laws.

Abstract:
Migratory game birds are those bird species so designated in conventions between the United States and several foreign nations for the protection and management of these birds. Under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (
16 U.S.C. 703-712
), the Secretary of the Interior is authorized to determine when “hunting, taking, capture, killing, possession, sale, purchase, shipment, transportation, carriage, or export of any such bird, or any part, nest, or egg” of migratory game birds can take place, and to adopt regulations for this purpose. These regulations are written after giving due regard to “the zones of temperature and to the distribution, abundance, economic value, breeding habits, and times and lines of migratory flight of such birds” (
16 U.S.C. 704(a)
). This responsibility has been delegated to the Service as the lead Federal agency for managing and conserving migratory birds in the United States. However, migratory bird management is a cooperative effort of State, Tribal, and Federal governments. Migratory game bird hunting seasons provide opportunities for recreation and sustenance; aid Federal, State, and Tribal governments in the management of migratory game birds; and permit harvests at levels compatible with migratory game bird population status and habitat conditions.
The Service adopted general regulations for migratory game bird hunting, which are set forth in
title 50 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) at
50 CFR part 20
. These regulations provide that the Service will establish the conditions (limits) from which States and Tribes may establish their seasonal migratory game bird hunting regulations. The limits include season dates, season lengths, shooting hours, bag and possession limits, areas where migratory game bird hunting may occur, and other restrictions, and are communicated via the Migratory Game Bird Hunting (MGBH) Memorandum and notice of availability in the
Federal Register
. These limits are necessary to allow harvest at levels compatible with migratory game bird population status and habitat conditions. After the limits are established, States and Tribes may establish their migratory game bird hunting regulations within the limits and in accordance with our general regulations at
50 CFR part 20
. We provided a detailed overview of the process for establishing the Federal limits for seasonal migratory game bird hunting in the August 31, 2026,
Federal Register
(
91 FR 55794
).
Migratory game birds use four primary migratory routes in North America. Because of the unique biological characteristics and the relative number of hunters in these routes, the Service adopted the flyway structure for administering migratory bird resources within the United States, referred to as the flyways (Atlantic, Mississippi, Central, and Pacific). Each administrative flyway has a Flyway Council established through the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies and is composed of one member from each State and province in that flyway. The Flyway Councils assist in researching and providing migratory game bird management information for Federal, State, Tribal, and provincial governments.
State and Territories Seasons
—After the Federal limits are established, States, including the U.S. Territories of Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, may establish their migratory game bird hunting regulations within the Federal limits and regulations at
50 CFR part 20
.
Tribal Seasons
—The Tribal process is very similar to the State process and largely uses the resulting Federal limits developed in the process described above.
Based on the demonstrated successful implementation of our Tribal guidelines since 1985 (
50 FR 23467
, June 4, 1985), and the historical and future expected minimal impacts to migratory game bird resources, we simplified the process for establishing special Tribal migratory game bird hunting regulations beginning with the (2023-2024) season (
88 FR 60375
, September 1, 2023). We removed the requirement that Tribes annually submit their proposed migratory game bird hunting regulations (and associated monitoring, anticipated harvest, and capabilities for regulation development and enforcement) for our review and approval. We also no longer publish special Tribal migratory game bird hunting regulations in the
Federal Register
(
i.e.,
a proposed and final rule). The regulations set forth in the 2023 rule adopt elements of our guidelines for establishing special migratory game bird hunting regulations on Federal Indian reservations (including off-reservation trust lands) and ceded lands. Tribes that comply with these regulations are authorized to independently establish special Tribal migratory bird hunting regulations.
By allowing Tribes to independently establish special migratory bird hunting regulations, the Service recognizes Tribal sovereignty to exercise reserved hunting rights and, for some Tribes, recognition of their authority to regulate hunting by both Tribal and nontribal members on their reservation. As an alternative to promulgating special Tribal migratory game bird hunting regulations, Tribes may choose to observe the hunting regulations established by the State or States in which the reservation is located.
For the regulatory cycle, Service biologists gather, analyze, and interpret biological survey data and provide this information to all those involved in the process through a series of published status reports and presentations to the Flyway Councils and other interested
(
printed page 67851)
parties. Because the Service is required to take abundance of migratory game birds and other factors into consideration, the Service undertakes a number of surveys throughout the year in conjunction with Service Regional Offices, the Canadian Wildlife Service, and State and provincial wildlife-management agencies. To determine the appropriate limits for each species, we consider factors such as population size and trend, geographical distribution, annual breeding effort, condition of breeding and wintering habitat, number of hunters, and anticipated harvest.
Federal regulations at
50 CFR 20.110
(Regulations for certain Federal Indian reservations and ceded lands) include requirements for Tribes to follow if they establish special Tribal migratory game bird hunting regulations, which are based on elements from the 1985 guidelines. The regulations provide that all Federal hunting regulations in
50 CFR part 20
apply to hunting by Tribal and nontribal members. These regulations provide for the continuation of Tribal members' harvest of migratory game birds on reservations where such harvest is a customary practice. We are supportive of this harvest provided it does not take place during the closed season (March 11 to August 31) mandated by the 1916 Convention Between the United States and Great Britain (for Canada) for the Protection of Migratory Birds and it is not so large as to adversely affect the status of the migratory game bird resource. Since the inception of the 1985 guidelines, we have reached annual agreement with Tribes for migratory game bird hunting by Tribal members on their lands or on lands where they have reserved hunting rights.
We note that migratory game birds are defined in
50 CFR 20.11(a)
as those birds included in the terms of conventions between the United States and any foreign country for the protection of migratory birds, belonging to certain families (Anatidae, Columbidae, Gruidae, Rallidae, and Scolopacidae), and for which open seasons are prescribed in this part. Open seasons for certain migratory game bird species are established by the Service annually as appropriate based on the biological status of these populations and published in the
Federal Register
as Federal limits. Tribes are encouraged to review each year the Federal limits to determine the list of migratory game bird species and species groups with authorized open seasons, and any special concerns regarding population status. Furthermore, annual review of the Federal limits for migratory game bird hunting seasons e nsures that Tribal regulations for nontribal members on reservation lands comply (as required by regulations) with opening and closing dates, season length, and daily bag and possession limits established by the Service.
As a result of the process explained above for authorizing seasonal migratory game bird hunting, information is requested from States annually on their proposed seasons. Therefore, this ICR incorporates the information requested from the States each year and other monitoring requirements for their seasons. We post all notices and rules electronically on the Service's website (
https://www.fws.gov/​policy/​frsystem/​default.cfm
). State and Tribal governments are aware of this process that affords them the opportunity to provide comments on the information collection requirements identified in the Paperwork Reduction Act section of each rule.
The information identified below, necessary to establish annual migratory bird hunting seasons, is solicited annually from State and U.S. territory governments:
1.
Information Requested from States and U.S. Territories to Establish Annual Migratory Bird Hunting Seasons
—State and U.S. territory governments that wish to establish annual migratory game bird hunting seasons are required to provide the requested dates and other details for hunting seasons in their respective States or Territories. The information is provided to the Service in a nonform format, usually via letter or spreadsheet, in response to solicitations for the information sent to the State governments each year via an emailed letter.
2.
Details Needed from Tribal Governments
—This requirement is not applicable to Tribes that choose to observe the hunting regulations established by the State or States in which the reservation is located or independently establish special migratory bird hunting regulations in accordance with our regulations at
50 CFR 20.110
. We will continue to consult with Tribes that wish to reach a mutual agreement (memorandum of understanding (MOU) or similar type of formal agreement) on conducting short-term (possibly several years) experimental hunting seasons using methods outside of the Federal hunting methods at § 20.21 for on-reservation and ceded lands hunting by Tribal members.
3.
Reports (
50 CFR part 20
)
—The following reports are requested from the States and are submitted either annually or every 3 years as explained in the following text.
a. Atlantic Flyway Council:
Maryland, New Jersey, and New York—Two-tier hunting regulations study (phase 2) during 2027-28 through 2030-31 seasons per the terms of the study plan and Memorandum of Agreement among these States and the Service (Yearly updates and Final report).
b. Central Flyway Council:
New Mexico and North Dakota—Two-tier hunting regulations study (phase 2) during 2027-28 through 2030-31 seasons per the terms of the study plan and Memorandum of Agreement among these States and the Service (Yearly updates and Final report).
c. Mississippi Flyway Council:
Michigan—Two-tier hunting regulations study (phase 2) during 2027-28 through 2030-31 seasons per the terms of the study plan and Memorandum of Agreement among these States and the Service (Yearly updates and Final report).
d. Pacific Flyway Council:
Arizona, Nevada, and Utah—Two-tier hunting regulations study (phase 2) during 2027-28 through 2030-31 seasons per the terms of the study plan and Memorandum of Agreement among these States and the Service (Yearly updates and Final report).
e.
Additional State-Specific Annual Reports:
Arizona—Sandhill crane season harvest and subspecies composition (3-year intervals).
New Mexico—Sandhill crane season harvest and subspecies composition in Estancia Valley.
Delaware, North Carolina and Virginia—Tundra swan season hunter participation and harvest.
Montana (Central Flyway portion), North Dakota, and South Dakota—Tundra swan season hunter participation and harvest.
Montana (Central Flyway portion) and South Dakota—Swan season hunter participation, harvest, species composition, and hunter compliance rates in providing species-determinant parts or bill measurements of harvested swans for species identification.
Idaho, Montana (Pacific Flyway Portion), Utah, and Nevada—Swan season hunter participation, harvest, species composition, and hunter compliance rates in providing species-determinant parts or bill measurements of harvested swans for species identification.
Reports and monitoring are used for a variety of reasons. Some are used to monitor species composition of the harvest for those areas where species intermingling can confound harvest management and potential overharvest
(
printed page 67852)
of one species can be a management concern. Others are used to determine overall harvest for those species and/or areas that are not sampled well by our overall harvest surveys due to either the limited nature/area of the hunt or season or where the harvest needs to be closely monitored.
Experimental season reports are used to determine whether the experimental season is achieving its intended goals and objectives, without causing unintended harm to other species and ultimately whether the experimental season should proceed to operational status. Most experimental seasons are 3-year trials with yearly reports and a final report. Most of the other reports and monitoring are conducted either annually or at 3-year intervals.
4.
Requests for Consultation (Tribes/States)
—The 2023 regulations also may be applied to the establishment of migratory game bird hunting regulations for non-Tribal members on all lands within the reservations where Tribes have full wildlife-management authority over such hunting, or where the Tribes and affected States otherwise have reached agreement over hunting by non-Tribal members on non-Indian lands within the reservation. Tribes usually have the authority to regulate migratory game bird hunting by nonmembers on Indian-owned reservation lands.
The question of jurisdiction is more complex on reservations that include lands owned by non-Indians, especially when the surrounding States have established or intend to establish regulations governing migratory game bird hunting by non-Indians on these lands. In those cases, we encourage the Tribes and States to reach agreement on regulations that would apply throughout the reservations. If appropriate, we will consult with a Tribe and State with the aim of facilitating an accord. We also will consult jointly with Tribal and State officials in the affected States where Tribes may wish to establish special migratory game bird hunting regulations for Tribal members on ceded lands.
It is incumbent upon the Tribe and/or the State to request consultation. We will not presume to make a determination, without being advised by either a Tribe or a State, that any issue is or is not worthy of formal consultation. Tribal and State requests for consultation with the Service should be sent to the Service's Assistant Director for the Migratory Bird Program. We note that our guidance on resolving issues of concern between Tribes and States on reservations and ceded lands is the same guidance we provided under the previous Tribal regulation process.
5.
Requests for Experimental Seasons (Tribes)
—We will continue to consult with Tribes that wish to reach a mutual agreement (MOU or similar type of formal agreement) on conducting short-term (possibly several years) experimental hunting seasons using methods outside of the Federal hunting methods at § 20.21 for on-reservation and ceded lands hunting by Tribal members. The Tribal-member-only experimental hunting season would provide data and evaluation criteria specified in an agreement for consideration if a Tribe would like to make the additional hunting method operational. Tribes should send such requests for consultation to the Service's Assistant Director for the Migratory Bird Program at least 9 months before the season or ceremony regarding hunting methods outside of the Federal regulations.

AGENCY:
Office of Government Ethics.
ACTION:
Final rule; technical amendments.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is updating its executive branch regulation on financial disclosure to reflect the retroactive statutory increase of the reporting thresholds for gifts and travel reimbursements. OGE is also updating the executive branchwide standards of ethical conduct regulation to raise the widely attended gatherings nonsponsor gifts exception dollar ceiling tied to these thresholds. This latter change is not retroactive.
DATES:
Effective date:
This final rule is effective October 28, 2026.
Applicability date:
The amendments to
5 CFR 2634.304
and
2634.907
are applicable as of January 1, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Christie Chung, Assistant Counsel, or Marjorie Levine, Assistant Counsel; Telephone: 202-482-9300.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is amending pertinent sections of its executive branchwide ethics regulations on financial disclosure and standards of ethical conduct, as codified at
5 CFR parts 2634
and
2635
, in order to update the thresholds for gifts and travel reimbursements, as well as the widely attended gatherings nonsponsor gifts exception dollar ceiling.
Increased Gifts and Travel Reimbursements Reporting Thresholds
First, OGE is revising its executive branch financial disclosure regulation at
5 CFR part 2634
to reflect the increased reporting thresholds for gifts, reimbursements, and travel expenses for both the public and confidential executive branch financial disclosure systems. The increased thresholds are applicable as of January 1, 2026. These increases conform to the statutorily mandated public disclosure reporting thresholds under the Ethics in Government Act as amended,
5 U.S.C. 13104(a)(2)(A)
and
(B)
, and are extended to confidential disclosure reporting by OGE's regulation. Under the Ethics in Government Act, the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds are tied to the dollar amount for the “minimal value” threshold for foreign gifts as the General Services Administration (GSA) periodically redefines it.
GSA raised the “minimal value” amount under the Foreign Gifts and Decorations Act,
5 U.S.C. 7342
, to $525 for the three-year period 2026-2028 (from the prior level of $480) in a December 29, 2025, Federal Management Regulation Bulletin. See Gen. Servs. Admin., GSA Bull. FMR B-2025-01, Foreign Gifts and Decorations Minimal Value (2025) (revising, effective January 1, 2026, the foreign gifts minimal value definition as codified at
41 CFR 102-42.10
).
Accordingly, applicable as of January 1, 2026, OGE is increasing the thresholds for reporting of gifts and travel reimbursements from any one source in
5 CFR 2634.304
and
2634.907(g)
. The thresholds have been raised to “more than $525” for the gifts and travel reimbursements aggregation thresholds and “$210 or less” for the de minimis exception for gifts and travel reimbursements that do not have to be aggregated. As noted, these regulatory increases implement the underlying statutory increases effective January 1, 2026. OGE is also updating the examples following those sections, including appropriate adjustments to gift values.
OGE will continue to adjust the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds in its part 2634 regulation in the future as needed in light of GSA's redefinition of “minimal value” every three years for foreign gifts purposes. See OGE's prior three-year adjustment of those regulatory reporting thresholds, as published at
88 FR 37753
(June 9, 2023) (for 2023-2025, the aggregate reporting thresholds were more than $480, with a $192 or less de minimis exception).
Increased Dollar Ceiling for the Exception for Nonsponsor Gifts of Free Attendance at Widely Attended Gatherings
OGE is also increasing the exception ceiling for nonsponsor gifts of free attendance at widely attended gatherings from $480 to $525 in the executive branch standards of ethical conduct regulation, as codified at
5 CFR 2635.204(g)(3)
(and as illustrated in the examples following paragraph (g)). This separate regulatory change is effective upon publication in the
Federal Register
, on October 28, 2026. As OGE noted in the preambles to the proposed and final rules on such nonsponsor gifts, that ceiling is tied to the financial disclosure gifts reporting threshold. See
60 FR 31415
(June 15, 1995) and
61 FR 42965
(Aug. 20, 1996). Thus, OGE is again increasing the nonsponsor gift ceiling to match the further increase in the gifts and travel reimbursements reporting thresholds described above. The nonsponsor gift ceiling was last raised in June 2023. See
88 FR 37753
(June 9, 2023). The other requirements for acceptance of such nonsponsor gifts, including an agency interest determination and expected attendance by more than 100 persons, remain unchanged.
II. Other Technical Changes
Designation of Notes and Examples
OGE is designating various notes and examples in §§ 2634.304 and 2634.907. The designation of those notes and examples are technical amendments involving no substantive changes to the regulations.
III. Matters of Regulatory Procedure
Administrative Procedure Act
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
and
(B)
, as Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I find that good cause exists for waiving the general notice of proposed rulemaking and public comment procedures as to these technical amendments. The notice and comment procedures are being waived because these amendments concern
(
printed page 67766)
matters of agency organization, procedure, and practice. Further, notice and comment is unnecessary because these are technical amendments unlikely to be of significant interest to the public. Finally, it is also in the public interest that the accurate and up-to-date information be contained in the affected sections of OGE's regulations as soon as possible. The increase in the reporting thresholds for gifts and reimbursements is based on a statutory formula and lessens the reporting burden. Therefore, that regulatory revision is retroactively applicable as of January 1, 2026, when the change became effective under the Ethics in Government Act. For the reasons described above, this rule may take immediate effect pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1)
and
(d)(3)
.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
As the Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I certify under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. chapter 6
) that this final rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it primarily affects current Federal executive branch employees.
Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act (
44 U.S.C. chapter 35
) does not apply because this regulation does not contain information collection requirements that require approval of the Office of Management and Budget.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
For purposes of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. chapter 25
, subchapter II), this final rule would not significantly or uniquely affect small governments and will not result in increased expenditures by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more (as adjusted for inflation) in any one year.
Congressional Review Act
The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has found that this amendatory rulemaking does not meet the criteria for a major rule under the Congressional Review Act (
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
). The Office of Government Ethics will submit a report thereon to the U.S. Senate, House of Representatives and Government Accountability Office in accordance with that law at the same time this rulemaking document is sent to the Office of the Federal Register for publication in the
Federal Register
.
Executive Order 13563
and
Executive Order 12866
Executive Orders 13563 and 12866 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select the regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity).
Executive Order 13563
emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, of harmonizing rules, and of promoting flexibility. In promulgating this rulemaking, OGE has adhered to the regulatory philosophy and the applicable principles of regulation set forth in Executive Orders 12866 and 13563. The rule has not been reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget because it is not a significant regulatory action for the purposes of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 12988
As Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I have reviewed this rule in light of section 3 of
Executive Order 12988
, Civil Justice Reform, and certify that it meets the applicable standards provided therein.

§ 2634.304
Gifts and reimbursements.
(a)
Gifts.
Except reports required under § 2634.201(f) and as indicated in § 2634.310(b), each financial disclosure report filed pursuant to this subpart must contain the identity of the source, a brief description, and the value of all gifts aggregating more than $525 in value which are received by the filer during the reporting period from any one source. Note 1 to paragraph (a):

(b)
Reimbursements.

The filer is not required to report travel reimbursements received from the filer's non-Federal employer.
