Section 212 of the Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act amended
12 U.S.C. 1789(b)(1)(A)
to require the NCUA Board (Board) to “on an annual basis and prior to the submission of the detailed business-type budget make publicly available and publish in the
Federal Register
a draft of the detailed business-type budget.” Although
12 U.S.C. 1789(b)(1)(A)
requires publication of a “business-type budget” only for the agency operations arising under the Federal Credit Union Act's subchapter on insurance activities, in the interest of transparency the Board is providing NCUA's entire draft budget for 2027-2028 in this Notice.
The draft budget details the resources required to support NCUA's mission. The draft budget includes personnel and dollar estimates for three major budget components: (1) the Operating Budget; (2) the Capital Budget; and (3) the Share Insurance Fund Administrative Budget. The resources proposed in the draft budget are to carry out the agency's operations in 2027 and 2028. This document is a draft, staff-level budget proposal made available to the NCUA Board and the public for their consideration and comment. The NCUA Board directed NCUA's Executive Director to develop the draft budget under delegated authority. The draft budget may change based on public comments, Board decisions, and staff's ongoing consideration of estimates and programs that impact the budget.
NCUA's Chief Financial Officer will present the draft budget at a hearing open to the public on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Eastern at NCUA's headquarters, 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, Virginia 22314. Interested parties unable to attend in person may visit the agency's homepage (
https://www.ncua.gov/​
) to access the provided webcast link.
If you wish to participate in the hearing and deliver a statement, you must email a request to
BudgetHearing@ncua.gov
by November 6, 2026. Your request must include your name, title, affiliation, mailing address, email address, and telephone number. Statements must be delivered in person at the hearing. NCUA will work to accommodate as many public statements as possible. The Board Secretary will inform you if you have been approved to make a presentation and you will be allotted five minutes during the budget hearing to deliver your remarks. A written copy of your statement must be delivered to the Board Secretary by email by 12 noon Eastern, November 12, 2026. In addition to delivering their remarks at the budget hearing, registered presenters will be provided the opportunity to ask questions of NCUA staff about the draft budget. The initial round of questions will be limited to five minutes per presenter, and one subsequent round of questions, limited to five minutes per
(
printed page 67863)
presenter, may be permitted by the Chairman if time allows.
Written comments on the draft budget will be accepted by November 30, 2026, through the Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
The docket number is NCUA-2026-2146. Commenters should follow the portal instructions for submitting comments.
All comments should provide specific, actionable recommendations about the draft budget rather than general remarks. NCUA's Board will review and consider any comments from the public before approving NCUA's 2027-2028 budget.
By the National Credit Union Administration Board on October 23, 2026.
Melane Conyers-Ausbrooks,
Secretary of the Board.
I. Introduction
About the National Credit Union Administration
Created by the U.S. Congress in 1970, the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) is the federal agency that insures deposits at federally insured credit unions, protects the members who own credit unions, and charters and regulates federal credit unions.
NCUA's mission is to enable access to financial services by facilitating safe, sound, and resilient credit unions.
The agency operates its headquarters in Alexandria, Virginia; its Asset Management and Assistance Center (AMAC) in Austin, Texas, which liquidates credit unions and recovers assets; and three regional offices, which carry out the agency's supervision and examination program.
Backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (Share Insurance Fund) provides up to $250,000 of federal share insurance to millions of account holders in all federal credit unions and most state-chartered credit unions.
As of June 30, 2026, NCUA regulates and supervises 4,214 federally insured credit unions, which have approximately 146 million members and $2.5 trillion in assets.
[
1
]
Statutory Authority
Pursuant to the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act), the NCUA Board (the Board) determines the resources needed for carrying out NCUA's responsibilities under the Act.
[
2
]
The Board is authorized to expend such funds and perform such other functions or acts as it deems necessary or appropriate, according to the rules, regulations, or policies it establishes.
[
3
]
The FCU Act authorizes two primary sources to fund NCUA: (1) Requisitions from the Share Insurance Fund “for such administrative and other expenses incurred in carrying out the purposes of [Title II of the Act] as [the Board] may determine to be proper” and (2) “fees and assessments (including income earned on insurance deposits) levied on insured credit unions under [the Act].”.
[
4
]
Pursuant to its authority to use the Share Insurance Fund to carry out its insurance-related responsibilities, the Board approved an Overhead Transfer Rate (OTR) methodology and authorized the Office of the Chief Financial Officer to transfer resources from the Share Insurance Fund to the Operating Fund to account for insurance-related expenses.
[
5
]
In December 2023, the Board approved and published in the
Federal Register
the current federal credit union annual operating fee methodology, which is the basis for how the operating fee is calculated.
[
6
]
The Board delegated authority to the Chief Financial Officer to calculate the annual operating fee for federal credit unions and to set the fee schedule as calculated using the approved method.
Pursuant to the FCU Act, NCUA deposits fees collected in the agency's Operating Fund at the Treasury of the United States, and NCUA uses those fees to defray the cost of carrying out the agency's operations, including examining and supervising federal credit unions.
[
7
]
NCUA's Annual Budget Process
The FCU Act requires NCUA to publish an annual draft budget in the
Federal Register
for public comment and hold a public hearing on the budget.
[
8
]
NCUA stands out as the only Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act (FIRREA) agency that releases a detailed draft budget and solicits public comments on it.
NCUA develops a two-year draft budget by identifying the necessary resources, including supporting justifications, to achieve the agency's mission, goals, requirements, and objectives. This effort includes a field-level review of every federally insured credit union to estimate the workload to examine and supervise the credit union in the forthcoming year, which is translated into the cost of the staff and associated expenses for such functions. In addition to this workload analysis, each NCUA office reviews its fixed and recurring expenses, including:
Employee travel.
Rental payments for leased property.
Operations and maintenance for owned facilities or equipment.
Supplies.
Telecommunications services.
Major capital investments.
Other administrative and contracted services costs.
Before arriving at the final budget, the NCUA Board reviews any comments from the public and evaluates other considerations. Once the budget is approved, the OTR and federal credit union annual operating fee rates are set for the first year of the two-year budget.
II. NCUA's Budget in Brief
Proposed 2027 and 2028 Budgets
NCUA's 2027-2028 draft budget includes three separate budgets: the Operating Budget, the Capital Budget, and the Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses Budget.
[
9
]
(
printed page 67864)
Combined, these three proposed 2027 budgets total $325.4 million, an increase of 2.9 percent compared to the 2026 Board-approved budget, and consistent with the 2027 funding level approved by the NCUA Board as part of the 2026-2027 budget.
There are three main factors contributing to the draft 2027 budget growth compared to 2026:
Growth in employee compensation budgets, reflecting the pay raise terms in the agency's compensation agreement with its employee union, inflationary adjustments for employee benefits, and five proposed additional positions required to meet emerging needs related to new legislation as well as the Administration's priorities.
An increase in contracted services budgets, resulting from inflationary cost increases, cybersecurity investments, and because the agency projects $10.0 million less in offsetting, prior-year surpluses than 2026.
An increase in the Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses Budget. NCUA used the proceeds from the sale of its Austin office building to offset the 2026 budget, which was a one-time offset.
These increases are partially offset by a comparative decrease to NCUA's Capital Budget for 2027. The 2026 Capital Budget included $16 million for reorganization-related investments in systems and process improvements that align with government efficiency goals and other Administration priorities. The 2027 Capital Budget does not include any additional funding for reorganization-related investments or projects.
Proposed 2028 Budget: $344.2 Million
The 2028 combined total for the three proposed budgets is $344.2 million, which is 5.8 percent higher than the proposed 2027 combined total.
For planning purposes, the 2028 draft budget projects the same rate of compensation growth as in 2027, and 3.0 percent budgetary growth in all non-compensation spending categories plus certain discrete adjustments in cases where project cost growth is expected to exceed 3.0 percent. The remaining growth results from a lower estimate of prior-year surpluses offsetting the 2028 budget compared to the surplus used in 2027.
While the agency presents a two-year draft budget for planning purposes, the Board's practice has been to revisit each year's budget before that budget year begins.
III. Key Themes of the Proposed 2027-2028 Budget
NCUA Reorganization
Since the start of its Voluntary Separation Program in 2025, which resulted in a 23 percent reduction to its staffing, NCUA has been developing reorganization plans to build more productive, efficient agency operations. Throughout 2025 and 2026, NCUA has increased its operational efficiency and improved service delivery. The agency has been removing unnecessary and burdensome regulations, streamlining its business processes, and identifying technological improvements, and will continue to do so in 2027 and 2028.
The draft 2027-2028 budget supports NCUA's strategic restructuring plans. The agency's reorganization process is actively underway and targeted for completion by December 2027. The agency's reorganization efforts focus on prioritizing NCUA's statutory authorities and its most critical work, reducing and consolidating business units with like functions, achieving a higher supervisor to employee ratio, and leveraging technology to increase staff efficiency.
Technology Modernization: Enhanced Cybersecurity and SI/AI Strategy
NCUA must continue investing in modern information technology to keep pace with innovation while defending against evolving threats that could impact its ability to supervise America's credit unions. By integrating its cybersecurity framework with a forward-looking super intelligence/artificial intelligence (SI/AI) strategy, NCUA seeks to optimize business operations, harden agency systems against evolving digital threats, and foster a secure environment that supports responsible innovation across the credit union landscape.
The draft 2027-2028 budget includes resources to expand the agency's zero-trust cybersecurity strategy, with investments in advanced threat protection to address evolving digital risks and fulfill new federal requirements. To comply fully with federal directives, NCUA must acquire enhanced cybersecurity capabilities. The draft budget's investments will reduce reliance on manual processes, reinforce the organization's IT infrastructure, and ensure that NCUA can continue innovating by integrating SI/AI tools into its operations.
When combined with a portion of the agency's 2026 reorganization and innovation funding, the draft budget provides funding to continue deploying SI/AI and advanced analytic tools across the agency. NCUA's SI/AI strategy aligns with the Administration's direction and will both enhance examination and supervision capabilities and deliver operational efficiencies.
(
printed page 67865)
Deregulation, Examination Priorities, and Workforce
The draft 2027-2028 budget includes resources to reduce regulatory burden on credit unions and focus NCUA's examination program on material risks.
NCUA's Deregulation Project is a multi-year initiative to review, streamline, and modernize the agency's regulatory framework. The Deregulation Project will continue in 2027, and will address more complex regulations with broader policy and operational implications. The draft budget supports this project and other rulemaking and related implementation efforts associated with new legislation and the Administration's priorities, such as the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act) for Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers.
NCUA continues to invest in its efforts to:
Focus examination attention on areas posing material risk.
Streamline examination practices to increase efficiency
Adopt advanced capabilities to improve risk and problem identification
Train, develop, and resource staff to ensure the agency has the necessary expertise to supervise complex and new activities
Facilitate responsible innovation by credit unions
IV. Operating Budget: $312.4 Million
Overview
The proposed 2027 Operating Budget is $312.4 million, which provides the resources required for the agency to conduct activities prescribed by the FCU Act. These mandates include but are not limited to:
Chartering new federal credit unions
Approving field of membership applications of federal credit unions
Promulgating regulations and providing guidance
Performing examinations, supervision, and enforcement
NCUA also implements requirements of other statutes and Executive Orders including those related to the Bank Secrecy Act, various consumer financial protection laws, and various requirements for federal agencies.
Operating Budget Categories
This section explains how the Operating Budget funds NCUA's major expense categories, as summarized in the following chart.
(
printed page 67866)
Pay and Benefits. Pay and benefits make up approximately 80 percent of the proposed 2027 NCUA Operating Budget. The proposed 2027 budget for pay and benefits increases by 4.2 percent compared to 2026, for a total of $250.5 million. There are three primary drivers of increased costs in 2027 for the pay and benefits category:
Merit and locality pay increases for NCUA's employees, which are paid according to the terms of the agency's compensation agreement with its employee union and its merit-based pay system.
[
10
]
Contributions for employee health insurance, which are set by OPM and cannot be changed by NCUA.
Costs associated with other mandatory employer contributions such as Social Security, Medicare, transportation subsidies, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation, which are set by other agencies and cannot be changed by NCUA.
The proposed 2028 budget for pay and benefits is estimated at $260.3 million, a 3.9 percent increase from the proposed 2027 level.
The proposed 2027 and 2028 Operating Budgets support a total agency staffing level of 972 positions.
[
11
]
This is an increase of five positions (0.5 percent) compared to the agency's 2026 approved position level. NCUA's Strategic Hiring Committee will allocate these new positions to address emerging needs related to new legislation, such as the GENIUS Act and the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, as well as for other emerging Administration and agency priorities, such as SI/AI implementation and cybersecurity enhancements.
Approximately 63 percent, or 609 proposed positions, would conduct NCUA's examination and supervision functions, while the remaining 37 percent, or 363 proposed positions, would perform other necessary functions, including legal services, policy development and analysis, and agency administration.
The following chart illustrates NCUA's approved position levels in recent years.
(
printed page 67867)
Travel.
The proposed travel budget decreases by $2.7 million (13.6 percent) compared to 2026, for a total of $17.4 million. The travel cost category includes expenses for employees' airfare, lodging, meals, auto rentals, reimbursements for privately owned vehicle usage, and other travel-related expenses. These are necessary expenses for onsite work in credit unions and other assignments involving travel.
The proposed 2028 budget for travel is estimated at $18.9 million, an 8.7 percent increase compared to the 2027 level. This budget level reflects travel-related cost inflation in 2028 and an agency-wide training event.
Rent, Communications, and Utilities.
The proposed budget for rent, communications, and utilities increases by $2.1 million in 2027 (43.5 percent) compared to 2026, for a budget of $7.0 million. The 2026 rent, communications, and utilities budget was reduced by a one-time offset of $1.7 million from the sale of the Austin, TX office building.
[
12
]
Excluding this change in the offset, the 2027 increase is $0.4 million.
Funding within this budget category pays for facilities-related costs, telecommunications services, data storage, and information technology network support. Telecommunications charges include leased data lines and data service subscriptions, Voice over Internet Protocol and mobile telephony, and other network charges. Facilities-related budgets pay for the cost of the leased offices and disaster recovery and continuity of operations sites, utilities, meeting space rental for offsite events, and postage.
The proposed 2028 budget for the rent, communications, and utilities category is a 3.0 percent increase compared to 2027.
Administrative.
The draft budget proposes a $0.8 million increase in administrative expenses for 2027 (21.1 percent) compared to 2026, for a budget of $4.6 million. Recurring costs in the administrative expenses category include employee relocation expenses, recruitment expenses, shipping, printing, subscriptions, examiner training and meeting supplies, office furniture, legal settlements, and employee supplies and materials. NCUA pays relocation costs to employees who are competitively selected for a promotion or new job within the agency in a different geographic area than where they live.
The proposed 2028 budget for administrative expenses is $4.8 million, an increase of 3.4 percent compared to the level proposed for 2027.
Contracted Services.
The proposed budget for contracted services increases by $13.5 million in 2027 (69.8 percent) compared to 2026, for a budget of $32.9 million. The substantial percentage increase in the contracted services budget is driven largely by a reduction in the amount of prior-year unspent budget surpluses used to offset the 2027 budget.
[
13
]
The proposed 2027 budget for contracted services assumes an offset of $39.3 million from prior-year unspent budget balances. Excluding the offset, the 2027 proposed budget assumes total contracted services expenditures of $72.2 million, compared to $68.7 million in 2026, a 5.1 percent increase.
NCUA uses contracted services because acquiring specific expertise or services from contract providers is often the most viable and cost-effective way for NCUA to accomplish its mission.
(
printed page 67868)
Contracted services include critical mission support such as information technology equipment and software development, accounting and auditing services, and specialized subject matter expertise that enable staff to focus on executing core mission requirements. The contracted services category supports NCUA's supervision framework, core NCUA systems such as accounting and payroll processing, and various recurring costs as described in the following seven major categories:
1. Information Technology Operations and Maintenance (50.7 Percent of Contracted Services)
IT network support services and help desk support
Contractor program and web support and network and equipment maintenance services
Administration of software products and audio-visual services
2. Administrative Support and Other Services (16.4 Percent of Contracted Services)
Examination and supervision program support
Technical support for examination and cybersecurity training programs
Equipment maintenance services
Legal services and other expert consulting support
FFIEC reimbursements
3. IT Security (16.9 Percent of Contracted Services)
Secure data storage and operations
Information security programs
Security system assessment services
4. Accounting, Procurement, Payroll, and Human Resources Systems (4.6 Percent of Contracted Services)
Accounting and procurement systems and support
Human resources, payroll, and employee services
Equal Employment Opportunity programs, as required by law
5. Building Operations, Maintenance, and Security (5.1 Percent of Contracted Services)
Headquarters facility operations and maintenance
Building security and continuity programs
Personnel security and administrative programs
6. Audit and Financial Management Support (4.4 Percent of Contracted Services)
Annual audit support services
Material loss reviews
Investigation support services

After adjusting for unspent prior-year budgets in both years, the 2028 budget level represents an increase of approximately $3.1 million, or 4.3 percent, over the proposed 2027 level.
V. Capital Budget: $7.9 Million
Overview
The proposed 2027 Capital Budget is $7.9 million, a decrease of $16.2 million (67.2 percent) compared to the 2026 Board-approved budget.
(
printed page 67869)
The proposed Capital Budget for 2028 is $8.0 million, an increase of 1.0 percent compared to the 2027 level.
Summary of 2027 Capital Projects
Each year NCUA carries out an extensive review of the agency's needs for improvement, repair, or replacement of information technology, facilities, equipment, and other capital investments. The proposed 2027 Capital Budget supports continuing investments in the agency's highest priority needs as follows:
[
14
]
Strengthening Agency Cybersecurity ($4.7 million).
The 2027 Capital Budget invests in multiple projects that directly strengthen cybersecurity at NCUA. These investments reinforce the agency's focus systems that are secure, available, and protected against emerging technological risks. Key projects within this category include:
Firewall Hardware Refresh—Strengthens network perimeter defenses and reduces outage risks, which are core requirements for safe operations.
Network Access Control / Network Segmentation—Supports identity-based cybersecurity, mitigating threats that target user identity.
Modernizing Network Internet Protocols—Ensures NCUA can communicate with the public and credit unions using the latest digital communications standards.
Identity Verification and Data Interchange Security—Modernizes and improves personal and system security through an enhanced technologies aligned to prevailing government and industry standards.
Modernizing Agency Systems and Workflow Transformation ($1.7 million).
The Capital Budget includes several investments to ensure the agency keeps pace with innovation across the credit union system. These projects adopt data-driven practices to expand access to financial services, support new credit unions, and strengthen the financial system. Key projects within this category include:
Community Development Revolving Loan Fund (CDRLF) Grant & Loan Management System—Modernizes the agency's outdated system to reduce staff workload and ensure compliance with federal grant management requirements.
Consumer Assistance Center / Relationship Management System—Modernizes customer relationship management infrastructure and supports interagency collaboration.
New Charter System Improvements—Fully digitizes chartering workflows, reduces burden for new credit union applicants, and meets requirements of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act.
eDiscovery Tool—Strengthens legal research capabilities and reduces manual discovery through a modern data-filtering and investigation engine.
Enhancing Engagement, Transparency, and Operational Reliability ($1.3 million).
The Capital Budget strengthens technological readiness through investments that modernize communication with customers and enable compliance with evolving regulatory requirements. Key projects within this category include:
Unified Communications and Collaboration Modernization—Improves hybrid meeting reliability for Board and public engagement functions.
Technical Support for Board Priorities—Maintains flexibility to act on emerging regulatory changes that require system reengineering, such as the GENIUS Act and the 21st Century Road to Housing Act requirements.
Headquarters Building Minor Construction and Maintenance Projects ($0.3 million).
The proposed 2027 Capital Budget supports NCUA's multi-year headquarters building improvement plan that identifies projects that can be completed incrementally, prioritizing the replacement of health and safety infrastructure. The ongoing multi-year approach recognizes the critical building management and maintenance needs while reducing the potential budgetary impact of such projects in a single budget year.
Reorganization and Technology Investment Fund.
The 2026 Capital Budget included a $16.0 million reorganization and technology investment fund—available over multiple years—to make appropriate information technology and process improvement investments that aid in the agency's reorganization. To ensure that NCUA can fully leverage SI/AI, the agency plans to allocate $4.3 million of these funds to develop a structured strategy that harnesses SI/AI-powered tools essential for future supervision, analytics, and fraud detection. Through September 2026, the agency also spent approximately $1 million on efficiency-related technology investments, business process analysis, and reorganization planning support.
VI. Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses Budget: $5.1 Million
Overview
The proposed 2027 Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses Budget is $5.1 million, which is $1.7 million, or 52.6 percent, higher than the 2026 Board-approved budget. The 2026 Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses Budget was reduced by a one-time offset of $1.7 million from the sale of the Austin, TX office building.
[
15
]
Excluding this change in the offset, the proposed 2027 increase is $0.04 million.
The Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses Budget funds direct costs associated with authorized Share Insurance Fund activities, including the following for 2027:
[
16
]
$2.7 million for operating and maintenance costs of the internal analytical capabilities to conduct supervisory stress testing analyses and
(
printed page 67870)
to perform other quantitative risk assessments of large credit unions.
$0.8 million for state examiner travel to NCUA-sponsored training classes and $0.2 million to ensure that state supervisory authorities can securely and efficiently access NCUA applications and NCUA's MERIT system for state examination and supervision activities.
$0.8 million for financial reporting, including the Share Insurance Fund's annual financial audit and support to ensure effective internal controls for the fund.
$0.4 million for certain insurance-related activities and AMAC expenses related to liquidations and conservatorships and for staff travel for consultation on complex or problem cases.
$64.0 thousand for corporate resolution program legacy asset valuation models, analytic support, and data.
$0.1 million in capital funding to modernize AMAC's liquidation support tracking tool. AMAC currently uses an end-of-life software platform to track various legal and financial claims during liquidation case management. In 2027, AMAC will deploy a modernized application to replace its current tool.
(
printed page 67871)
The proposed 2028 Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses budget is $5.2 million, an increase of 2.0 percent compared to the proposed 2027 budget.
VII. Financing NCUA's Programs
Overview
NCUA incurs various expenses to satisfy its statutory requirements, including those involved in examining and supervising federally insured credit unions. The NCUA Board adopts an Operating Budget, a Capital Budget, and a Share Insurance Fund Administrative Expenses Budget each year to fund most of the costs to operate the agency.
[
17
]
When formulating the annual budget, NCUA is mindful that its funding comes from credit unions and strives to operate in an efficient, effective, transparent, and fully accountable manner.
The FCU Act authorizes two primary sources to fund the Operating and Capital Budgets:
(1) Requisitions from the Share Insurance Fund “for such administrative and other expenses incurred in carrying out the purposes of [Title II of the Act] as [the Board] may determine to be proper,”
[
18
]
and.
(2) “[F]ees and assessments (including income earned on insurance deposits) levied on insured credit unions under [the Act].”
[
19
]
Among the fees levied under the Act are annual Operating Fees, which are required for federal credit unions under
12 U.S.C. 1755
“and may be expended by the Board to defray the expenses incurred in carrying out the provisions of [the Act,] including the examination and supervision of [federal credit unions].”
Taken together, these authorities effectively require the Board to determine which expenses are appropriately paid from each source while giving the Board broad discretion in allocating expenses.
In 1973, the U.S. Government Accountability Office recommended NCUA adopt a method for allocating Operating Budget costs—that is, the portion of NCUA's budget funded by requisitions from the Share Insurance Fund and the portion covered by operating fees paid by federal credit unions.
[
20
]
NCUA has since used an allocation methodology known as the OTR to determine how much of the Operating and Capital Budgets to fund with a requisition from the Share Insurance Fund.
NCUA uses the OTR methodology to allocate agency expenses between these two primary funding sources. Specifically, the OTR is the formula NCUA uses to allocate insurance-related expenses to the Share Insurance Fund under Title II of the FCU Act. Almost all other operating expenses are funded by collecting annual operating fees from federal credit unions.
[
21
]
Two statutory provisions directly limit the Board's discretion with respect to Share Insurance Fund requisitions for NCUA's Operating Budget and the OTR. First, expenses funded from the Share Insurance Fund must carry out the purposes of Title II of the FCU Act, which relates to share insurance.
[
22
]
Second, NCUA may not fund its entire Operating Budget through charges to the Share Insurance Fund.
[
23
]
Overhead Transfer Rate
The OTR represents the percentage of the agency's operating budget paid for by a transfer from the Share Insurance Fund. The OTR is designed to cover NCUA's costs of examining and supervising the risk to the Share Insurance Fund posed by all federally insured credit unions, as well as the costs of administering the Share Insurance Fund.
Federally insured credit unions are not billed for and do not have to remit the OTR amount; instead, it is transferred directly to the Operating Fund from the Share Insurance Fund. This transfer, therefore, represents an indirect cost to all federally insured credit unions.
The NCUA Board approved the current methodology for calculating the OTR at its November 2017 open meeting.
[
24
]
In 2023, the Board published a request for comment in the
Federal Register
regarding the OTR methodology but did not propose or adopt any changes to the current methodology.
[
25
]
The minor variations in the OTR since 2018 are the result of routine, small fluctuations in the variables that affect the OTR, including normal variations in the workload budget from one calendar year to the next.
NCUA conducts a comprehensive workload analysis annually. This analysis estimates the amount of time necessary to conduct examinations and supervise federally insured credit unions to carry out NCUA's dual mission as insurer and regulator. This analysis starts with a field-level review of every federally insured credit union to estimate the number of workload hours needed for the year. These estimates are informed by the overall parameters of NCUA's examination program, including workload estimates that are refined by regional managers and submitted to NCUA headquarters for the annual budget proposal. The OTR methodology excludes state regulator costs, including state examiner hours.
Based on the Board-approved methodology and the proposed budget, the OTR for 2027 is estimated to be 62.0 percent, which is an increase of 20 basis points from 2026. Thus, 62.0 percent of the proposed 2027 Operating Budget is estimated to be paid out of the Share Insurance Fund. The remaining 38.0 percent of the proposed 2027 Operating Budget is estimated to be paid for by operating fees collected from federal credit unions. (
printed page 67872)
The following chart illustrates the share of the proposed 2027 Operating Budget that would be paid by federal credit unions (70.4 percent) and federally insured, state-chartered credit unions (29.6 percent).
Operating Fee
The Board delegated authority to the Chief Financial Officer to calculate the annual operating fee for federal credit unions and to set the fee schedule as calculated using the approved methodology. In December 2023, the Board approved and published in the
Federal Register
the current operating fee methodology, which forms the basis for how the operating fee is calculated.
[
26
]
Under the current methodology to determine the annual operating fee assessed on natural person federal credit unions, NCUA first calculates the average of total assets reported in the preceding four calendar quarters available at the time of the calculation, net of any reported Paycheck Protection Program loans.
[
27
]
Natural person federal credit unions with assets less than approximately $2.3 million are not assessed an operating fee and their assets are therefore excluded from this calculation.
[
28
]
Corporate federal credit unions also pay an annual operating fee based on a different scale.
Based on the Board-approved operating fee methodology, as shown in the following tables, the share of the proposed 2027 budget funded by the operating fee is $116.9 million. The calculated operating fee rate for 2027 decreases by 49 basis points compared to the rate in 2026.
(
printed page 67873)
As part of the Board-approved operating fee methodology, NCUA analyzes the agency's future cash flow requirements compared to available balances. Any projected surplus cash from past years' fee collections that is not required to finance agency operations can be used to lower the operating fee share of the proposed budget. Because these cash surpluses result from past years' operating fee collections, they do not offset the portion of the budget funded by the OTR. As the final 2027-2028 budget is prepared for consideration by the NCUA Board, the Chief Financial Officer will evaluate the agency's cash position and make a recommendation about any surplus cash that can be credited to the operating fee.

AGENCY:
Research, Education, and Economics, United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).
ACTION:
Solicit applications for memberships for the National Agricultural Research, Extension, Education, and Economics (NAREEE) Advisory Board and Citrus Disease Subcommittee (CDS).
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) announces the opening of the solicitation for applications to fill vacancies on the National Agricultural Research, Extension, Education, and Economics (NAREEE) Advisory Board and the Citrus Disease Subcommittee (CDS) for Fiscal Year 2027.
DATES:
Visit the NAREEE Advisory Board website:
https://nareeeab.ree.usda.gov/​membership
to review a complete list of the Board and committee and subcommittee membership categories. If you wish to be considered for the seats listed above, electronic applications should be submitted by close of business on Monday, November 30, 2026. Applications submitted through the mail should be postmarked no later than Monday, November 30, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Please submit a complete nomination package with the nominee's name, resume or CV, completed and signed Form AD-755, and any letters of support or recommendation must be submitted via one of the following methods: (1) Email to
NAREEE@usda.gov
;
or (2) By mail delivery service to Attention, Richard Derksen, NAREEE Advisory Board, U.S. Department of Agriculture, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Room 6020, South Building, Washington, DC 20250-2255.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Dr. Richard Derksen, Deputy Director, Office of the Chief Scientist, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Room 6020, South Building, Washington, DC 20250-2255; email:
rich.derksen@usda.gov
.
NAREEE Advisory Board website:
https://nareeeab.ree.usda.gov/​
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
All Board members serve without compensation, but may be allowed reimbursement for travel expenses, including per diem, authorized by
5 U.S.C. 5703
of the Federal Travel Regulation for persons employed intermittently in government service to attend meetings or conduct board-related business away from their homes or regular places of business.
Applications:
Please note, individuals may not serve on more than one USDA Federal Advisory Committee. Individuals who are federally registered lobbyists, appointed to committees to exercise their own individual best judgment on behalf of the government (
e.g.,
as Special Government Employees), are ineligible to serve.
Applications from individuals from across the agricultural sector—including scientists, educators, producers, interest group advocates, and other industry experts, are welcome to self-nominate and apply for a vacant position on the Advisory Board. Applications for membership to the CDS should represent stakeholders and have knowledge of citrus industry opportunities and barriers, especially citrus diseases. All applicants will be carefully reviewed for their relevant experience, expertise, and leadership. Appointed members will serve one-, two-, or three-year terms to properly stagger term rotation. All applicants will be vetted before selection.
Instructions:
To apply, submit the following: a resume/curriculum vitae (CV) (required); form AD-755 (required), a cover letter (optional); and letters of recommendation (optional). Resumes/CVs should be no longer than five (5) pages and should include the following information: the position for which you are applying; current and past organization affiliations; areas of expertise; education; career positions held; and any other notable, relevant positions held. Previous applicants/members who wish to be considered must reapply. The application may be found on the USDA website:
https://www.usda.gov/​sites/​default/​files/​documents/​ad-755-advisory-committee-commodity-board-background-information.pdf
.
Applicant Selection:
Appointments to the NAREEE Advisory Board and its committees and subcommittees will be made by the Secretary of Agriculture. The selection is based on how well the applicants meet the required qualifications and the current needs of the Board and its committees/subcommittees. It is anticipated that the members will start serving on the Advisory Board and/or the subcommittee in Fiscal Year 2027.
USDA will consider Committee Membership appointments, to the extent practicable and consistent with applicable laws, to ensure the needs of all Americans are served.
Equal opportunity practices in accordance with USDA's policies will be followed in all appointments to the Committee. USDA is an equal opportunity provider, employer, and lender.
In accordance with Federal civil rights law and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) civil rights regulations and policies, the USDA, its Agencies, offices, and employees, and institutions participating in or administering USDA programs are prohibited from discriminating based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, disability, age, marital status, family/parental status, income derived from a public assistance program, political beliefs, or reprisal or retaliation for prior civil rights activity, in any program or activity conducted or funded by USDA (not all bases apply to all programs).
(
printed page 67813)
Remedies and complaint filing deadlines vary by program or incident.
Persons with disabilities who require alternative means of communication for program information (
e.g.,
Braille, large print, audiotape, American Sign Language, etc.) should contact the State or local Agency that administers the program or contact USDA through the Telecommunications Relay Service at 711 (voice and TTY). Additionally, program information may be made available in languages other than English.

ACTION:
Notice of re-establishment of a matching program.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the provisions of the Privacy Act, as amended, this notice announces the re-establishment of a matching program with the Department of War (DOW), Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC). Under this matching program, DOW will disclose military retirement payment and survivor benefit payment data to SSA. SSA will use the military retirement payment and survivor benefit payment data to verify information provided by applicants, recipients, deemors (
i.e.,
someone other than the eligible individual or eligible spouse whose income and resources are considered when determining an individual's eligibility for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and the amount of their payment), and beneficiaries of SSI payments and Special Veterans Benefits (SVB).
DATES:
The deadline to submit comments on the proposed matching program is November 27, 2026.

ACTION:
Notice of Intent (NOI) to Transfer Federally Assisted Land or Facility.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) issues this notice to advise Federal agencies that New Jersey TRANSIT (NJ TRANSIT) intends to transfer a 2.17-acre portion of a 9.27-acre parcel to the Jersey City Municipal Utilities Authority (JCMUA).
DATES:
Any Federal agency interested in acquiring the Subject Property must notify the FTA Region II Office of its interest no later than November 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Interested parties should notify FTA Region II by writing to Michael Culotta, Regional Administrator, Federal Transit Administration, One Bowling Green, Room 428 New York, NY 10004.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Michael Culotta, Regional Administrator, Federal Transit Administration, One Bowling Green, Room 428, New York, NY 10004, or at (212) 668-2170.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
New Jersey TRANSIT (NJ TRANSIT) intends to transfer a 2.17-acre portion of a 9.27-acre parcel (the 2.17-acre portion is referred to herein as the Subject Property) to the Jersey City Municipal Utilities Authority (JCMUA). NJ TRANSIT has not used the Subject Property since the mid-1990s and it has remained vacant. NJ TRANSIT has determined it no longer needs the Subject Property for public transportation purposes, and requests FTA approval to transfer it to the JCMUA if no Federal agency is interested in acquiring the Subject Property for Federal use. JCMUA will utilize the Subject Property for its proposed stormwater pump station, which will assist in alleviating flooding in parts of Jersey City, NJ.
Background
Federal public transportation law (
49 U.S.C. 5334(h)
) sets forth requirements for the transfer of capital assets. Specifically, if a recipient of FTA assistance decides an asset acquired with assistance under
49 U.S.C. Chapter 53
is no longer needed for the purpose for which it was acquired, FTA may authorize the recipient to transfer the asset to a local governmental authority to be used for a public purpose with no further obligation to the Government.
49 U.S.C. 5334(h)(1)(A)
.
Determinations
FTA may authorize a transfer for a public purpose other than mass transportation only if FTA determines:
(i) The asset will remain in public use for at least five (5) years after the date the asset is transferred;
(ii) There is no purpose eligible for assistance under
Chapter 53 of title 49, United States Code
, for which the asset should be used;
(iii) The overall benefit of allowing the transfer is greater than the interest of the Government in liquidation and return of the financial interest of the Government in the asset, after considering fair market value and other factors; and
(iv) Through an appropriate screening or survey process, that there is no interest in acquiring the asset for Government use if the asset is a facility or land.
FTA has determined the above requirements (i), (ii), and (iii) have been met.
Federal Interest in Acquiring Land or Facility
This Notice implements the requirements of
49 U.S.C. 5334(h)(1)(A)(iv)
. Accordingly, FTA hereby provides notice of the availability of the Subject Property further described below. Any Federal agency interested in acquiring the Subject Property should promptly notify the FTA. If no Federal agency is interested in acquiring the Subject Property, FTA will transfer the property.
Additional Description of Land
The Subject Property is a 2.17 acre unimproved parcel located at 510 Pacific Avenue, Jersey City, in the County of Hudson, New Jersey, Block 15801, Part of Lots 2 & 65.

I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose of Deregulatory Action
Since the inception of the ONC Health IT Certification Program (Certification Program) (
42 U.S.C. 300jj-11(c)(5)
), ONC has aimed to implement and administer the Certification Program in the least burdensome manner that supports an administration's policy goals. Throughout the years, we have worked to improve the Certification Program with a focus on ways to reduce burden, offer flexibility to both developers and providers, and support innovation. Over the past 15 years, we have established a set of regulatory requirements that have provided a foundation for our voluntary Certification Program. As we look to the future, we reviewed the existing requirements and made updates. Through both formal notice and comment rulemaking and informal engagements, we received suggestions on how to update the Certification Program to meet current market needs. This final rule includes deregulatory actions that: take into consideration suggestions and comments received on the Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: ASTP/ONC Deregulatory Actions To Unleash Prosperity Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60970
) (“Proposed Rule”); account for the current and future state of technology; reduce burden on health IT developers; and promote innovation for health IT developers, providers, and other interested parties.
These efforts directly align with Administration goals as outlined in
E.O. 14192
(Unleashing Prosperity through
(
printed page 67917)
Deregulation)
[
1
]
and
E.O. 14267
(Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers).
[
2
]
By removing burdensome and unnecessary requirements of the Certification Program, this final rule supports providers in caring for their patients. Developers of certified health IT will have more time to support providers' specific technological needs. Further, by increasing competition in the certified health IT market that will come from reduced barriers to entry for the certification of health IT, providers also will have more choices to meet their health IT needs.
America's interoperability arc in healthcare has bent decisively toward Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR®)-based application programming interfaces (APIs). An open, interoperable health data ecosystem invites entrepreneurship, drives innovation, and cements American leadership and competitiveness in the expanding digital health marketplace. As discussed in this deregulatory final rule, we aggressively reduce and remove long-standing functionality-oriented and non-FHIR-based certification criteria from the Certification Program. While this approach will directly and rapidly reduce compliance burdens for health IT developers that participate in the Certification Program, more broadly, it will enable ONC to reset the Certification Program's regulatory scope and establish a new foundation on which to build FHIR-based API requirements in the future. This will allow more creative super intelligence
[
3
]
(SI)-enabled interoperability solutions that combine FHIR with newer standards to emerge, such as Model Context Protocol (MCP), which “standardizes how applications provide context to Large Language Models (LLMs),”
[
4
]
and will further embrace the 21st Century Cures Act (
Pub. L. 114-255
) (Cures Act)'s reference to successor technology and standards in the API Condition of Certification.
[
5
]
While FHIR provides the potential for better, faster, and more consistent ways to address emerging market needs and policy imperatives, more work is needed for certain use cases. We intend to continue to fully engage industry and our Federal partners, such as CMS, to rapidly advance FHIR specifications for regulatory readiness. We also intend to sharpen the Certification Program's future focus to prioritize FHIR-based APIs that, consistent with all legal requirements: (1) enhance automation and API performance; (2) move beyond read-only interactions; and (3) expand the scope of data available to support clinical efficiency, patient-centered care, and use cases focused on timely reporting (
e.g.,
public health, quality, government programs).
The transition to a FHIR-based API ecosystem is a strategic imperative and an investment in the US's interoperability future. Successful execution of this vision will require a collective commitment from clinicians, patients, payers, policymakers, and software developers, alike. Together, we can build interoperable solutions that meet today's challenges and anticipate tomorrow's opportunities.
In this final rule, we have finalized the removal or revision of certain certification criteria that are consistent with our drive toward and our support for the FHIR standard. The push toward universal adoption of FHIR is not just important for secure, streamlined data access, it is a critical step toward modernizing our healthcare system with the ultimate goal of Making America Healthy Again.

C. Severability
It is our intent that each provision of this final rule be severable from other provisions of this final rule. This means that if any provision of this final rule is held to be invalid or unenforceable facially, or as applied to any person or plaintiff, or stayed pending further judicial or agency action, we intend that such provision shall be severable from other provisions of this final rule, and from rules and regulations currently in effect. We provided notice of this intent in the HTI-5 Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60974
). It is also our intent that, unless such provision shall be held to be utterly invalid or unenforceable, it be construed to give the provision maximum effect permitted by law including in the application of the provision to other persons not similarly situated or to other, dissimilar circumstances from those where the provision may be held to be invalid or unenforceable.
In this final rule, we have finalized provisions that are intended to and will operate independently of each other, even if multiple of them serve the same or similar general purpose(s) or policy goal(s). Where a provision is necessarily dependent on another, the context generally makes that clear (such as by cross-reference to a particular standard, requirement, condition, or pre-requisite). Where a provision that is dependent on one that is stayed or held invalid or unenforceable (as described in the preceding paragraph) is included in a subparagraph, paragraph, or section within part 170 of
45 CFR
, our intention is that other provisions of such subparagraph(s), paragraph(s), or section(s) operate independently of said provision and would remain in effect.
If any revision to any provision of part 170 (such as a revision to a certification criterion in part 170) were stayed or held to be invalid or unenforceable as applied to any person, plaintiff, or circumstance, we explained our intent that such provision—and any section or paragraph of part 170 that may reference such provision—be construed to give the provision maximum effect permitted by law including in the application of the provision to other persons not similarly situated or to other, dissimilar circumstances from those where the provision may be held to be invalid or unenforceable.
D. Costs and Benefits
The Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) includes an updated analysis of the costs and benefits associated with the finalized proposals in this final rule. The finalized deregulatory actions provide substantial relief for developers of certified health IT and significant cost savings realized from the revision and removal of certain Certification Program requirements. The cost savings have been estimated using the best available data and modeled on the costs estimated and finalized in prior ONC rulemakings. The finalized deregulatory actions reduce the effort for developers of certified health IT to meet ongoing Certification Program requirements and reduce entry barriers for new Certification Program participants. The finalized actions, importantly, return resources back to developers of certified health IT to innovate with their technology, improve interoperability and third-party integration, and focus on the needs of their customers. We do not expect costs to be associated with these finalized deregulatory actions. We expect the finalized deregulatory actions to result in significant benefits for health IT developers, providers, ONC-Authorized Certification Bodies (ONC-ACBs), ONC-Authorized Testing Laboratories (ONC-ATLs), and ONC. Generally, these benefits are in the form of cost and time savings and reductions in administrative burden to comply with Certification Program requirements. The finalized actions reduce the scope and breadth of Certification Program requirements.
The analysis included in this final rule indicates that the finalized updates to the Certification Program would result in $0 in implementation and compliance costs on developers of certified health IT. However, we estimated some costs for reviewers who reviewed this final rule. We estimated those costs to be $1,293,508 in total for an estimated 616 reviewers, which include developers, medical associations, and other health and health IT community members. We did not quantify benefits for this final rule and instead rely on our calculation of cost savings to developers of certified health IT to quantify in dollars the time and effort developers would have

II. Background
A. Statutory Basis
The Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act (HITECH Act), Title XIII of Division A and Title IV of Division B of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 (
Pub. L. 111-5
), was enacted on February 17, 2009. The HITECH Act amended the Public Health Service Act (PHSA) and created “Title XXX—Health Information Technology and Quality” (Title XXX) to improve healthcare quality, safety, and efficiency through the promotion of health IT and electronic health information (EHI) exchange.
The 21st Century Cures Act (
Pub. L. 114-255
) (Cures Act) was enacted on December 13, 2016, to accelerate the discovery, development, and delivery of 21st century cures, and for other purposes. The Cures Act, through Title IV—Delivery, amended the HITECH Act by modifying or adding certain provisions to the PHSA relating to health IT.
1. Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria
The HITECH Act established two Federal advisory committees, the Health IT Policy Committee (HITPC) and the Health IT Standards Committee (HITSC). Each was responsible for advising the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (National Coordinator) on different aspects of standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria.
Section 4003(e) of the Cures Act amended sections 3002 and 3003 of the PHSA by replacing, in an amended section 3002, the HITPC and HITSC with one committee named the Health Information Technology Advisory Committee (Health IT Advisory Committee or HITAC). Section 3002(a) of the PHSA, as added by the Cures Act, establishes that the HITAC recommends to the National Coordinator policies and standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria, relating to the implementation of a health information technology infrastructure, nationally and locally, that advances the electronic access, exchange, and use of health information. Further described in section 3002(b)(1) of the PHSA, this includes recommending to the National Coordinator a policy framework to advance interoperable health information technology infrastructure, updating recommendations to the policy framework, and making new recommendations, as appropriate. Section 3002(b)(2)(A) of the PHSA specifies that in general, the HITAC shall recommend to the National Coordinator for purposes of adoption under section 3004, standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria and an order of priority for the development, harmonization, and recognition of such standards, specifications, and certification criteria. Like the process previously required of the former HITPC and HITSC, section 3002(b)(5) of the PHSA requires the HITAC to develop a schedule, updated annually, for the assessment of policy recommendations, which the Secretary publishes in the
Federal Register
.
[
9
]
Section 3004 of the PHSA establishes a process for the adoption of health IT standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria and authorizes the Secretary to adopt such standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria. As specified in section 3004(a)(1), the Secretary is required, in consultation with representatives of other relevant Federal agencies, to jointly review standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria endorsed by the National Coordinator in section 3001(c) and subsequently determine whether to propose the adoption of such standards, implementation specifications, or certification criteria. Section 3004(a)(3) requires the Secretary to publish all such determinations in the
Federal Register
.
Section 3004(b)(3) of the PHSA, titled Subsequent Standards Activity, provides that the Secretary shall adopt additional standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria as necessary and consistent with the schedule published by the HITAC. We consider this provision in the broader context of the HITECH Act and Cures Act to grant the Secretary the authority and discretion to adopt standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria that have been recommended by the HITAC and endorsed by the National Coordinator, as well as other appropriate and necessary health IT standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria.
2. Health IT Certification Program(s)
Section 3001(c)(5) of the PHSA provides the National Coordinator with the authority to establish a certification program or programs for the voluntary certification of health IT. Section 3001(c)(5)(A) specifies that the National Coordinator, in consultation with the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), shall keep or recognize a program or programs for the voluntary certification of health IT that is in compliance with applicable certification criteria adopted in section 3004 of the PHSA.
The certification program(s) must also include, as appropriate, testing of the technology in accordance with section 13201(b) of the HITECH Act. Overall, section 13201(b) of the HITECH Act requires that, with respect to the development of standards and implementation specifications, the Director of NIST shall support the establishment of a conformance testing infrastructure, including the development of technical test beds. The HITECH Act also indicates that the development of this conformance testing infrastructure may include a program to accredit independent, non-Federal laboratories to perform testing.
Section 4002(a) of the Cures Act amended section 3001(c)(5) of the PHSA by adding section 3001(c)(5)(D), which requires the Secretary, through notice-and-comment rulemaking, to require conditions of certification and maintenance of certification for the Certification Program. Specifically, the health IT developers or entities with technology certified under the Certification Program must, in order to maintain such certification status, adhere to certain conditions and maintenance of certification requirements concerning information blocking; assurances regarding appropriate exchange, access, and use of electronic health information; communications regarding health IT; APIs; real world testing; attestations regarding certain conditions and maintenance of certification requirements; and submission of reporting criteria under the EHR Reporting Program in accordance with section 3009A(b) of the PHSA.

C. General Comments on the Proposed Rule
Comments.
Many commenters were supportive of modernizing the Certification Program around FHIR-based APIs and reducing outdated or duplicative requirements, stating that it would have the benefit of reducing administrative burden, improving standards-based interoperability, and supporting automation, innovation, and more scalable exchange. They also noted that this modernization would allow vendors and implementers to redirect effort away from low-value compliance activities and toward real-world interoperability, reliability, scalability, and more granular exchange. Some of these commenters emphasized that a “FHIR-forward” approach should advance computable interoperability, where exchanged data are reliably structured, attributable, and usable, not simply accessible. The commenters noted that this would reduce integration burden, improve data quality, and accelerate innovation across care delivery, payer, public health, and third-party application ecosystems.
Response.
We thank commenters for their support for America's FHIR-forward future. We may take these comments into consideration to inform future rulemaking.
Comments.
We received numerous comments that were not supportive of the deregulatory approach to reducing or removing certification and related interoperability guardrails without replacement safeguards. These commenters expressed significant concerns that such approaches would weaken baseline functionality, increase fragmentation and cost, and shift operational, compliance, and financial burdens to providers, public health agencies, and other end users. Some of these commenters expressed concerns that when foundational capabilities are no longer required, they reappear as optional modules, implementation fees, or premium features that providers must purchase to achieve necessary functionality. A commenter recommended prompt release of the next future rulemaking stating difficulties commenting on the Proposed Rule without knowing future plans for the Certification Program. These commenters noted that our proposal for a transition toward a FHIR-based API ecosystem would require additional guidance or specification of phased timelines, readiness thresholds, implementation best practices, testing and performance expectations, and the continued role of existing exchange pathways during transition.
Some commenters highlighted that many organizations continue to operate in a hybrid environment where document-based exchange remains foundational to many workflows. Several commenters also warned that, absent a required, standardized, and patient-accessible FHIR-native alternative, removal of Consolidated Clinical Document Architecture (C-CDA)-based summary functionality could leave patients and caregivers with technically complete but clinically fragmented information during care transitions. Many of these commenters also expressed similar concerns in relation to specific proposals, which we address in their respective sections throughout this final rule.
A couple of commenters urged ONC to be mindful of financial and workforce strain on rural and other low-resourced providers. Commenters suggested ONC create grants for small and rural providers to implement APIs and electronic health record upgrades. Another commenter requested clarification on whether the rule limits State authority to require certain standards if certification no longer guarantees certain capabilities.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback. We first clarify that the removal of certain certification criteria does not limit State authority as States remain able to establish their own requirements as permitted by law. Generally, we note that these concerns are likely mitigated by our final decisions to retain the majority of certification criteria and to give additional transition time for certain C-CDA certification criteria. In addition, we have further addressed these comments in section III below as they relate to specific proposals to remove criteria or functionality. We have also addressed timelines for certification criteria relevant to the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program and the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category in their respective sections.
We acknowledge commenters' concerns that capabilities no longer included in the Certification Program could be offered as optional or premium features. The purpose of the Certification Program is to establish the minimum criteria that health IT must meet to obtain certification. We do not believe that users will see a significant increase in overall costs because the costs for certain functionalities were likely included in the costs that customers currently pay to use a particular certified Health IT Module. As noted by commenters, functionalities associated with removed criteria were part of the certified Health IT Module that a customer purchased or licensed for a fee, which presumably included the costs of the functionality. To the extent that health IT developers continue to charge for specified functionalities, customers may now be able to see the cost of a specific functionality independent of the certified Health IT Modules, providing further price transparency to the decision-making and purchasing processes.

III. Health Information Technology Standards, Implementation Specifications, and Certification Criteria and Certification Programs for Health Information Technology (Part 170)
Reading This Final Rule
In this preamble, we present our finalizations in an order that begins with the certification criteria we finalized for removal and subsequently the standards, definitions, and other related Certification Program provisions finalized for removal or revision. This approach should make it easier for readers to follow our finalized Certification Program removals, in part, due to the natural cascading effects of finalizing to remove or revise a certification criterion.
Additionally, we finalized the removal of standards when they are no longer referenced by existing certification criteria. In very limited circumstances, we retained a standard that is cross-referenced in a certification criterion that we finalized for removal. We did this because the standard is cross-referenced in another criterion and/or supports health IT interoperability alignment. Further, as noted above, we finalized the removal of certain Conditions and Maintenance of Certification requirements and other Certification Program requirements.
As stated above, for the purposes of this final rule, we have reviewed and responded to comments on a narrowed set of proposals from the Proposed Rule. Comments received in response to other Proposed Rule proposals remain under review and consideration. The Proposed Rule proposals not discussed in this final rule may, in the future, be included in subsequent final rules or as revised proposals in subsequent proposed rules.
RFI Feedback
Recently, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the Department, and CMS-ONC issued requests for information (RFIs) related to deregulation. We reviewed comments related to ONC. In response to the CMS-ONC Request for Information; Health Technology Ecosystem (
90 FR 21034
) (CMS-ONC RFI), commenters expressed a strong desire to modernize the Certification Program to be more modular, API-focused, and less centered on specific EHR functionalities. Commenters recommended simplifying the process, reducing costs, and expanding certification requirements to ensure payers and other health IT systems adhere to the same interoperability standards. There was an overwhelming demand to strengthen, expand, and mandate the use of FHIR-based APIs. Commenters strongly advocated for retiring outdated, less efficient standards to reduce complexity. A central theme from commenters was the need for regulatory modernization to reduce administrative and financial burdens on providers and technology developers. Commenters also expressed concern that existing certification requirements are often too rigid, costly, and not aligned with emerging care models like value-based care or specialized technologies such as SI and remote monitoring. A commenter that responded to the HHS RFI expressed concerns with the Real World Testing and Insights Conditions of Certification, stating that the requirements are overly burdensome and offer limited value to providers or patients. The commenter also recommended retiring low-value certification criteria requirements that add complexity without improving care. A commenter that responded to the OMB RFI suggested that revisions could be made to the Conditions and Maintenance of Certification requirements that focus on streamlined and meaningful oversight without placing undue demands on developers, especially where those demands offer limited direct benefit to health care provider customers or their patients. The commenter also suggested the removal of “non-interoperability-focused, redundant, or valueless” criteria and a focus on promoting standardized and scalable interoperability. ONC addresses a number of these comments below, specifically the suggestions to remove non-interoperability-focused and non-essential certification criteria. Commenters were strongly supportive of our focus on FHIR-based standards. Some commenters, however, included suggestions related to new regulatory actions. As noted in the Proposed Rule, these suggestions are out of scope for this deregulatory rule, but we may consider the suggestions for a future rulemaking (
90 FR 60979
).

Therefore, removing § 170.315(a)(9) from the CFR will not result in any further substantive effects, and delaying its removal is unnecessary.

We proposed to reduce the scope of the criterion to focus on enabling the receipt of a Consolidated CDA (C-CDA) document as a way to position this criterion for a future evolution to receipt of FHIR-formatted data. We proposed to remove the requirements in § 170.315(b)(1)(i) “send and receive via edge protocol” and in § 170.315(b)(1)(iii) “create” and to simplify the requirements in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii) “validate and display” to focus on the ability to receive and validate C-CDA documents. We proposed to remove the requirements in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(B) and (C). We also proposed to move the requirements in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(A) “validate C-CDA conformance—system performance” to § 170.315(b)(1)(i) and to rename § 170.315(b)(1) to read “transitions of care—receive and validate.” Additionally, in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(A) we proposed to remove the references to § 170.205(a)(3) and to replace the references to § 170.205(a)(5), which expired on January 1, 2026, with references to § 170.205(a)(6).
Comments.
The majority of commenters were not supportive of our proposal to revise the transitions of care certification criterion to remove or narrow C-CDA creation and transmission capabilities for transitions of care/referral summaries, primarily due to concerns about timing and readiness with respect to transitioning to FHIR-based document exchange for transitions of care. Many commenters stated that C-CDA-based document exchange is still widely used, and some stressed that certain settings, including long-term and post-acute care (LTPAC), behavioral health, small, rural and safety net providers, are particularly reliant on C-CDA-based document exchange in current transitions of care workflows. Several commenters expressed concerns that both C-CDA and Direct secure messaging serve as core national exchange mechanisms at this time. Several commenters stated that readiness for FHIR-based exchange is uneven across settings, and thus the proposal could increase disparities. Several commenters stated that C-CDA-based document exchange functions as the current means of sharing structured health information with dental providers, who are less FHIR-ready. Another commenter noted that many public health systems are dependent on C-CDA-based document exchange and may face data quality or compatibility challenges without a viable alternative. Many commenters stressed that there is currently no mature and broadly adopted FHIR-based replacement for C-CDA-based document exchange and had concerns that without a replacement, removal of C-CDA creation and transmission capabilities would weaken interoperability, increase burden, disrupt care coordination, and increase patient safety risks. Additionally, many commenters expressed concern that there is no phased migration plan, readiness criteria, sunset roadmap, or clear bridge between current C-CDA-based document exchange requirements and future FHIR-based exchange requirements. Several commenters stated that C-CDA-based document exchange remains a necessary backup, and several stated that C-CDA-based document exchange supports migration to FHIR.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing their concerns regarding FHIR readiness and the removal of the current C-CDA-based document exchange requirements in § 170.315(b)(1). We appreciate the concerns expressed by commenters about the impact the proposal would have on C-CDA-based document exchange, which continues to be widely used, particularly in specific settings, as well as the impact on Direct secure messaging. We have reconsidered our proposed policy and have decided to finalize our proposal with modification by extending the timeline for removing the Direct requirements and the C-CDA-based document exchange requirements in § 170.315(b)(1) to January 1, 2030. Specifically, we have finalized our proposed removal of § 170.315(b)(1)(i) “send and receive via edge protocol,” § 170.315(b)(1)(iii) “create,” § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(B) “display,” and § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(C) “display section views” with an effective date of January 1, 2030. We have finalized the proposed removal of references to § 170.205(a)(3) in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii) and replacement of references to § 170.205(a)(5) in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii) with references to § 170.205(a)(6) as of the effective date of this final rule. We have not finalized the proposed renaming of the criterion and renumbering of the requirements in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(A). We note that in the Proposed Rule we did not propose to remove references to § 170.205(a)(3) or replace references to § 170.205(a)(5) with references to § 170.205(a)(6) in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(B) and (C) and in § 170.315(b)(1)(iii) because we proposed to remove § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(B) and (C) and § 170.315(b)(1)(iii) entirely. However, because we have not finalized our proposal to remove § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(B) and (C) and § 170.315(b)(1)(iii) as of the effective date of a final rule, but the references to § 170.205(a)(3) and (5) remain outdated, we have finalized removal of references to § 170.205(a)(3) and replacement of references to § 170.205(a)(5) with references to § 170.205(a)(6) in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(B) and (C) and in § 170.315(b)(1)(iii) as of the effective date of this final rule, similar to how we proposed and finalized removal of references to § 170.205(a)(3) and replacement of references to § 170.205(a)(5) with references to § 170.205(a)(6) in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii).
Delaying the effective date of removal of § 170.315(b)(1)(i) “send and receive via edge protocol” and § 170.315(b)(1)(iii) “create” to January 1, 2030, helps address commenter concerns regarding our proposed removal of C-CDA-based standards requirements and Direct secure messaging requirements from the Certification Program. Significant advances are occurring in the development and adoption of FHIR-based standards, and the revised deadline of January 1, 2030, allows for a more gradual and achievable adoption of FHIR-based exchange. In response to concerns regarding C-CDA being considered a necessary backup, we note that while we anticipate that the extended timeline will allow increased adoption of FHIR-based exchange, the removal of C-CDA-based exchange requirements in § 170.315(b)(1) does not prevent the use of C-CDA-based exchange standards where necessary for users. In response to comments expressing concerns regarding the lack of a phased transition plan or roadmap for moving from C-CDA-based exchange to FHIR-based exchange, we note that providing this extended deadline will serve as a helpful timeline and migration pathway for moving from C-CDA-based document exchange to FHIR-based document exchange. Additionally, ONC will continue to provide resources related to transitioning to FHIR-based exchange.

b. Clinical Information Reconciliation and Incorporation
We proposed to remove the “clinical information reconciliation and incorporation” certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) with an effective date of January 1, 2027, and to reserve that section. The clinical information reconciliation and incorporation (CIRI) certification criterion allows health care providers to reconcile and incorporate patient health information in C-CDA format sent from external sources to maintain a more accurate and up-to-date patient record. The CIRI certification criterion is not currently included in the Base EHR definition. However, the criterion is required in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program and the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category for the Support Electronic Referral Loops by Receiving and Reconciling Health Information measure and also is specified as an example of a criterion that may be used to support the actions of the HIE Bi-Directional Exchange and Enabling Exchange under TEFCA measures in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program and the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category.
