Response.
We appreciate these concerns regarding FHIR readiness and removal of the current C-CDA-based document exchange requirements in § 170.315(b)(2) prior to a mature and widely adopted FHIR-based alternative being in place. Additionally, we understand that C-CDA-based document exchange is currently widely used, particularly in certain settings. Further, we appreciate the concerns expressed by commenters that due to a perceived lack of mature and widely adopted FHIR-based replacements, removal of the criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) could increase manual reconciliation burden and shift administrative burden to clinicians and providers. We also appreciate the recommendation to consider retaining the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) as a functional requirement and agree that would provide developers of certified health IT more flexibility to adopt FHIR-based solutions.
We have reconsidered our proposed policy and have not finalized complete removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2). Instead, we have reduced the burden for certification to this criterion and increased flexibility for certification. First, we have provided that health IT can demonstrate conformance with the criterion in a broader range of workflows instead of only upon receipt of a transition of care/referral summary. For example, health IT could demonstrate the ability to reconcile information according to the certification criterion's requirements when received from a patient, during internal patient transitions within a health care system, or when a patient is discharged to any external entity. Second, we have finalized removal of the references to standards for exchanging electronic health information in § 170.315(b)(2), thus making it a functional criterion, effective with the effective date of this final rule. Last, we have finalized the removal of the requirement to simultaneously display the data from at least two sources in a manner that allows a user to view the data and their attributes. We believe this finalized policy will not result in provider burden from manual reconciliation or provider burden from increased cost for electronic reconciliation functions, and at the same time will allow movement toward innovative, FHIR-based solutions. Additionally, as noted in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60984
) and discussed in more detail in a comment response below, the criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) is required for certain CMS measures, and maintaining it as a functional criterion ensures that certified functionality is available to support the actions identified in those measures.
We have finalized removal throughout § 170.315(b)(2) of the requirements to use the content exchange standards and implementation specifications specified in § 170.205(a)(3), (4), and (6) for exchanging electronic health information, as well as made conforming revisions for clarity and readability related to the removal of references to those standards. As noted above, we have also finalized removal of references to the standard in § 170.205(a)(5) which expired on January 1, 2026. In addition, we have finalized removal of the requirement to simultaneously display (
i.e.,
in a single view) information received from another source. We believe removal of this requirement is consistent with our objective of providing greater flexibility under the criterion while reducing unnecessary burden. We understand that the simultaneous display requirement may, in some cases, have constrained the development and implementation of improved workflows. We are also aware that some health IT developers are pursuing more automated approaches to reconciliation, including approaches for data received from trusted sources. Accordingly, we expect removal of this requirement will afford health IT developers greater flexibility to design and implement more efficient and innovative reconciliation workflows that better support clinician users, including automated approaches to reconciliation. As finalized, the criterion requires the ability to match data received from a transition of care/referral summary or other workflow with the correct patient; create a single reconciled list of medications, allergies and intolerances, and problems; enable user review and validation of the accuracy of a final set of data; and upon a user's confirmation, automatically update the list and incorporate medications, allergies and intolerances, and problems expressed according to, at a minimum, the version of the standard in § 170.213. We note that we do not expect that a health IT developer with a Health IT Module currently certified to § 170.315(b)(2) would need to make any changes to the certified Health IT Module to meet the revised criterion, because if a health IT developer's Health IT Module was previously conformant to the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2), then the Health IT Module would also be conformant to the revised criterion. Since we have not removed this certification criterion in its entirety, we have made the revisions effective with the effective date of this final rule. This will provide health IT developers with the discussed flexibility and reduced burden as soon as practical.

Several commenters stated that removal of the certification criterion would weaken care coordination, continuity of care, referrals, and integrated or team-based care. Multiple commenters stated that certification was like a national safety floor or baseline safeguard and removing the criterion would reduce accountability, transparency, uniformity, and assurance that
