important capabilities remain available, ultimately impacting patient safety. Another commenter stated that removing the certification criterion could reduce motivation to provide or use reconciliation functionality uniformly, which could affect accurate quality reporting.
Response.
We appreciate commenter concerns regarding patient safety, and we understand the importance of ensuring that health information is exchanged reliably during transitions of care and reconciliation. We have not finalized complete removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) as proposed and instead have finalized removal of the requirements in § 170.315(b)(2) to use the content exchange standards and implementation specifications in § 170.205(a)(3), (4), and (6) for exchanging electronic health information, thus making it a functional criterion. We believe this addresses concerns from commenters by ensuring that certified health IT has the capability of reconciling and incorporating patient health information appropriately.
Comments.
There were a number of comments related to burden. Many commenters stated that the proposal would increase manual reconciliation, transcription, and workflow burden on clinicians and staff. A commenter stressed that when certified health IT lacks reliable reconciliation functionality, reconciliation burden is shifted directly onto physicians and clinical staff, increasing manual work, workflow inefficiencies, and the risk of incomplete or inaccurate records. Another commenter stated that removing the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) would remove the expectation that reconciliation is supported and increase reliance on manual transcription, significantly raising the risk of errors. Some commenters stated that removal of the certification criterion would shift verification, compliance, operational burden, and in some cases liability from developers or government to providers, and some stressed that this would especially impact small, independent, and rural practices that rely on certified systems to meet regulatory, reporting, and security obligations.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing their concerns that removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) would shift burden to providers. We appreciate the importance of not increasing burden on providers or introducing manual workflows. We have not finalized complete removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) as proposed and instead have finalized removal of the requirements in § 170.315(b)(2) to use content exchange standards and implementation specifications for exchanging electronic health information, thus making it a functional criterion. We believe this addresses these burden-related concerns from commenters by ensuring that certified health IT has the capability to reconcile and incorporate patient health information electronically.
Comment.
There were several comments about timing, and commenters generally stated that the proposed timing was too aggressive, allowed insufficient time to transition to FHIR-based standards, and provided a poorly defined path from current C-CDA-based requirements.
Response.
We appreciate concerns regarding the timeline of the proposal and the need for additional time to transition to FHIR-based solutions. We have not finalized removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) as proposed and instead have finalized removal of the requirements in § 170.315(b)(2) to use content exchange standards and implementation specifications for exchanging electronic health information, thus making it a functional criterion. We believe this in effect provides additional time for the transition to FHIR-based solutions while at the same time ensuring that certified health IT maintains the capability to appropriately reconcile and incorporate patient health information electronically.
Comments.
Several commenters expressed concerns about aligning with CMS. Another commenter stated that the current proposed timelines would not give CMS time to determine if Promoting Interoperability measures require changes and, if changes are required, it would be impossible for health IT developers to have the changes in place by the start of the 2027 Promoting Interoperability reporting performance year, resulting in significant additional burden for hospitals and providers participating in these programs.
Response.
We thank commenters for these comments regarding alignment with CMS. Currently, the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) is required by CMS for the Support Electronic Referral Loops by Receiving and Reconciling Health Information measure and specified as an example of a criterion that may be used to support the actions of the HIE Bi-Directional Exchange and Enabling Exchange under TEFCA measures in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program (see
86 FR 45490
and
87 FR 49330-49331
, respectively) and the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category (see
85 FR 84889
and
87 FR 70084
, respectively). We have not finalized removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) as proposed and instead have finalized revisions to § 170.315(b)(2) to make it a functional criterion, thus ensuring that certified functionality is available to support the actions identified in the CMS measures noted above. Therefore, we do not anticipate that our finalized policy will require any changes to the references to this certification criterion in either the Medicare Promoting Interoperability or MIPS programs.
Comments.
There were several comments rejecting the “widespread adoption” rationale for removing a certification criterion. Commenters stated that adoption results from certification is not uniform across settings and may not persist after deregulation. Another commenter stated that ONC has not provided data demonstrating that these capabilities are uniformly implemented across all practice sizes, specialties, and healthcare settings and that “widespread” among large health systems is not the same as “widespread” among small practices, rural clinics, behavioral health providers, or SI health applications. Several commenters stated that market incentives do not guarantee continued support and that functionality could become an add-on, be left unmaintained, or be sunset. Another commenter stated that removing certification does not create incentives for improvement but instead risks stagnation.
Response.
We thank commenters for these comments regarding our rationale for proposing removal of certification criteria that have been widely adopted. In the Proposed Rule, we explained how we determined which certification criteria could be considered “widely adopted” (
90 FR 60979
through
60980
). We also referenced recent Real World Testing results regarding routine use of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) that demonstrate its widespread implementation and use in certified health IT at this time and indicate that the functionality is not likely to be removed (
90 FR 60985
). While we maintain that the current broad adoption and use of CIRI capabilities would ensure retention of that functionality in certified health IT, we have not, as discussed in detail above, finalized removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) as proposed. This action provides further assurance that this functionality
(
printed page 67936)
will be maintained in certified health IT.
Comments.
Some commenters expressed support for removal or simplification of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2), stating that it is widely adopted, overly prescriptive, and could permit more flexible and innovative approaches.
Response.
We thank commenters for their support of our proposal. We agree with commenters that removal of the criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) would provide room for innovation in this space. However, the finalized functional requirement in § 170.315(b)(2) also will give health IT developers greater flexibility to adopt FHIR-based solutions and innovative approaches, while at the same time ensuring that certified health IT maintains the capability to appropriately reconcile and incorporate patient health information electronically.
Comments.
Several commenters expressed concerns that the certification criterion does not address automated or computational reconciliation or define guardrails for SI-assisted reconciliation, human review, auditability, and accountability.
Response.
We thank commenters for these comments. While automated, computational, or SI-assisted reconciliation could be workflows and technology used to now meet the requirements of this certification criterion, we did not propose to make them functionalities required to meet the criterion. We also did not propose any form of “guardrails” (
e.g.,
human review or auditability) for inclusion in the CIRI certification criterion. Therefore, these recommendations are generally outside the scope of this rulemaking, and we decline to adopt them in this final rule.
c. Security Tags—Summary of Care
We proposed to remove the “security tags—summary of care—send” certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(7) and the “security tags—summary of care—receive” certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(8) and reserve those sections. Together, these certification criteria are designed to support the application and persistence of security labels for document-based exchange. The security tags—summary of care—send certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(7) enables a user to create a summary record that is tagged as restricted and subject to restrictions on re-disclosure, while the security tags—summary of care—receive certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(8) enables a user to receive a summary record that is tagged as restricted and subject to restrictions on re-disclosure. These criteria are not currently included in the Base EHR or CEHRT definitions. We proposed to remove the security tags—summary of care—send certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(7) and the security tags—summary of care—receive certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(8) as of the effective date of this final rule.
Comments.
The majority of commenters were not supportive of removing the security tags—summary of care—send certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(7) and the security tags—summary of care—receive certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(8), primarily due to concerns that C-CDA-based standards are still widely used at this time and FHIR-based standards are not sufficiently mature or widely adopted. Commenters were concerned that there was not an adequate replacement in place, and many opposed removal of the certification criteria without a transition plan, clear alternative pathway, or FHIR-based replacement. Commenters expressed concerns that removal of the criteria without an adequate replacement would weaken privacy protections for sensitive data, increase variability in implementation, and create risks of over-sharing, under-sharing, or manual workarounds during exchange and transitions of care. A commenter stated that readiness to transition to FHIR is uneven across care settings and that removal without sufficient transition time could increase interoperability gaps, reduce transparency into whether certified technology works reliably across settings, and worsen disparities. Some commenters noted that certain settings have resource limitations and would benefit from retaining the criteria or delaying removal. Several commenters stressed that current C-CDA-based exchange still has meaningful utility and value during the transition to FHIR-based approaches. Some commenters recommended changing certification to attestation or keeping the criteria optional while more progress is made on FHIR standards, and some recommended retaining the criteria or extending timelines for removal. Several commenters recommended a transition plan to minimize disruption and ensure that segmentation capabilities are not lost and that consent and restricted data indicators continue to function consistently across networks.
Response.
We appreciate the concerns raised regarding the removal of the C-CDA-based security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (b)(8). We recognize that C-CDA-based standards are frequently used for health information exchange at this time; however, as we stated in the Proposed Rule, there has been limited certification to the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) (
90 FR 60985
). We believe this indicates that the criteria are not as beneficial as some commenters suggest, thus lacking sufficient value as part of the Certification Program, and that there is promising movement toward FHIR-based solutions in the industry (
90 FR 60985
). We have heard repeatedly that the criteria present implementation challenges and are not effective in managing complex sensitive data. We appreciate that technical solutions to issues around patient consent and data segmentation are notoriously challenging and that current technology does not allow for segmenting specific health data and controlling its disclosure in a way that matches most expectations. Removal of these under-adopted certification criteria from the Certification Program will allow for greater focus on the continued development of a robust and effective FHIR-enabled data privacy and segmentation standard. We believe this focus can lead to more innovation in this area and enable us to propose more effective solutions in the future. Finally, we note that where users are successfully implementing C-CDA based data tagging solutions, including those that have been certified, our removal of the voluntary criteria from the Certification Program does not necessitate removal of such functionality from implemented systems or real world use. We are simply no longer certifying such technology by any means, including through attestation,
21
as we believe the burden on the Certification Program and health IT developers to be greater than the benefit derived specifically from certification to these criteria. Accordingly, we have finalized removal of the criteria as proposed.
We reassure commenters that we support and encourage technical approaches that offer patients a range of consent choices,
[
22
]
as we have noted in
(
printed page 67937)
prior rulemaking exploring both the C-CDA and the FHIR Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) standards and related security label taxonomy (See for example
89 FR 1299
through
1305
). We intend to maintain our focus on this area in future rulemaking as well as in our work with standards development organizations and health IT innovators. For example, ONC's Leading Edge Acceleration Projects (LEAP) in Health IT program has supported efforts around scalable consent frameworks for the advancement of interoperability with FHIR-based APIs.
[
23
]
With respect to comments regarding a transition plan or alternative pathway, we note that the C-CDA exchange requirement in § 170.315(b)(1) would remain in effect until January 1, 2030, providing a clear transition period for developers to support continued use of the security tag capabilities where implemented by users for C-CDA document exchange. We reiterate that the removal of the certification criteria does not necessitate removal of the functionality from health IT systems for users who may have these functions implemented, nor does it prohibit continued use of the referenced standards in existing and new health IT implementations.
Comments.
A number of commenters noted that the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) are the only existing mechanism in the Certification Program to support the segmentation of sensitive health information and had concerns about removal. Several commenters stressed that the criteria are still needed to protect especially sensitive categories of information, including behavioral health, substance use disorder, and adolescent data, and that removal could limit participation in health information exchange. Some commenters expressed concerns that removing the criteria would lower the security floor for health IT and create more variability in whether and how segmentation tags and security tags are implemented. Several commenters stated that removal of the criteria could increase the risk of over-sharing, under-sharing, or unauthorized sharing of data, especially during referrals and transitions of care. Another commenter stated that removal could encourage under-documentation or make records less reliable if providers avoid documenting sensitive information or rely on nonstandard workarounds.
Response.
We appreciate concerns that the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) are the only criteria in the Certification Program that support data segmentation and the protection of sensitive health information. As stated above, we support and encourage technical approaches that allow for the electronic capture, management, and exchange of an individual's consent preferences and offer patients a range of choices related to the use and sharing of health information under applicable law. We also note promising industry initiatives in this area, including an increasing availability of consent management tools on the market as well as State and HIE/HIN efforts to advance consent management approaches.
[
24
]
Comments.
Several commenters expressed concern that patients may disengage from or lose trust in health information exchange if computable privacy controls are unavailable. Some commenters expressed concern that removal of the criteria could erode public trust. Some commenters expressed concern that patients with sensitive health information may be harmed or avoid care if the criteria are removed.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns and understand how critical it is to ensure patient trust in the electronic exchange of health information. As noted above, we support initiatives exploring the capture, management, and exchange of patient consent preferences. Additionally, we note that as described in detail in section III.A.4 of this final rule, we have retained the privacy and security certification criteria in § 170.315(d) and the associated Privacy and Security Certification Framework under § 170.550(h) that we had proposed to remove in the Proposed Rule. We appreciate the concern that patients may disengage or lose trust in health information exchange if computable privacy controls are unavailable. Research indicates that public expectations and preferences for what “computable privacy controls” should deliver are growing,
[
25
]
and we believe that neither § 170.315(b)(7) nor § 170.315(b)(8) are optimal approaches to meeting those expectations. As document-based approaches tied to summary record exchange, these criteria are not aligned with granular controls pertaining to the release of information, as an individual would expect from modern API-based interactions. Again, we note that removal from the program does not necessitate removal from systems where the standards and functionality have been successfully implemented. Based on input from clinicians and health IT developers, we do understand that some such implementations exist although they are not widely in use. We believe that ongoing development in FHIR can better meet growing public expectations.
Comments.
Several commenters stated that developers may deprioritize segmentation capabilities or create proprietary, non-interoperable segmentation and consent solutions if the certification expectation is reduced or removed.
Response.
We appreciate these concerns regarding potential actions of developers to deprioritize segmentation capabilities due to removal of the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8). However, as previously noted, these criteria are not included in the Base EHR or CEHRT definitions, and have not been required to meet any measures under the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program or the Promoting Interoperability performance category of MIPS. The inclusion of these criteria in the Certification Program has not driven uptake within the industry, in large part because prioritization of these functionalities that are generally held to be only partially effective would divert resources from other efforts that may have greater efficacy. We understand the importance of ensuring the appropriate capture, management, and exchange of patient consent preferences. As described above, we believe that removal of the certification criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) will allow more space for innovation in this area, and we intend to maintain a focus on supporting and encouraging technical approaches that offer patients a range of consent choices, including in future rulemaking.
Comments.
A number of commenters expressed concerns about burden and warned that removing this functionality without a mature replacement would shift burden to providers. Some commenters stated that removal of the criteria could result in manual redactions based on patient preference, separate documentation, manual
(
printed page 67938)
collation, and other workarounds that would shift work to providers and staff.
Response.
We appreciate these comments regarding burden shifting due to removal of the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) and we understand the importance of not increasing burden on providers. We reiterate that we have heard repeatedly that the criteria present implementation challenges, are not meeting expectations, and are not effective in managing the sharing and/or release of complex sensitive data. Additionally, we note that certification to the criteria is voluntary, and as mentioned in the Proposed Rule and above, few Health IT Modules are currently certified to the criteria (
90 FR 60985
). Therefore, due to the small number of products certified to these criteria and low implementation, we do not expect that removal of these criteria will result in a significant burden shift to providers. We believe that removal of the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) will allow health IT developers and others in industry to move toward more effective technical solutions in this space, and we will continue to support and encourage technical approaches that enable operationalizing patient choices, including through future rulemaking.
Comments.
Several commenters rejected “low uptake” as a sufficient reason for removal, arguing that the underlying privacy need remains. Another commenter stated that low adoption is not a valid reason to remove protections when an underlying need persists.
Response.
We thank commenters for these comments regarding the low level of certification to the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8). As stated above, we believe the relatively small number of products certified to these criteria indicates that they do not have sufficient value to the users or implementers. In addition to the low level of certification, we have received multiple complaints that the criteria present implementation challenges and can be ineffective, which also influenced our proposal to remove these criteria. For example, industry has reported that security labels required by § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) can be difficult to use consistently because different systems may label, interpret, and enforce sensitive information differently, which limits how reliably those labels protect data when information is exchanged between organizations.
[
26
]
We agree with commenters that privacy needs are important to address. We believe that removal of the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) will allow health IT developers and industry to develop and adopt more effective solutions in this space, and we will continue to focus on identifying and supporting technical approaches that enable a range of consent choices.
Comments.
A commenter stated that maintaining these voluntary criteria would not add burden but would continue to signal the importance of a standards-based approach to computable consent.
Response.
We thank the commenter for this comment, and we agree that standards-based approaches to computable consent are very important. As stated above, ONC supports initiatives working to improve the capture, management, and exchange of patient consent preferences, and we note promising growth in industry initiatives in this area and an increasing availability of consent management tools. We support and encourage technical solutions that enable computable consent, and we intend to maintain a focus on this issue in future rulemaking.
Comments.
A commenter had concerns about alignment with CMS and recommended delaying removal of these criteria until at least 2028 so that ONC can work with CMS to ensure alignment between its program requirements and evolving ONC certification criteria.
Response.
We thank the commenter for this comment. We note that currently there are no CMS requirements requiring health care providers to adopt or use health IT certified to the certification criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8). We do not believe that removal of these criteria will lead to regulatory alignment concerns for health care providers participating in CMS programs. Additionally, we note that the criteria are not included in the definition for Base EHR at
45 CFR 170.102
.
Comments.
Some commenters expressed support for removal, noting that the criteria have had low adoption and limited real-world utility.
Response.
We thank commenters for these comments in support of our proposal to remove the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8). We agree with commenters that the criteria have been poorly adopted and have limited utility. We have repeatedly heard complaints that the criteria present implementation challenges and can be ineffective. We have finalized the proposal to remove the security tags criteria in § 170.315(b)(7) and (8) as of the effective date of a final rule.
d. Care Plan
We proposed to remove the “care plan” certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) and reserve that section as of the effective date of a final rule. The certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) helps improve coordination of care by providing a structured format for documenting patient information such as goals, health concerns, health status evaluations, and interventions. The criterion is not currently included in the Base EHR definition.
As of September 2026, 48 unique Health IT Modules are certified to the criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) out of a total of 714 active and non-suspended certifications listed on the Certified Health IT Product List (CHPL),
[
27
]
indicating low interest by health IT developers in certifying to this criterion. We also noted in the Proposed Rule that the industry is moving away from C-CDA-based standards to the use of FHIR-based standards, and we highlighted the development of FHIR-based care plan implementation guides (IGs), including the Multiple Chronic Condition eCare Plan and the Electronic Long Term Services & Support Care Plan IGs (
90 FR 60986
). Additionally, we noted input from industry that the care plan document type is less frequently adopted than other C-CDA document types, and where it is utilized, health IT developers are not likely to cease supporting the functionality if the criterion is removed from the Certification Program (
90 FR 60986
).
Comments.
The proposal received relatively few comments, and the majority of commenters were not supportive of removing the care plan certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9), primarily due to concerns that FHIR adoption and readiness were uneven and immature and there was not a viable replacement standard or plan for transitioning to FHIR. Commenters noted a lack of widespread use of FHIR push capabilities, interoperability issues with legacy systems, uneven adoption of FHIR across organizations, maintenance burdens, and inconsistent use of terminologies and value sets as examples of FHIR challenges and readiness issues. Commenters expressed
(
printed page 67939)
concerns that removing a criterion that relies on C-CDA-based standards at a time when FHIR-based standards are not mature and widely adopted would weaken care coordination, increase patient safety risks, and exacerbate interoperability gaps during the transition from C-CDA-based exchange to FHIR-based exchange. Several commenters cautioned that removing this requirement prematurely could increase administrative burden, create fragmentation across care settings, and disproportionately affect rural, small, safety net, dental, and other providers that continue to rely on existing C-CDA-based document exchange. Several commenters stressed that some settings were less ready to transition to FHIR, such as LTPAC, behavioral health, small, rural, safety-net, and dental settings, and that removal of the criterion could widen interoperability gaps and disparities.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns regarding the removal of the care plan certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9). We appreciate the points expressed by commenters that FHIR-based alternatives are not mature and widely available at this time and that certain settings are not ready to transition to FHIR. However, we note that the care plan certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) is just one of several certification criteria in the Certification Program that require use of C-CDA-based document exchange standards. The transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1) includes C-CDA-based requirements, and as discussed earlier in section III.A.2.a, we have extended the timeline for removing the C-CDA-based creation and transmission requirements in § 170.315(b)(1) until January 1, 2030. Also, we are retaining the requirements in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(A) to validate C-CDA performance beyond January 1, 2030. We believe this addresses commenter concerns regarding the removal of C-CDA-based requirements from the Certification Program. Further, as we noted in the Proposed Rule, adoption of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) is currently very low and removal of the certification criterion would help promote greater innovation and advancement in this area (
90 FR 60986
). Given these factors, we have finalized the removal of the criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) as of the effective date of this final rule as proposed.
Comments.
Several commenters expressed concerns about patient safety and stated that removal of the criterion could result in incomplete, delayed, lost, duplicated, or insufficiently supported health information. Several commenters stated that the criterion was still viewed as providing baseline safeguards and that removal could lead to degradation, inconsistency, loss of capability, or less transparency about whether certified tools perform reliably.
Response.
We appreciate commenter concerns about patient safety, and we understand the importance of ensuring that health information is exchanged reliably as part of patient care and care coordination. As stated above, we note that the care plan certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) is not the only certification criterion in the Certification Program that requires use of C-CDA-based standards and helps ensure reliable exchange of clinical data for patient care. The transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1) includes C-CDA-based requirements, and as discussed earlier in section III.A.2.a, we have extended the timeline for removing the C-CDA-based creation and transmission requirements in § 170.315(b)(1) until January 1, 2030. This extension should provide time for certified health IT to move from C-CDA-based standards to FHIR-based standards for exchange without sacrificing patient safety and help address commenter concerns. Also, we are retaining the requirements in § 170.315(b)(1)(ii)(A) to validate C-CDA performance beyond January 1, 2030. We do not believe it is necessary to also maintain requirements in § 170.315(b)(9) because health IT developers are likely to continue supporting C-CDA-based exchange under § 170.315(b)(1), which also contains requirements to support C-CDA document templates. Additionally, as we stated in the Proposed Rule, we do not believe that health IT developers are likely to cease supporting the functionality in § 170.315(b)(9) if the criterion is removed from the Certification Program (
90 FR 60986
). We also note that USCDI v3 includes data elements supporting the exchange of the components of a care plan, including Problems, Clinical Tests, Procedures, and Patient Goals. Additionally, USCDI v6 adds a Care Plan data element, and the USCDI standard follows the Standards Version Advancement Process (SVAP) to allow health IT developers to update their systems to newer version of USCDI and provide these updates to their customers.
[
28
]
We note that beginning August 29, 2026, health IT developers participating in the Certification Program may voluntarily use the 2026 SVAP-approved standards, which include USCDI v6, in their certified Health IT Modules.
[
29
]
Comments.
Several commenters stated that removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) without ensuring support for the functionality while transitioning to FHIR could shift burden to providers, clinicians, and system administrators. Commenters stated that this could result in manual workflows, manual transcription, and added operational burden, especially for smaller or under-resourced practices.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns about burden and appreciate the importance of not imposing additional burden on providers. As stated above, we have extended the deadline for removal of C-CDA-based creation and transmission requirements in the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1), and this extension will provide time for certified health IT to move from C-CDA-based standards to FHIR-based standards without significantly increasing burden on providers. We do not believe it is necessary to also maintain requirements in § 170.315(b)(9) because health IT developers are likely to continue supporting C-CDA-based exchange under § 170.315(b)(1). Further, as discussed above we do not believe that health IT developers that currently support this functionality are likely to cease supporting the functionality in § 170.315(b)(9) if the criterion is removed from the Certification Program, and therefore we do not anticipate additional burden on providers associated with removal of the criterion or a shifting of burden to providers.
Comments.
Several commenters disagreed that vendors would voluntarily keep the same functionality after deregulation and stated that vendors may stop maintaining the functionality, let the functionality become obsolete, or charge extra for the functionality. Another commenter stressed that the care plan criterion was one of the few certification signals to developers that care planning matters and recommend that ONC identify alternative pathways to accelerate adoption of care planning functionality.
Response.
We appreciate these concerns from commenters regarding developers ceasing to support C-CDA-based exchange and care plan documents or charging more for the functionality. We understand the importance of ensuring that support for C-CDA-based exchange and Care Plan
(
printed page 67940)
functionality is continued during a transition to FHIR-based exchange. However, because this functionality is so widely adopted, we are not persuaded that developers will cease supporting C-CDA-based exchange and care plan documents, or charge more for such functionality, due to removal of the criterion in § 170.315(b)(9). As stated above, other certification criteria in the Certification Program also require use of C-CDA-based standards, including the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1), and can help ensure support of C-CDA-based standards during a transition from C-CDA-based exchange to FHIR-based exchange. We have extended the deadline for removal of C-CDA-based creation and transmission requirements in the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1) to January 1, 2030. We do not believe it is necessary to also maintain requirements in § 170.315(b)(9) because health IT developers are likely to continue supporting C-CDA-based exchange under § 170.315(b)(1). Regarding alternative means of encouraging care planning functionality, we note that USCDI v3 includes data elements supporting the exchange of the components of a care plan, including Problems, Clinical Tests, Procedures, and Patient Goals, and that USCDI v6 includes a Care Plan data element.
Comments.
Some commenters stated that our proposal for removing the care plan certification criterion and related C-CDA-based certification criteria would require transition timelines and additional guidance and safeguards to ensure continued baseline functionality. Commenters requested phased or delayed implementation, clearer transition strategies, support for participation in national exchange frameworks, or replacement criteria, such as FHIR-based care plan requirements, before removing the existing criterion.
Response.
We appreciate these concerns from commenters regarding the need for timelines, strategies and resources related to transitioning from C-CDA-based exchange to FHIR-based exchange. We also understand the importance of ensuring that support for care plan functionality is continued during a transition to FHIR-based exchange. As stated above, we have extended the deadline for removal of C-CDA-based creation and transmission requirements in the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1) to January 1, 2030. This extension helps provide a timeline and pathway for transition to FHIR for developers of certified health IT. As stated earlier, we do not feel it is necessary to also maintain requirements in § 170.315(b)(9) because health IT developers are likely to continue supporting C-CDA-based exchange under § 170.315(b)(1). Additionally, we will continue to provide resources related to transitioning to FHIR-based exchange on our website. Regarding replacement criteria, we did not propose a FHIR-based replacement for the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9), and therefore, we are not finalizing a FHIR-based replacement here. However, as we stated in the Proposed Rule, there have been advancements in this area, and we may consider whether to propose a replacement in future rulemaking (
90 FR 60986
). We also note that USCDI v6 includes a Care Plan data element, which we believe may alleviate some of commenters' concerns regarding lack of continuity for care plans.
Comments.
A commenter had concerns about CMS alignment.
Response.
We thank the commenter for this comment. We note that currently there are no CMS requirements requiring health care providers to adopt or use health IT certified to the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9). Therefore, we do not believe that removal of this criterion will lead to regulatory alignment concerns for health care providers participating in CMS programs.
Comments.
Commenters who supported removal of the care plan criterion stated that it would reduce burden and that the criterion is no longer tied to active regulatory program requirements or widely used. These commenters noted that the criterion had been associated with the Comprehensive Primary Care Plus (CPC+) program, which is no longer active, and that its removal would not compromise Certification Program integrity.
Response.
We thank commenters for these comments in support of the proposal. We agree with commenters that removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) will reduce burden, including costs to maintain certification. We also agree with commenters that the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) is no longer associated with an active CMS program or other incentive program and that removal will not compromise Certification Program integrity. We have finalized the proposal to remove the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(9) as of the effective date of a final rule as proposed.
e. Decision Support Interventions
We proposed to revise the “decision support interventions” (DSI) certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(11) in order to reduce burden and promote innovation of SI in healthcare (
90 FR 60986
through
60988
). The DSI certification criterion ensures that users can leverage health IT for clinical decision-making by supporting their selection of both evidence-based and predictive DSIs (PDSIs) and enabling users' access to transparent information on DSI performance and quality. In particular, the source attribute requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) support “model cards” for PDSIs, which essentially function as nutrition labels and provide important information for providers using a PDSI, such as how a PDSI's algorithm was trained, its intended use and limitations, and how it performs across different patient groups. However, as discussed in more detail below, we did not find that users of certified health IT have relied on these requirements to review such information or that the requirements have positively impacted patient care (
90 FR 60987
). We have finalized removal of the requirements related to “model cards” as well as other revisions for the reasons discussed in detail below.
We proposed to remove the requirement in § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B) to enable interventions when a patient's medications, allergies and intolerance, and problems are incorporated from a transition of care or referral summary received and pursuant to paragraph § 170.315(b)(2)(iii)(D), and we proposed to redesignate the certification criterion requirement currently in § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(C) as § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B). We also proposed to remove the parenthetical reference in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii) to “drug-drug and drug-allergy contraindication checking” upon the effective date of this final rule. Additionally, we proposed to revise the requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii)(B), which currently relate to enabling predictive DSIs that use any data expressed in the standards in § 170.213, to limit the application of the certification criterion to just data expressed in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii)(A) as well as data expressed in the Clinical Notes and the Assessment and Plan of Treatment data classes in the standards in § 170.213. Finally, we proposed to remove the requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(iv) and (v) regarding source attribute support, access, and modification and in § 170.315(b)(11)(vi)
(
printed page 67941)
regarding intervention risk management for predictive DSIs.
Comments.
A large majority of commenters were not supportive of our proposal, primarily due to concerns about removing DSI transparency and risk-management requirements in § 170.315(b)(11). Concerns included that reducing transparency and accountability for SI-enabled tools would shift evaluation, governance, and liability burdens to providers and health systems and undermine patient safety, clinician trust, and the ability to evaluate bias, performance, and appropriateness. Many commenters expressed concerns that eliminating “model card” requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) was premature since the requirements have been in effect for less than two years and have not been fully evaluated. Commenters stated that removal of the model card requirements would create a significant regulatory gap in SI governance at a time when SI adoption is accelerating. Some commenters stated that providers would lose important information about intended use, provenance, training data, limitations, performance, and known risks. Some commenters stated that the loss of information would make it more difficult to determine the appropriateness of a tool for particular patient populations or settings. Another commenter noted that in behavioral health and substance use cases, reduced transparency may complicate safe and lawful use of tools that process sensitive information, creating confidentiality and compliance concerns. Several commenters noted as a distinct benefit of model cards or source attribute disclosures that funding-source disclosures help detect hidden commercial or pharmaceutical influence on CDS recommendations.
Over half of the commenters expressing concerns about transparency wanted ONC to retain the model cards requirements, or the full criterion, while the other commenters with transparency concerns wanted some form of guardrails even if model card requirements are removed. Commenter suggestions for guardrails included establishing voluntary transparency standards, creating a voluntary transparency designation for predictive SI, retaining the useful elements of predictive DSI transparency and risk management requirements, retaining the criterion in § 170.315(a)(9), clarifying developer responsibilities related to transparency, acknowledging transparency as a best practice, or public model cards as a means of ensuring transparency.
Response.
We appreciate these commenter concerns and understand the importance of ensuring appropriate transparency around decision support interventions. However, as we stated in the Proposed Rule, developers of certified health IT have reported that during care delivery, most clinical users lack the time or technical background to engage with source attribute information for DSIs (
90 FR 60987
). Further, we have identified no evidence through peer reviewed publication or trade press indicating that users of certified health IT have relied on the transparency requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) to access, record, or modify source attributes, or that the requirements have led to positive impacts on patient care (
90 FR 60987
). We have also found no evidence that source attribute transparency requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) have improved healthcare delivery organizations' evaluation and effective use of SI (
90 FR 60987
). We believe that we have had a sufficient amount of time to evaluate the effectiveness of the transparency requirements in § 170.315(b)(11), including via peer reviewed publication, articles in the press, and reports from developers of health IT, and are not persuaded of their value, particularly given the feedback we have received from developers that the requirements are burdensome and detrimental to innovation (
90 FR 60987
). We do, however, believe it is important to continue to ensure the ability for users to leverage health IT for clinical decision-making and to select both evidence-based and predictive DSIs, and we encourage users of certified health IT to discuss SI quality and performance before deploying DSIs supplied by the developer of their certified health IT. We note that removing requirements for DSI performance and quality as part of the Certification Program does not mean that such information about intended use, provenance, training data, limitations, performance, and known risks is unknown or unavailable to users of certified health IT, or that such information could not be communicated to them. We encourage users of certified health IT to ask their developers for such information, and in particular we remind users of certified health IT of the importance of complying with applicable requirements to identify potential bias in PDSIs and to avoid discrimination through the use of such tools.
See
45 CFR 92.210
. We note that we did not propose to remove requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(C) for evidence-based DSIs regarding electronic feedback data, which support transparency by enabling providers to share, export, and report on the performance of DSIs in real-world settings. We did, however, propose to redesignate § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(C) as § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B).
Specifically, we have finalized as proposed revisions in § 170.315(b)(11) to remove the requirement in § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B); redesignate § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(C) as § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B); remove the reference in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii) to “drug-drug and drug-allergy contraindication checking”; revise the requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii)(B) to limit the application of the certification criterion; and remove the source attribute support, source attribute access and modification, and intervention risk management requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(iv), (v), and (vi). While we have retained a revised CIRI certification criterion in this final rule, we believe that removal of the requirement in § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B) is still appropriate. The requirement prescribed enabling DSI in a specific circumstance with limited data elements (
i.e.,
transition of care/referral summary focused on only medications, allergies and intolerance, and problems). Such prescription has minimal value for certification, particularly compared to the DSI certification criterion requirement to support selection of interventions based on a wider breadth of data as identified in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii). This requirement further provides flexibility for health IT developers and their customers to determine how interventions are incorporated into customer workflows.
We acknowledge that the prior CDS “source attributes transparency” requirements (§ 170.315(a)(9)(v)) for evidence-based interventions have been part of the Certification Program for many years and may not present significant burden or costs for health IT developers with health IT previously certified to the CDS certification criterion. As such, we will further consider for future rulemaking whether these or similar requirements should be reinstated in the Certification Program.
Comments.
A number of commenters expressed concerns regarding burden. Commenters stated that the proposal would shift evaluation, governance, and liability burdens related to SI tools to providers and health systems. Some commenters stated that the burden shift would be especially problematic for small, rural, safety-net, shared-network, community healthcare, and LTPAC
(
printed page 67942)
organizations that lack data-science, governance, legal, or IT capacity.
Response.
We appreciate these concerns expressed by commenters regarding evaluation, governance, and liability burden shifting to providers and healthcare systems. We understand the importance of ensuring that additional burdens related to selecting DSIs or DSI functionality are not placed on providers and health systems. As discussed above, we did not propose removal of requirements related to feedback tools for evidence-based DSIs in redesignated § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B), and we believe these requirements can help provide assurances regarding the performance of evidence-based DSI functionality in Health IT Modules certified to § 170.315(b)(11). As also discussed above, we are not persuaded of the value of the transparency requirements in § 170.315(b)(11), and thus we do not believe that our finalized removal of the requirements to enable access to source attributes for evidence-based and predictive DSIs will significantly impair the ability to evaluate DSI tools. We believe the finalized revisions to § 170.315(b)(11) provide sufficient assurances and transparency to make any significant increase or shift in the evaluation, governance, or liability burden of providers and healthcare systems unlikely.
Comments.
A number of commenters expressed concern that the proposal would undermine patient safety. Commenters expressed concern that the proposal would impair the ability to evaluate bias, performance, and appropriateness. Some commenters stated that the proposal could result in unsafe recommendations, preventable harm, inappropriate reliance, and weaker clinician oversight. A couple of commenters expressed concern that loss of transparency could increase automation bias, salience bias, or other overreliance problems. Several commenters expressed concern that the proposal removes a core safeguard. Several commenters also stressed that certain populations and settings need population-specific validation and transparency because they are especially vulnerable to underrepresentation or inappropriate extrapolation. A commenter expressed concern that removing the DSI reference to drug-drug and drug-allergy contraindication checking could negatively affect patient care.
Response.
We appreciate these comments expressing concerns about patient safety, and we understand the importance of ensuring that the use of DSI tools does not harm patients or negatively impact patient care. We note that, as we stated in the Proposed Rule, we are not aware of any publicly available evidence showing that transparency requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) led to positive impacts on patient care, including removal of defective algorithms (
90 FR 60987
). In response to commenters' concerns regarding a need for population-specific validation and transparency, we agree that such information is important, especially for patients belonging to underrepresented groups, and we encourage users of certified health IT to discuss these facets of SI quality and performance before deploying their developer's supplied PDSIs. We do not believe that our policy to remove requirements for user transparency will significantly impair efforts to evaluate DSI tools or discuss such matters with health IT developers. Regarding removal of the reference to drug-drug and drug-allergy contraindication checking, we note that, as stated in the Proposed Rule, the retention of requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii)(A)(
2
) and (
3
) regarding enabling evidence-based DSIs that include “Medications” and “Allergies and Intolerances” as data types ensures support for such interaction checks by Health IT Modules certified to § 170.315(b)(11) (
90 FR 60986
through
60987
).
Comments.
Some commenters stated that the proposal would weaken provider and patient trust in SI-enabled decision support and that this could slow responsible adoption of SI-enabled decision support.
Response.
We appreciate these comments regarding trust in SI-enabled decision support. We are committed to encouraging trust in health IT and health information exchange, including trust in SI-enabled decision support. We do not believe that our revisions to § 170.315(b)(11) will significantly lessen trust in SI-enabled decision support because, as described above, we found that the requirements lacked utility. Additionally, the retained requirements related to feedback tools in redesignated § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B) help provide assurances regarding the performance of DSI functionality in Health IT Modules certified to § 170.315(b)(11). We believe the finalized revisions to § 170.315(b)(11) provide sufficient assurances and transparency, and that our finalized policies will not contribute to an erosion in provider or patient trust in health IT and SI-enabled DSI.
Comments.
Some commenters rejected the premise that low clinician use at the point of care means the information lacks value, arguing that the real users are governance, procurement, implementation, compliance, and safety teams.
Response.
We appreciate these comments regarding clinician use of source attribute information and the value of that information. We noted in the Proposed Rule that developers of certified health IT reported that during care delivery, most clinical users did not have the time or technical background to engage with source attribute information for either evidence-based DSIs or predictive DSIs supplied by the developer of certified health IT (
90 FR 60987
). We recognize that there is value in transparency regarding DSIs, however we remain cognizant of the need to minimize burden on developers of certified health IT, especially when the required functionality is not widely used and may not be equally applied to other developers that do not participate in the Certification Program. We note that we have retained requirements related to feedback tools for evidence-based DSI in redesignated § 170.315(b)(11)(ii)(B), which we believe help ensure transparency.
Comments.
Some commenters expressed specific concerns about removing risk-management requirements, including that it would weaken drift monitoring, control over updates and changes, auditability, root-cause analysis, and ongoing quality review.
Response.
We appreciate concerns regarding the removal of risk-management requirements, including concerns related to monitoring drift, updates, auditability, root-cause analysis, and ongoing quality reviews. While we understand the importance of ensuring that predictive DSI functions appropriately and effectively, we also seek to minimize burden on developers of certified health IT and encourage innovation in this evolving area. We believe that removal of the risk-management requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(vi) provides substantial burden relief for developers of certified health IT without hindering developer's ability to work with their customers to institute ongoing monitoring of predictive DSI performance and effectiveness. Requirements to apply risk management to supplied PDSIs may still be considered best practices and may still be incentivized through other policies, such as those established by the FDA for premarket approvals.
Comments.
Several commenters expressed concern about fragmentation and variability that might occur if requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) are removed. Some commenters stated that removing the Federal framework could
(
printed page 67943)
produce fragmented oversight, including divergent State requirements or weaker cross-agency alignment. Several commenters stated that resulting variability across developers could make SI less portable, less comparable, or less predictable across health systems. A commenter stated that removing the requirements soon after HTI-1 implementation would undercut recent compliance investments and create regulatory instability.
Response.
We appreciate these comments regarding fragmentation and variability that could occur if requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) are removed. We note that we are retaining a number of requirements in the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(11), including requirements to support DSI selection. We do not agree that our revisions to § 170.315(b)(11) will create regulatory instability. Rather, we anticipate that by removing requirements for developers of certified health IT to supply their customers with access to DSI performance and quality information, we are reducing the Department's regulatory footprint and concentrating requirements solely within other Department authorities, such as those exerted by the FDA.
Comments.
Some commenters expressed concerns about the proposal's data support and selection requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii). Some commenters stated that the requirements were confusing, ambiguous, or misaligned with the FHIR API framework, especially where no clear standard for “selection” was specified. Some commenters objected to narrowing the scope of predictive DSIs because certain tools may need broader clinical context, including longitudinal history and social or behavioral context. A commenter stated that ONC needed a standard for enabling third-party predictive DSIs in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii)(B).
Response.
We appreciate these comments expressing concerns regarding requirements in § 170.315(b)(11)(iii). As we stated in the Proposed Rule, we have received feedback from developers of certified health IT that requiring support of predictive DSIs that use
any
data element in one of the USCDI standards in § 170.213 is overly burdensome and costly (
90 FR 60986
). We also noted in the Proposed Rule that many USCDI data elements, such as phone number and phone number type data elements, are not likely to be used as inputs for predictive DSIs (
90 FR 60986
). We believe that revising the requirements to focus on fewer data elements will simplify requirements and significantly reduce burden for health IT developers without diminishing users' ability to activate a wide variety of predictive DSIs (
90 FR 60987
). With respect to the comment regarding the need for a standard for enabling “selection” of third-party predictive DSIs according to § 170.315(b)(11)(iii), we continue to maintain a flexible and non-prescriptive posture regarding how a health IT developer supports selection of DSIs according to § 170.315(b)(11)(iii). We reiterate long-standing Certification Program expectations that health IT developers with Health IT Modules certified to § 170.315(b)(11) support a user's selection of DSIs based on whether a DSI uses specified data, and we decline to dictate how developers support selection of such DSIs at this time.
Comments.
Some commenters expressed support for our proposed revisions to the DSI certification criterion. These commenters stated that the revisions would reduce burden from rarely used or overly prescriptive requirements and allow more flexible or voluntary approaches to transparency. Many supporters of our proposal noted extremely low use of the required functionality and a lack of value for clinicians at the point of care. Several supporters of our proposal stated that the SI landscape is rapidly evolving and that industry-led frameworks are more appropriate than Federal transparency requirements that could quickly become outdated. A supporter of our proposal noted that the current requirements in § 170.315(b)(11) exceed those of other Federal Government programs utilizing SI, and that the FDA is best situated to ensure SI safety. Another supporter of our proposal stated that most SI solutions function as downstream consumers of interoperable data and are not components of certified EHRs. A supporter of our proposal stated that source attribute information embedded into clinical interfaces risks alert fatigue without providing benefit to patients.
Response.
We appreciate these comments in support of our proposal. We agree with commenters that our proposed revisions to § 170.315(b)(11) would reduce burden related to under-utilized requirements and allow for greater innovation in this area. We also agree that, as several commenters stated, the SI landscape is rapidly evolving and industry-led efforts to provide transparency have promise. We have finalized our proposed revisions to § 170.315(b)(11) as proposed.
Comments.
Several commenters commented on issues that were out of scope for our proposal, including broader audit trail and data preservation requirements, patient-facing notice regarding downstream SI-related uses of data, contractual issues, and support for emerging interoperability approaches beyond existing standards.
Response.
We appreciate these comments; however, these comments were outside the scope of this rulemaking.
3. Clinical Quality Measures Certification Criteria
a. Clinical Quality Measures—Report
In the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
), we proposed to revise the “clinical quality measures (CQM)—report” certification criterion in § 170.315(c)(3) as of the effective date of this final rule. This certification criterion enables a user to electronically create a data file for transmission of clinical quality measure data. In the Cures Act Interim Final Rule, we revised § 170.315(c)(3) to include a corrected compliance transition timeline for the criterion in § 170.315(c)(3)(ii), which specified the use of standards in §§ 170.205(h)(2) and (k)(1) and (2), for the period before December 31, 2022 (
85 FR 70075
and
70083
). In the Proposed Rule, we proposed to remove § 170.315(c)(3)(ii) because that transition time period had elapsed (
90 FR 60988
). We also proposed to move the requirements in § 170.315(c)(3)(i) to § 170.315(c)(3), thus removing all subparagraphs and including all certification criterion requirements in the main paragraph for § 170.315(c)(3). For further background and history on this certification criterion, we refer readers to the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
).
Comments.
The majority of commenters supported our proposal to revise the CQM—report certification criterion to remove expired transition language, stating that the proposal would streamline outdated regulatory requirements with little or no practical impact. Several of these commenters characterized the proposal as a narrow cleanup that would align the regulation with current practice and remove obsolete references to expired standards.
Some commenters used their discussion of this certification criterion to recommend broader changes to quality measurement policy, including recommending: revising § 170.315(c)(3) to permit technology-neutral quality reporting, allowing certified Health IT Modules to satisfy the certification criterion requirement using either Quality Reporting Document Architecture (QRDA) or FHIR-based quality reporting implementation guides, and establishing a transition
(
printed page 67944)
pathway toward FHIR-based quality reporting. A few commenters expressed concern that continued reliance on QRDA is inconsistent with FHIR-based modernization efforts because it limits quality reporting to legacy document standards. Other commenters also noted that continued reliance on QRDA-based reporting introduces architectural inconsistency with interoperability efforts that are transitioning to FHIR-based APIs and may require developers to maintain parallel infrastructure, limiting their available modernization resources. A cross-cutting concern expressed by a few commenters was that revisions to certification requirements should not risk continuity by creating a gap in quality reporting infrastructure before FHIR-based or other modernized approaches are fully implemented. Additionally, many of the commenters who recommend broader changes to quality measurement policy encouraged broader API-driven quality measurement approaches and strengthening post-certification oversight and transparency regarding the quality measurement capabilities of certified health IT products, including tracking which quality measurement capabilities are included versus offered as paid add-ons to products. A few other commenters expressed concerns regarding the continuity of quality reporting infrastructure, workflow burden and costs for providers, comparability and auditability of quality measurement outputs, maintaining a consistent baseline for interoperability and quality reporting, and supporting digital quality measures, including measures that use patient-reported data.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback. We have finalized our proposal to revise § 170.315(c)(3), including the removal of § 170.315(c)(3)(ii) and transfer of the requirements in former § 170.315(c)(3)(i) to § 170.315(c)(3), as of the effective date of this final rule. We note that the revisions to § 170.315(c)(3) do not alter the substantive requirements a Health IT Module must meet to obtain certification to § 170.315(c)(3) that remain applicable under the CQM—report certification criterion.
We acknowledge commenters' recommendations that we use this final rule to adopt broader revisions related to quality measurement modernization efforts, including technology-neutral QRDA or FHIR-based quality reporting implementation guides, a sequenced transition pathway for broader FHIR-based quality reporting, as well as concerns expressed by commenters regarding provider burden. However, we did not propose these broader revisions to § 170.315(c)(3) in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
), and therefore, we have not adopted these revisions in this final rule.
Comments.
Some commenters opposed removal of the CQM—report certification criterion and recommended coordinating certification changes related to quality reporting with CMS program requirements and requested that any future substantive changes to quality reporting certification requirements include mechanisms to evaluate impacts on CMS program compliance. A number of these commenters recommended that such substantive changes to quality reporting certification requirements be delayed until 2028 or until alignment with CMS program timelines can be achieved.
Response.
We acknowledge commenters' recommendations to coordinate changes to certification criteria related to quality reporting with CMS program requirements and to include mechanisms to evaluate potential impacts on CMS program compliance. We also recognize commenters' requests that substantive changes be delayed until alignment with CMS program timelines can be achieved. However, we did not propose to remove the CQM—report certification criterion, therefore, these comments are out of scope for this rulemaking. The revisions we have finalized are limited to removal of expired transition language and reorganization of regulatory text in the CFR, and they do not alter the substantive requirements a Health IT Module must meet to obtain certification to § 170.315(c)(3) that remain applicable under this certification criterion. We will continue to coordinate with CMS, as appropriate, on any future proposals to substantively change this certification criterion in future rulemaking in order to support alignment of Certification Program criteria with CMS program needs.
b. Clinical Quality Measures—Filter
In the Proposed Rule, we proposed to remove the “clinical quality measures (CQM)—filter” certification criterion in § 170.315(c)(4) with an effective date of January 1, 2027 (
90 FR 60988
). This certification criterion assesses whether a Health IT Module can filter quality data based on a set of standardized data elements for electronic clinical quality measures (eCQM) calculated using certified health IT. As stated in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
), we proposed to remove this certification criterion because we identified that the administrative costs of certification for CQM—filter are no longer offset by the benefits of advancing the specific functionality supported by the criterion. Additionally, quality reporting programs, such as those required by States and CMS programs, require broader supplemental data and capabilities beyond what we currently require for certification. We also stated in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
) that health IT developers have widely implemented technology solutions that expand beyond the baseline requirements of the CQM—filter certification criterion. We further stated that § 170.315(c)(4) is not included in the Base EHR definition in § 170.102 but is included in the CEHRT definition used by programs including MIPS in
42 CFR 414.1305
. We clarify here that § 170.315(c)(4) is specified as optional for inclusion as part of CEHRT necessary to report on clinical quality measures in paragraph (2) of the definition. We also explained that health care providers participating in CMS alternative payment models, as well as health IT developers supporting quality initiatives, reported using different options to filter eCQM results, including customized systems and support from third parties to meet particular quality measure reporting needs. For further background and history on this certification criterion, we refer readers to the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
).
Comments.
Many commenters opposed the removal of the CQM—filter certification criterion. These commenters expressed concerns that removal could shift responsibility for maintaining quality reporting, stratification, and workflow functionality from health IT developers to clinical providers, increase provider burden and costs, require manual workarounds or third-party tools, and reduce comparability and confidence in quality measure outputs across systems. Some commenters recommended that we not remove the CQM—filter certification criterion until a fully functional, low cost, standardized replacement is available, noting that § 170.315(c)(4) serves as a baseline capability supporting consistency across systems.
Several commenters representing providers stated that the CQM—filter certification criterion is important for day-to-day quality reporting workflows and for supporting some Federal, State, and other programmatic reporting requirements. Another commenter specified that these reporting workflow functions support demographic stratification, validating measure denominators and numerators, generating clinician-facing lists for gap closure, and reconciling measure
(
printed page 67945)
discrepancies across systems. Several commenters, including payer- and plan-affiliated organizations, echoed concerns expressed by providers, particularly with respect to workflow integration and the potential for disruption to existing reporting processes, including for safety-net providers and organizations that rely on certified functionality to support Uniform Data System (UDS) and other program reporting requirements.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback. We have finalized our proposal to remove the CQM—filter certification criterion in § 170.315(c)(4) with an effective date of January 1, 2027.
We continue to believe that the administrative costs of certification for § 170.315(c)(4) are no longer offset by the benefits of maintaining this specific certification requirement. As noted in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
), quality reporting programs generally require broader supplemental data and capabilities than the limited functionality described in § 170.315(c)(4), and health IT developers have widely implemented technological solutions that extend beyond the criterion's minimum certification requirements.
While we recognize the importance of functionality within EHRs to filter quality data by common variables, current rates of certification indicate that such functionality is not being driven by compliance with this certification criterion. As of May 2026, CHPL
[
30
]
data indicates there is low interest by health IT developers in certifying their Health IT Modules to § 170.315(c)(4). For example, there are 326 active Health IT Modules certified to § 170.315(c)(1), (2), or (3), but only 62 active Health IT Modules certified to § 170.315(c)(4). Additionally, we find from publicly available 2024 Promoting Interoperability data that less than 2 percent of MIPS-eligible clinicians and less than 8 percent of eligible hospitals and critical access hospitals reported using health IT certified to the CQM—filter certification criterion, showing that few healthcare providers used technology certified to this criterion.
[
31 32
]
These findings are consistent with feedback received through listening sessions with a wide range of health care provider types and sites of service, as well as through public correspondence.
We appreciate comments recommending that we do not remove this certification criterion until a fully functional, low cost, standardized replacement is available. However, based on the utilization data described above, removal of the CQM—filter certification criterion is not expected to result in a decrease in the availability of quality measure filtering functionality in health IT, as developers and users have existing options to support filtering and stratification functions beyond the limited functionality described in § 170.315(c)(4).
We acknowledge concerns expressed by commenters surrounding the importance of supporting reliable and efficient quality measure data reporting workflows across Federal, State, and other programmatic reporting requirements. We also acknowledge that some providers, particularly safety-net providers and organizations with limited resources, may rely on filtering functionality within their EHRs to support specific reporting workflows, including those related to UDS reporting. Additionally, we acknowledge concerns expressed by commenters that removal could shift responsibility for maintaining quality reporting functionality from health IT developers to clinical providers resulting in an increase in provider burden. However, given the low rates of certification to this criterion, we believe health IT developers provide this functionality in response to customer needs, rather than to obtain certification for their Health IT Modules to this certification criterion. Therefore, we do not believe removing the availability of § 170.315(c)(4) for certification will result in a loss of quality measure filtering functionality from health IT systems, in a shift of responsibility from health IT developers to clinical providers, or in a potential disruption to workflow integration or existing reporting processes. We also do not believe that removing the CQM—filter certification criterion will increase provider burden and costs, require additional manual workarounds or third-party tools, or affect existing comparability and confidence in quality measure outputs across systems. As noted in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60988
), developers and providers have implemented a range of approaches to support filtering, stratification, and validation functions that extend beyond the limited baseline established by this certification criterion.
Comments.
Some commenters who opposed removal of the CQM—filter certification criterion recommended a transition plan instead of immediate removal of the criterion. A commenter recommended that any changes to certification requirements should allow a two-year window of voluntary compliance following publication of a requirement in final rulemaking. Several commenters recommended a phased or delayed sunset in coordination with CMS program timelines. A few of these commenters recommended we adopt a phased transition as more standardized approaches to digital quality measurement and API-based quality data exchange mature.
Response.
We appreciate commenters' requests that we coordinate the timing of removal of the CQM—filter certification criterion with CMS program timelines and future quality measure modernization efforts. We acknowledge the cross-cutting concern expressed by commenters; however, the certification criterion is specified as optional under the definition of CEHRT in
42 CFR 414.1305
, which is referenced by certain CMS programs, including MIPS. As a certification criterion that may “optionally” be included in the definition of CEHRT with respect to criteria necessary to support the calculation and reporting of clinical quality measures, health care providers are not subject to program requirements to use EHR technology certified to this criterion in order to meet the definition of CEHRT in
42 CFR 414.1305
.
