4. Privacy and Security Certification Criteria
We proposed to remove all the privacy and security (P&S) certification criteria in § 170.315(d) and the associated Privacy and Security Certification Framework (P&S Certification Framework) under § 170.550(h) as of the effective date of this final rule. We proposed to remove the P&S certification criteria and P&S Certification Framework for a multitude of reasons that led to our conclusion that the costs and burden of these certification criteria and Certification Program requirements far exceed their intended purpose and benefits (
90 FR 60989-60990
). We reiterate these reasons below.
First, we have found that health IT developers have changed their development processes to build in P&S capabilities to meet these certification requirements rather than attempting to demonstrate that their technology could interface with other health IT that provides these capabilities. This has led to negative experiences for health care providers who have sought to use a best-of-breed, non-certified security technology to work across their deployed enterprise (
e.g.,
a third-party audit log).
Second, certified health IT (which is generally EHR-focused technology) is often implemented in enterprise-wide settings (
e.g.,
group practices, large healthcare systems, multi-provider cloud-supported services). However, it cannot, in isolation or independently, provide the necessary P&S capabilities across all relevant technologies in the enterprise-wide setting for covered entities to comply with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) Security Rule (
45 CFR part 160
and subparts A and C of part 164).
Third, while certified health IT has always been “linked” to the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program and the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, those programs have not required participating health care providers to use or implement the P&S capabilities included in certified health IT for purposes of meeting the security risk analysis measure. Rather, the health care providers must “have” such certified health IT. As such and as discussed in more detail below (and in the Proposed Rule), health care providers participating in the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program or the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category are required to adopt certified capabilities that they may not use because, for example, they may prefer a non-certified security health IT product to meet their overall security needs, including compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule.
Fourth, many interested parties have overinterpreted the Certification Program's limited scope and policy purpose with respect to health IT security and instead have assumed that the Certification Program assessed discrete specific security capabilities at significant depths, such as when and how the capabilities are implemented in health care provider or system settings. For example, interested parties have expressed incorrect expectations of certified health IT and developers, such as expectations that the Certification Program required health IT developers of certified health IT to implement and conduct penetration testing of certified health IT or ensure that certified authentication and authorization capabilities protect against known or unknown vulnerabilities. In contrast, to allow for significant scalable deployment flexibility, a certified Heath IT Module must only, for example, demonstrate support for basic authentication and role-based access control.
Fifth, there remains a disconnect between health IT certified to the P&S certification criteria under the Certification Program and the implementation and compliance responsibilities of most purchasers and users of certified health IT with the requirements of the HIPAA Privacy
[
33
]
and Security Rules. This disconnect has led to the introduction of unnecessary regulatory burden and duplication, as well as unwarranted opportunity costs for innovation. As we noted above and in our prior rulemakings related to the P&S certification criteria, the adoption of health IT certified to the P&S certification criteria does not guarantee compliance with the requirements of the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules. Further, the adoption of health IT certified to the P&S certification criteria does not serve as an affirmative defense, has not been identified as a mitigating factor in assessing HIPAA civil money penalties, and does not exempt a HIPAA-regulated entity from having to comply with any applicable provision of the HIPAA Privacy or Security Rules (or the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule
[
34
]
). These facts alone have created unnecessary burden for health care providers that adopt certified health IT and health IT developers of certified health IT that also meet the definition of a covered entity or business associate, respectively, and are subject to the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules.
[
35
]
In fact, we have heard from interested parties both arguing that our certification requirements go beyond the HIPAA Security Rule requirements (
75 FR 44619
,
80 FR 62707
) or do not go far enough in meeting the requirements of the HIPAA Privacy Rule and Security Rule (
80 FR 62691
,
62706
). Considering these opposing perspectives, our Certification Program requirements may be diverting financial resources and efforts from innovative, agile, and comprehensive solutions that can address the threats faced by health care providers and meet their regulatory obligations under the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules. As highlighted in the Proposed Rule, by removing the P&S certification requirements under the Certification Program, we would provide health IT developers with the flexibility to innovate in this area and to develop new solutions to address the needs of their customers. Such an approach should also spur competition and give health care providers, including small practices, the opportunity to choose the best P&S technologies that fit their needs at the best price as opposed to being forced to accept those capabilities included in certified health IT that may not fit their health information P&S needs for various reasons. Finally, we noted that we did not plan to completely forego the adoption of P&S capabilities within the
(
printed page 67947)
Certification Program. Instead, going forward, we stated that we intend to prioritize the adoption of P&S capabilities that are fit for purpose, use case specific, and deliver much needed technical consistency in the market when paired with specific conformance requirements. As an example, we stated that as we pursue more API-focused certification criteria, if the standards and implementation guides adopted for them do not specify or leave optional specific security requirements, we may look to add further constraints (
e.g.,
multi-factor authentication support). Further, we stated that, in all cases, we intended to make security capability conformance a built-in part of a certification criterion's conformance and not the separate and stand-alone conformance assessment that currently exists.
In lieu of removing, on the effective date of this final rule, all of the P&S certification criteria in § 170.315(d) and the associated P&S Certification Framework under § 170.550(h), we offered an alternative proposal. We proposed to retain the “auditable events and tamper resistance” (§ 170.315(d)(2)), “audit report(s)” (§ 170.315(d)(3)), and “auditing actions on health information” (§ 170.315(d)(10)) certification criteria and associated P&S Certification Framework certification requirements. We stated that these certification criteria and included functionality may serve to help identify fraud and abuse. We noted that the functionality may also support health care provider compliance obligations and investigations by relevant entities, including both civil and criminal matters at the Federal and State levels. As mentioned in the Proposed Rule, identifying and addressing fraud and abuse increases confidence in the nation's healthcare system, reduces inappropriate and wasteful spending, and protects taxpayer dollars when it comes to government spending on healthcare (
90 FR 60990
).
Comments.
We received some comments supporting our proposal to completely remove the P&S certification criteria and the associated P&S Certification Framework. These commenters strongly agreed with our rationale, including noting that removal would eliminate regulatory duplication. These commenters asserted that certification involved intensive and costly testing. Some of these commenters also advocated for a “system-wide approach” to certification and a uniform national governance structure for privacy and security. Another commenter highlighted the availability of alternative certification processes, such as HITRUST.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback. We have ultimately decided not to finalize our proposal to remove the P&S certification criteria and the P&S Certification Framework for the reasons we discuss hereafter.
Comments.
The vast majority of commenters did not support our proposal to remove all of the P&S certification criteria and the P&S Certification Framework. With limited exceptions, these commenters generally did not comment on or respond to our rationale for proposing to remove the P&S certification criteria and the P&S Certification Framework. Rather, they offered different rationales for keeping the P&S certification criteria and P&S Certification Framework. Commenters stated that certification provides a minimum baseline of P&S capabilities and a mechanism for verifying that these capabilities exist in health IT products that health care providers purchase, license, and use. Further, health care providers expressed concern that removal of the certification requirements will both shift burden to health care providers to verify the existence of the capabilities and lead to developers removing P&S capabilities due to costs and burden. These concerns were particularly acute for small and rural providers that stated they had limited resources to address these concerns and negotiate inclusion of capabilities in health IT. A few commenters asserted that privacy and security capabilities also support patient safety (
e.g.,
ensuring health information remains reliable).
Commenters who responded to our rationale that P&S certification criteria do not guarantee compliance with the requirements of the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules, do not serve as an affirmative defense, have not been identified as a mitigating factor in assessing HIPAA civil money penalties, and do not exempt a HIPAA-regulated entity from having to comply with any applicable provision of the HIPAA Privacy or Security Rules, recommended that we work with the HHS Office for Civil Rights to find ways to leverage the adoption and use of health IT certified to P&S certification criteria for compliance with the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules.
In response to our alternative proposal, commenters expressed strong support for retaining the three “auditing” certification criteria. However, many of these same commenters pointed out that the criteria-incorporated audit standard (ASTM E2147-18) is outdated and should be updated.
Some commenters argued for the specific retention of other P&S certification criteria such as the authentication (§ 170.315(d)(1)) and encryption (§ 170.315(d)(7) and (9)) criteria.
A few commenters suggested using testing alternatives to lower burden.
Response.
We appreciate the robust response from commenters and their strong views in favor of preserving the P&S certification criteria and the P&S Certification Framework. As noted above, commenters generally did not respond to our rationale for removal. Further, we were not persuaded by the comments that did respond to some of our rationale because we expect that developers would remove P&S capabilities that are redundant or could be replaced by a health care provider with a better alternative and this would be preceded by discussions with customers (
e.g.,
health care providers). However, we have reassessed our proposals in light of commenters' explanations for why we should retain some (and update) P&S certification criteria. As we stated in the Proposed Rule, we have always supported strong P&S health IT infrastructure and plan to continue to incorporate P&S capabilities into the Certification Program. The Proposed Rule did not address all potential options for revisions to the P&S certification criteria and the P&S Certification Framework. Rather, it focused primarily on a binary choice between removing all the P&S certification criteria and P&S Certification Framework (with a discrete alternative proposal focused on three P&S certification criteria) or not. We have decided not to finalize our proposal to remove any of the P&S certification criteria, the P&S Certification Framework, or the alternative proposal to retain the “auditing” certification criteria only. We will continue to consider the best regulatory approach for the P&S certification of health IT under the Certification Program in anticipation of future rulemaking. This will also provide additional time to consider comments related to alignment of the P&S certification of health IT under the Certification Program with policies and requirements of the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules. Future rulemaking may include proposing to remove all or some P&S certification criteria, updating certain P&S certification criteria, changing the P&S Certification Framework, or other options to address the concerns we have expressed in this
(
printed page 67948)
rulemaking and those concerns raised by commenters.
We also draw readers' attention to the fact that we did not include the following certification criteria in the P&S Certification Framework when we adopted the criteria: § 170.315(g)(31) “provider prior authorization API—coverage requirements discovery”; § 170.315(g)(32) “provider prior authorization API—documentation templates and rules”; § 170.315(g)(33) “provider prior authorization API—prior authorization support”; § 170.315(j)(20) “workflow triggers for decision support interventions—clients”; and § 170.315(j)(21) “subscriptions—client.” As part of any future rulemaking, we will consider whether to add them to the P&S Certification Framework if such framework is retained or revised.

WCAG
Comments.
Comments from developers of certified health IT supported removing the WCAG standard and conformance requirement. These commenters noted that the WCAG conformance requirement appears duplicative and redundant with accessibility requirements imposed elsewhere, most specifically the nondiscrimination requirements rooted in section 1557 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (“Affordable Care Act”). These commenters also emphasized that removing the outdated standard and conformance requirement would reduce certification burden and provide design flexibility.
The majority of commenters argued that we should not remove the WCAG standard and conformance requirement. These commenters asserted that certification provides explicit compliance verification and reinforces existing Federal obligations. Commenters also suggested that developers would stop including accessibility requirements and would charge more for accessibility tools. A commenter asserted that not all developers are subject to the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA) obligations. Some commenters contended that removing the conformance requirement would shift burden to health care providers. A few commenters suggested that removal of the WCAG conformance requirement would have a negating impact on patient access and usability.
Response.
We appreciate the comments submitted that supported and opposed our proposal. We recognize that the WCAG conformance requirement in the Certification Program served a function distinct from the obligations imposed by Federal civil rights laws because certification provides an evaluation of specified health IT functionality, while the other laws impose obligations on entities covered by those laws. We also considered commenters' concerns that removing the certification requirement could reduce accessibility for patients with disabilities or place greater responsibility on health care providers to evaluate the accessibility of the health IT they purchase and use. Overall, we disagree with and are not persuaded by the commenters that opposed our proposal.
As noted in the Proposed Rule, the baseline certification standard of WCAG 2.0 Level A was adopted with the 2014 Edition in 2012 and has been part of the voluntary Certification Program and specifically the VDT certification criterion since that time. The functionality is now sufficiently widespread among certified health IT and health care providers who adopt such technology. This is true because the VDT certification criterion has been part of the CEHRT definitions and specifically supports the “Provide Patients Electronic Access to their Health Information” measures under the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program and MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category since the 2014 Edition. By removing the WCAG conformance requirement (WCAG 2.0, Level A or optional Level AA), developers of health IT currently certified to § 170.315(e)(1) will likely not abandon accessibility functionality for that certified health IT. Rather, they will have the opportunity to consider other innovative ways to provide patients with accessible viewing functionality. In short, the purpose of certification under the Certification Program has been achieved in drawing attention to accessibility design and in establishing a baseline functionality for such design.
Further, as we noted in the 2011 Edition Interim Final Rule and again in response to comments on the 2011 Edition Interim Final Rule, in providing patients with access to their online health information, the accessibility requirements of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 still apply to entities covered by these Federal civil rights laws (
75 FR 2036
,
75 FR 44643
). In addition, this final rule does not alter the obligations of any entity under the ADA,
[
36
]
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act,
[
37
]
Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act,
[
38
]
or any other applicable Federal or State law.
Even if a developer of certified health IT was not covered by relevant laws as suggested by a commenter, we expect developers to include, as requested by their clients (
e.g.,
health care providers), accessibility functionality needed to support their clients' compliance with applicable laws. In response to commenters' suggestions that the removal of the WCAG conformance requirement will increase both burden and costs for health care providers, we respectfully disagree. We recognize commenters' concern that removing the WCAG conformance requirement could place greater responsibility on health care providers to evaluate the accessibility of the health IT they purchase and use for compliance with relevant laws. However, the legal obligations of health care providers under applicable disability and accessibility laws are not affected by this final rule. In addition, costs of certification to the adopted WCAG standard are likely built into the certified health IT licensed or purchased by the health care provider. Costs for such functionality are also likely to be
(
printed page 67949)
the same or less if purchased or licensed without certification.
For all these reasons, we expect health IT developers will continue to provide accessibility functionalities within their products certified to the VDT certification criterion and have finalized our proposal to remove the WCAG conformance requirement from the certification criterion (found in § 170.315(e)(1)(i)).
Comments.
A commenter encouraged ONC to consider revising the certification requirement to an attestation-based approach. Another commenter suggested that we adopt a functionally equivalent, testable accessibility baseline. Some commenters suggested further revising the criterion to withdraw the “view” requirements enumerated under sub-paragraph (i)(A) to have the flexibility to support basic “viewing” in more innovative and user-friendly formats and methods, while retaining the ability to “download” and “transmit” health information in the standardized HL7 CDA C-CDA document format for interoperability purposes. Another commenter suggested that we removed the VDT criterion completely.
Response.
These comments were outside the scope of the proposal and were not considered for finalization.
Network Time Protocol
Comments.
We received few comments on the proposal to remove the NTP conformance requirement. Those comments directly focused on the proposal offered support for removing the NTP conformance requirement. Commenters stated that aligning with a NTP standard was an established industry functionality. Commenters also noted that time synchronization is handled at the infrastructure or operating-system level; and that most environments already maintain accurate time through domain controllers or equivalent mechanisms. Commenters also expressed agreement with our assessment that certification adds little value and that developers will continue using NTP regardless of conformance requirements.
Response.
We thank commenters for their support. As noted in the Proposed Rule and supported by comments received on the Proposed Rule, the NTP functionality is not native to the EHR technology (rather part of the operating system within which the EHR technology runs) and unnecessary for certification because EHRs use of underlying operating system clocks is commonplace. Consistent with our overall goal to reduce regulatory burden, we agree that there is currently little value, and unnecessary burden, in maintaining the conformance requirement as part of certification. As noted in the Proposed Rule and confirmed by developers in comments of the Proposed Rule, we do not expect that developers will stop using NTP with their certified health IT. Rather, we expect that developers will continue to use NTPs, due to ongoing evolution in the industry. Accordingly, we have finalized our proposal to remove the NTP requirements from the VDT certification criterion.

b. Patient Health Information Capture
We proposed to remove and reserve the “patient health information capture” certification criterion in § 170.315(e)(3) with an effective date of January 1, 2027. The patient health information capture certification criterion allows health care providers to incorporate unstructured patient generated health data or data from a non-clinical setting into a patient record. The criterion is not currently included in the Base EHR definition; however, the criterion is included in the definitions of CEHRT established by CMS in
42 CFR 495.4
and
42 CFR 414.1305
for programs including the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program and the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category.
We have reviewed and evaluated the patient health information capture certification criterion in § 170.315(e)(3) and sought to identify ways to reduce burden while still supporting our policy goals. As we have stressed in prior rulemaking, we take an incremental approach to improving health IT interoperability and performance, relying on factors such as market prevalence and industry readiness to harmonize current and future standards and phase out standards and certification criteria as needed (
75 FR 2021
).
As we mentioned in the Proposed Rule, removing the patient health information capture certification criterion in § 170.315(e)(3) on January 1, 2027, would reduce administrative burden as well as burden for health IT developers of certified health IT and health care providers while still allowing us to achieve our policy goals (
90 FR 60991
and
60992
).
Comments.
Of the commenters who specifically commented on the patient health information capture proposal, they were generally evenly split on supporting or not supporting removal of the patient health information capture certification criterion (§ 170.315(e)(3)) with those in support noting that it would reduce burden by eliminating a criterion they described as widely implemented, poorly defined, or not delivering value.
Commenters not supporting removal (or recommending delay/retention) expressed concerns that removing the criterion could reduce support for incorporating patient- and caregiver-contributed information (including unstructured patient-generated health data) in certain settings, including Long Term and Post Acute Care, weaken patient engagement and accessibility, and create challenges for providers seeking to meet other program and interoperability expectations. Another commenter, who did not support the removal, recommended that we add the patient health information capture certification criterion to the Base EHR definition in § 170.102.
In particular, commenters noted that our proposal for removing the patient health information capture criterion would require additional guidance or specification of transition planning and impact evaluation (including coordination with other Federal program requirements). A commenter stated that ONC would also need to clarify how the shift toward FHIR-based APIs would support family caregiver access, including proxy access
(
printed page 67950)
mechanisms, delegation workflows, and caregiver-contributed data capture through third-party applications.
Another commenter suggested delaying the removal of the criterion until at least 2028 to support alignment with CMS requirements.
Response.
We thank commenters for their input and support of our proposal to remove the patient health information capture certification criterion. We have finalized the removal of the patient health information capture certification as proposed with an effective date of January 1, 2027. As mentioned in the Proposed Rule and supported by a number of commenters, the capabilities described in the criterion are widely implemented and used in health IT at this time, suggesting that these capabilities will remain in health IT products even if the corresponding criterion is removed from the Certification Program (
90 FR 60991
). We also noted in the Proposed Rule that removing the criterion from the Certification Program could spur greater development and innovation in this area (
90 FR 60991
). We stated that there are other certification criteria that support patient engagement, such as the “view, download, and transmit to 3rd party” and “standardized API for patient and population services” certification criteria (
90 FR 60991
). We have seen developers integrate the functionality in the patient health information capture certification criterion as part of other patient engagement features, such as patient portals. With these considerations in mind, we believe removing this criterion from the Certification Program will help reduce burden and costs, while also spurring further innovations in patient engagement (
90 FR 60991
).
Because the certification criterion in § 170.315(e)(3) is a requirement for CEHRT definitions established by CMS, we proposed to remove the patient health information capture certification criterion in § 170.315(e)(3) effective January 1, 2027 (
90 FR 60991
), and we have finalized this date for removal in this final rule. Because patient health information capture is a requirement of the CEHRT definition, and both the Medicare Promoting Interoperability program and the MIPS program are on a calendar year rulemaking cycle, it is appropriate to align changes to the certification criteria that are included in the definition of CEHRT to a calendar year cycle as well. In the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule, CMS proposed to update the definition of CEHRT in
42 CFR 495.4
to remove the cross-reference to the certification criterion in § 170.315(e)(3) (
91 FR 19620
). CMS finalized this proposal in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule, which appeared in the
Federal Register
on August 4, 2026 (
91 FR 50033
). CMS made similar proposals for the definition of CEHRT in
42 CFR 414.1305
in the 2027 Physician Fee Schedule proposed rule (
91 FR 43842
). This final action and proposed policy will (or would in the case of proposed policies) enable CMS to ensure that requirements in the definitions of CEHRT are updated to align with our final policy regarding the removal of this certification criterion. ONC will continue to coordinate with CMS to ensure alignment around changes resulting from the policies in this final rule.
We also appreciate commenters who opposed removal or recommended delaying removal based on concerns about patient- and caregiver-contributed information (including unstructured patient-generated health data) in Long Term and Post Acute Care settings, patient engagement, accessibility, and providers' ability to meet other program and interoperability expectations. We recognize the importance of enabling patients, families, caregivers, and other authorized representatives to contribute information. However, we do not believe that continued certification to § 170.315(e)(3) is necessary to preserve or advance those capabilities. The removal of the certification criterion does not prohibit health IT developers from continuing to offer these functions, does not prevent providers from using or procuring such capabilities, and does not limit the ability of health IT products to support patient- or caregiver-contributed information. Rather, removal means that this specific functionality will no longer be addressed through a certification criterion under the Certification Program. We acknowledge commenters' specific concerns regarding family caregiver access, proxy access, delegation workflows, and caregiver-contributed data capture through third-party applications. We agree that these are important use cases. However, § 170.315(e)(3) does not establish detailed requirements for proxy access, caregiver delegation, identity proofing, authorization management, or application-based caregiver contribution workflows. Retaining this criterion would therefore not, by itself, ensure that those more specific capabilities are available or implemented consistently across health IT products. We also decline to add the patient health information capture certification criterion to the Base EHR definition in § 170.102. Because we are finalizing removal of § 170.315(e)(3), adding the criterion to the Base EHR definition would be inconsistent with our determination that the availability of a certification criterion for this specific functionality is no longer necessary. The Base EHR definition reflects certification capabilities that remain necessary as a minimum foundation for certified health IT. Based on the widespread implementation of this functionality, the availability of other patient engagement and API criteria, and the burden associated with maintaining certification to § 170.315(e)(3), we do not believe this criterion should be added to the Base EHR definition. We also considered the recommendation to delay removal until at least 2028. We do not believe a further delay is necessary. The January 1, 2027, effective date allows for regulatory alignment with CMS program requirements under the CEHRT definitions while avoiding the continued burden of maintaining a certification requirement that no longer provides sufficient incremental value. Extending the criterion beyond that date would prolong certification and compliance costs for developers and providers without materially advancing patient engagement beyond what is already supported through existing product functionality, other certification criteria, and applicable Federal policies. ONC has a history of recognizing the importance of patient engagement as a core component of modern healthcare, driving improved outcomes, enhanced safety, and lower costs by leveraging technology and intends to continue doing so with future policies. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule implemented parts of section 4006(a) of the Cures Act to support patients' access to their EHI in a form convenient for patients, such as making a patient's EHI more electronically accessible through the adoption of standards and certification criteria and the implementation of information blocking policies that support patient electronic access to their health information at no cost (
85 FR 25644
). Specifically, the ONC Cures Act Final Rule supported patient access to their health information by: (1) enabling patients to securely access their EHI using smartphone applications of their choice through standardized APIs; (2) emphasizing under the information blocking “fees exception” that an actor's practice of charging for the electronic access to EHI by a patient, their personal representative, or another person or entity designated by the patient, would be inherently suspect under an information blocking review; and (3)
(
printed page 67951)
permitting actors regulated by the information blocking regulations to educate and advise individuals about privacy and security risks posed by applications they use to steward their information while also fully supporting an individual's right to choose which application(s) they want to share their EHI with—if any. The HTI-1 Final Rule further supported patients by requiring developers certified to the “view, download, and transmit to 3rd party” certification criterion to support an “internet-based method” for patients to request a restriction on the use or disclosure of their data (
89 FR 1299
). We will continue to prioritize patient and caregiver engagement and monitor future developments. ONC seeks to further the advancement of patient engagement by promoting electronic access to health data and increasing resources dedicated to curbing the practice of information blocking.

Some commenters stated that many receiving public health systems are not ready to operationalize FHIR at scale. Several commenters stated that the current CDA-based reporting approaches are still necessary and relied upon by registries and providers, and the criterion encourages developers to support cancer registry reporting functionality. Many commenters expressed support for moving toward FHIR-based solutions but stated that we should retain the current CDA-based criterion until FHIR is consistently implemented by providers and cancer registries and can be included in an updated criterion. We thank commenters for expressing these concerns regarding removing the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(4), including concerns that developers would no longer support cancer registry reporting and that standardized reporting and interoperability would be disrupted. In light of issues raised by commenters and our reconsideration of the proposal in response thereto, we have decided not to finalize the proposal to remove the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(4). However, we also agree with the multiple comments supporting movement toward FHIR-based solutions, and we have confidence in the future progression of FHIR in this space. We appreciate these comments regarding the potential for burden shifting due to the proposed removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(4). We have not finalized the proposed removal of the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(4) for the reasons noted in the response directly above.

Some commenters viewed certification to the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(4) as an important safeguard or accountability mechanism to ensure against disruption in cancer reporting.

We thank commenters for these comments expressing concern regarding a potential disruption of cancer reporting. We agree with comments regarding the importance of cancer reporting and its impact on cancer care and research. b. Transmission to Public Health Agencies—Electronic Case Reporting
We proposed to revise the “transmission to public health agencies—electronic case reporting” (eCR) certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(5). This criterion enables a user to create case reports that can be transmitted electronically to public health agencies. We proposed to revise the eCR certification criterion to be a functional requirement in order to reduce burden and allow for industry innovation. In particular, we proposed to rescind the expiration date for the functional requirements defined in § 170.315(f)(5) as of the effective date of this final rule. We proposed to revise the introductory text of the criterion to enable a user to create a case report for electronic transmission meeting the functional requirements described in paragraph (f)(5)(i) of this section. Additionally, we proposed to remove the standards-based requirements defined in § 170.315(f)(5)(ii) as of the effective date of this final rule and to reserve that section.
Comments.
The vast majority of comments, including those from health care providers, developers and public health, were not supportive of revising the eCR certification criterion to remove standards-based requirements and rely on a functional-only approach, primarily due to concerns that FHIR-based standards for eCR are still maturing and not ready as a replacement for CDA-based standards. Several commenters also stressed that many receiving public health systems were not ready for FHIR-based reporting. Some commenters recommended retaining flexibility for either CDA-based or FHIR-based standards for eCR in the short-term and moving exclusively to FHIR-based requirements only after the FHIR standard fully matures and there is sufficient implementation time to ensure that the CDC, Public Health Authorities (PHAs), and physicians have the technology and standards in place to transition to FHIR. Some commenters stressed that the current requirement provides an opportunity to use CDA-based or FHIR-based standards and to migrate as needed, thus serving as a clear glidepath to FHIR-based standards and enabling progress toward exclusively FHIR-based eCR in the future. Many commenters indicated support for FHIR-based eCR in the future but expressed concerns that
(
printed page 67953)
revising the eCR certification criterion to remove standards-based requirements prior to a FHIR-based standard being widely available would increase variability in implementations, shift burden to providers and public health agencies, and reduce the timeliness, completeness, and reliability of public health reporting.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns regarding revising the eCR certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(5) to be a functional requirement prior to having a mature FHIR-based standard widely available. We recognize that there is still a significant amount of reliance on CDA-based standards for eCR as well as limited adoption of FHIR-based standards for eCR on both the sending and receiving ends of transactions. Having considered the points raised by commenters, we have decided not to finalize the proposal to revise the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(5) to be a functional requirement. However, we also have confidence in the future progression of FHIR in this space and agree with commenters that retaining the ability to certify to either CDA-based standards or FHIR-based standards for eCR in the meantime can provide a helpful glidepath and encourage progress toward a fully FHIR-based future.
Comments.
A number of commenters expressed concerns about removing standards in the eCR criterion and making it a functional criterion. Several commenters stressed that a functional-only approach would undermine interoperability, consistency, and predictability. Some stressed that the shift to functional requirements could degrade data quality, integrity, completeness, timeliness, reliability, usability, and comparability. Some commenters stated that a functional requirement could result in increased integration burdens on downstream systems such as public health agencies. Some commenters stated that the proposal would disrupt significant progress that has been made through standards-based eCR adoption. These commenters stated that standards-based eCR adoption has steadily increased and has reduced burden on both public health and healthcare organizations to meet reporting requirements. Another commenter stated that removal of standards-based requirements may result in fragmented and jurisdiction-specific reporting. Some commenters stressed that standards are needed to prevent inconsistencies and variability that would undermine public health efforts, including outbreak response and real-time surveillance, and require burdensome workarounds. Several commenters noted specific benefits of the eCR criterion, including detecting and responding to communicable diseases impacting the population. Another commenter stated that having the eCR criterion as part of CEHRT has been vital to advancing eCR and that if it becomes a functional requirement only, PHAs would have the burden of processing non-standardized formats and providers may revert to fax-based reporting, eroding efficiency and reversing progress.
Response.
We appreciate the concerns expressed by commenters regarding removal of standards in the eCR criterion and instead relying on functional requirements, including concerns that it would result in fragmentation and variability that would impede public health efforts and increase burden. While functional requirements are appropriate in some instances, we recognize that may not be the case where there is ongoing modernization of standards. We agree with commenters that the current criterion requirements, which allow the use of either CDA-based standards or FHIR-based standards for eCR, have been successful in moving eCR forward to date and that retaining them for the time being can help ensure continued progress. We have not finalized the proposal to revise the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(5) to be a functional requirement. We will continue to monitor advancements in the use of FHIR-based standards for eCR.
Comments.
A number of commenters expressed concerns that the proposal would reduce public health situational awareness, create public health operations issues, and weaken emergency preparedness, including disease surveillance and outbreak detection and response.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns, and we understand the importance of not impeding vital public health operations. We have not finalized the proposal to revise the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(5) to be a functional requirement.
Comments.
A number of commenters expressed concern about burden. Some commenters stated that burden would move from certification and developers to providers, public health agencies, and governments. Some commenters stressed that small, rural and under-resourced providers would be particularly impacted by increased burden. In addition, some commenters stated that public health agencies lacked the infrastructure, workforce, funding, or governance capacity to transition to FHIR. Some commenters stated that the proposal will shift the burden of assessing health IT functionality and standards adoption away from ONC to the users of health IT, imposing additional burden on individuals, governments, and healthcare organizations as they evaluate and select health IT to purchase and implement. Several commenters characterized the proposal as an unfunded mandate.
Response.
We appreciate these commenter concerns regarding burden. We understand that for many under-resourced settings moving toward FHIR-based standards for eCR could be burdensome. We have not finalized the proposal to revise the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(5) to be a functional requirement and are retaining the current criterion requirements, which require the use of either CDA-based standards or FHIR-based standards for certification to the eCR criterion. This addresses commenter concerns about burden and, as stated above, provides a helpful glidepath toward more ubiquitous FHIR-based eCR in the future.
Comments.
Several commenters stated that developers who already invested in the current standards-based options in § 170.315(f)(5)(ii) would be penalized. Another commenter was concerned that all developers were required to comply with paragraph § 170.315(f)(5)(ii) by February 28, 2026, and that developers would now be required to revert back to meeting the requirements of § 170.315(f)(5)(i). c. Transmission to Public Health Agencies—Antimicrobial Use and Resistance Reporting
We proposed to revise the “transmission to public health agencies—antimicrobial use and resistance reporting” certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(6). This criterion assesses whether Health IT Modules can create and properly format an antimicrobial use and resistance report for electronic transmission, following specified sections of a CDA-based implementation guide. We proposed to revise the criterion requirements to be functional only and proposed to remove the reference to the standard in § 170.205(r)(1) as of the effective date of this final rule.
Comments.
The majority of commenters were not supportive of revising the transmission to public health agencies—antimicrobial use and resistance reporting certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(6) to remove referenced standards and rely on a functional requirement, often due to concerns that FHIR was not fully mature or widely adopted. Several commenters stated that receiving public health agencies were not ready for full FHIR-based reporting, and some stated that the existing CDA-based standards for reporting to public health have been adopted in a number of settings and are important for continuity. Some commenters expressed concerns about timing due to lack of FHIR readiness and did not support revising the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(6) to remove the referenced CDA-based standard until a FHIR-based replacement was operationally ready. Another commenter supported an effective date no earlier than January 1, 2029, for any changes to the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(6) and for removal of the CDA-based public health-related certification criteria and adoption of FHIR-based approaches to reporting. Commenters had concerns that without a FHIR-based replacement available, removal of the referenced standard in § 170.315(f)(6) would reduce standardization, increase variability, shift burden and costs to providers and public health agencies, and disrupt public health reporting and surveillance.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns regarding FHIR readiness and removing the CDA-based standards from the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(6). We recognize that for certain public health use cases CDA-based standards are widely used for public health reporting and FHIR-based standards are still in development. However, antimicrobial use and resistance reporting is made to the CDC's National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN), and the CDA-based standard referenced in § 170.315(f)(6) is currently not aligned with NHSN requirements. Additional rulemaking to address this misalignment would likely require several years to complete, and we believe that lack of alignment with NHSN requirements will undermine the effectiveness of the certification criterion in § 170.315(f)(6) until such steps can be completed. As we noted in the Proposed Rule, the CDC is working to move reporting to FHIR-based standards
[
43
]
and has already implemented a more recent version of the CDA-IG. Further, we identified trends within the industry regarding a shift in reporting approach that supports revision of this criterion (
90 FR 60993
).

Accordingly, we have adopted our revisions as proposed. We will continue to monitor the development of FHIR-based standards in this area as they mature.

s. Several commenters requested that ONC provide a clearer transition path toward FHIR-based reporting, and another commenter who supported the proposal suggested ongoing monitoring and implementation guardrails as reporting transitions from the C-CDA standards required in the criterion.
