c. Safety-Enhanced Design
In the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60995
), we proposed to remove the “safety-enhanced design” (SED) certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(3) and the reference to this certification criterion in § 170.550(g)(1) as of the effective date of this final rule. The safety-enhanced design certification criterion specifies the user-centered design testing that must be applied to certain health IT capabilities submitted for certification. Certification to this certification criterion is conditional as its scope and applicability depends on the other certification criteria for which a Health IT Module is presented for certification.
As discussed in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60995
and
60996
), we anticipated that removal of this certification criterion would reduce costs and burden for health IT developers and health care providers.
Comments.
The majority of commenters were not supportive of removing the SED certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(3). These commenters stated that the SED certification criterion remains an important patient safety, usability, and human factors engineering safeguard and expressed concerns that removal of this certification criterion would weaken a baseline certification expectation for user-centered design, increase the risk of technology-induced errors, promote inefficiency and inconsistency, and shift responsibility for identifying and mitigating such risks to providers and purchasers. Some commenters noted that if safety verification became the responsibility of providers and purchasers, then smaller, rural, or low-resource practices would incur the most burden, as they may have limited technical resources and expertise to independently evaluate the safety and security of their software systems.
A few commenters who opposed removal of the SED certification criterion expressed concerns that removal may cause health IT developers to revert to engineering-centric interfaces or reduce incentives to prioritize the clinician-user experience and could create a scenario where provider organizations are charged for design techniques that were previously included in health IT products. A few other commenters stated that removal of § 170.315(g)(3) could create an unlevel playing field between established developers and new market entrants, particularly if new entrants are not held to comparable usability and safety expectations. Some commenters who opposed removal also noted that safety-enhanced design and usability testing
(
printed page 67959)
may become more important as SI-enabled functionality is incorporated into certified health IT and recommended that safety validation approaches evolve rather than be eliminated.
Some of the commenters who recommended retaining the certification criterion emphasized that the SED certification criterion, and related usability requirements, were originally implemented in response to real-world patient safety incidents and that the certification criterion continues to serve as an important safeguard against technology-induced harm. Another commenter expressed concerns that removal without first putting critical safeguards in place could result in unsafe practices and billing fraud.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback. We have not finalized our proposal to remove the SED certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(3) or the reference to this certification criterion in § 170.550(g)(1). Instead, we have finalized § 170.315(g)(3) with revisions, as of the effective date of this final rule. Specifically, we have finalized the revision of § 170.315(g)(3) to an attestation-based certification requirement by removing the requirements in § 170.315(g)(3)(ii), (iv), and (v), making conforming revisions to paragraph (g)(3), and retaining the reference to § 170.315(g)(3) in § 170.550(g)(1).
We acknowledge comments that recommended we retain § 170.315(g)(3) and stated that removal of the SED certification criterion would not be appropriate without a clearly defined replacement mechanism that preserves baseline expectations for user-centered design and safety validation. We also recognize commenters' statements that the SED certification criterion, and related usability requirements, were implemented in response to real-world patient safety incidents and that the certification criterion continues to serve as an important safeguard against technology-induced harm. We agree with these commenters that § 170.315(g)(3) continues to serve an important safety function in the Certification Program by maintaining baseline assurance that developers of certified health IT apply user-centered design processes to certain health IT capabilities.
In the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60995
), we proposed to remove the SED certification criterion to reduce costs and burden associated with certification for health IT developers and health care providers. Specifically, we identified the testing and reporting requirements associated with certification to § 170.315(g)(3) as contributing to health IT developers' burden and stated that removal of the SED certification criterion could allow health IT developers to redirect time and resources toward more innovative approaches to support and improve safety-enhanced design in their products (
90 FR 60996
). In consideration of commenters' explanations for why we should retain the SED certification criterion, we reassessed whether our proposal to completely remove the criterion is necessary to achieve our objective of reducing costs and burden. We determined that revising § 170.315(g)(3) to establish an attestation-based certification requirement addresses these considerations by reducing the testing and reporting requirements associated with certification while retaining the certification expectation for the application of user-centered design practices to certain certified health IT capabilities.
Comments.
Some commenters recommended that if the SED certification criterion was removed, we should adopt alternative mechanisms to support continued usability and safety oversight. A commenter suggested prioritizing the use of post-market data to identify usability failures. A few other commenters recommended that we provide explicit transition guidance for products currently certified to § 170.315(g)(3) to ensure continuity of safety expectations and avoid gaps during any transition. Another commenter recommended that we provide a model risk assessment framework, particularly tailored to rural and low-resource providers, to support evaluation of health IT usability and safety in the absence of this certification requirement.
Response.
We acknowledge commenters who recommended alternatives to our proposal, including prioritizing the use of post-market data to identify usability failures, providing explicit transition guidance, and offering additional tools to support providers in evaluating usability and safety. While we have not adopted these suggested alternatives in this final rule, the revisions that we have finalized to § 170.315(g)(3) take into consideration comments that urged us to continue to support usability and safety oversight certification requirements rather than eliminate them completely.
Comments.
A smaller number of commenters expressed support for removing or streamlining the SED certification criterion. Of the commenters who supported removal of § 170.315(g)(3), most stated that current summative usability testing and related documentation requirements are costly and administratively burdensome, have limited practical value, and divert resources from formative usability testing and other product improvement activities. Additionally, commenters who supported removal of this certification criterion agreed that there is widespread market adoption of safety-enhanced design practices. Other commenters recommended that, rather than remove the certification criterion, we should retain and modernize or streamline it. These recommendations included adopting a lean form of SED by narrowing requirements, focusing on higher-risk workflows, adopting a lighter-weight attestation-based approach, reducing prescriptive reporting, and aligning with recognized usability engineering frameworks such as those defined by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). Many of these commenters stated that formative usability testing conducted during development is more effective than the required summative testing model and that removing the current certification requirements would allow resources to be redirected toward more impactful usability practices. Another commenter specified that conducting user-centered design testing after development practices limits the ability to incorporate findings into products and that clients rarely access or use the detailed reports required by the SED certification criterion. Another commenter stated that safety-enhanced design features should be decided by markets.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback and perspectives on how safety-enhanced design continues to play an important role in supporting safe and effective use of certified health IT but that current summative usability testing and related documentation requirements are costly and administratively burdensome. As discussed above, we have finalized revisions to § 170.315(g)(3) that reduce prescriptive testing and reporting requirements while retaining a meaningful certification expectation for user-centered design. This approach is intended to balance the need to maintain baseline safety and usability expectations with the goal of reducing unnecessary burden and allowing health IT developers to redirect time and resources towards more innovative approaches to support and improve safety-enhanced design in their products. We refer readers to section VII
(
printed page 67960)
(Regulatory Impact Analysis) of this final rule for more detailed information on cost estimates of safety-enhanced design and estimated cost savings.
We have determined that the current reporting requirements for the SED certification criterion can be reduced to an attestation-based approach that retains a meaningful certification expectation for SED. Therefore, we have finalized the SED certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(3) to an attestation-based certification requirement by removing the requirements in § 170.315(g)(3)(ii), (iv), and (v), making conforming revisions to paragraph (g)(3), and retaining the reference to § 170.315(g)(3) in § 170.550(g)(1). All revisions to the SED certification criterion are effective as of the effective date of this final rule.
d. Quality Management System
In the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60996
), we proposed to remove the “quality management system” (QMS) certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(4) and the reference to this certification criterion in § 170.550(g)(2), as of the effective date of this final rule. The QMS certification criterion states for each capability that a technology includes and for which that capability's certification is sought, the use of a QMS in the development, testing, implementation, and maintenance of that capability must be identified and satisfied in one of the following ways: either the QMS used is established by the Federal Government or a standards development organization (SDO) or the QMS used is mapped to one or more QMS established by the Federal Government or an SDO. Per § 170.550(g), this certification criterion is mandatory for all certified Health IT Modules.
As discussed in the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60996
), we proposed to remove this certification criterion because industry and other interested parties now widely implement quality management principles in comparison to when this certification criterion was initially adopted. We determined as a result, that the certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(4), and the related requirement that all Health IT Modules be certified to it, have become duplicative.
Comments.
The majority of commenters were not supportive of removing the QMS certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(4). These commenters expressed concerns that removal would weaken baseline safety, quality, and reliability expectations for certified health IT and shift verification responsibilities from developers to providers and purchasers. Many of these commenters also expressed concerns that removal of the certification criterion could reduce assurances for quality practices, increase the likelihood that immature products enter clinical and operational workflows, and result in inconsistent adoption of quality management practices, including by new market entrants.
Some commenters also noted that removal of this certification criterion could introduce new challenges in evaluating health IT developer safety practices and managing risk, particularly for rural or low-resourced providers with limited technical resources and expertise to independently evaluate the safety, security, and quality of their software systems. Some commenters who opposed removal of the QMS certification criterion recommended that, if the criterion was removed, we provide additional guidance on a replacement approach and how safety, quality, and reliability expectations would be maintained through modernization efforts, including API-based ecosystems and other programmatic mechanisms. Several of these commenters also recommended adopting post-certification oversight and transparency mechanisms to assess the impact of removing this certification requirement and to offer providers information about developers' capabilities and associated costs.
A small number of commenters supported removing the certification criterion or expressed a neutral view, stating that the requirement can be seen as duplicative since many developers already maintain quality management system practices as part of routine operations.
We received mixed comments regarding the level of burden associated with the QMS certification criterion and whether removal of the criterion would meaningfully reduce burden. As noted above, a few commenters who expressed a neutral view or supported removal of this certification criterion stated that many mature development organizations would continue to maintain quality management practices and follow the ISO industry standard regardless of certification requirements. Other commenters noted that the current QMS certification criterion was burdensome for developers and system administrators and recommended that we should modernize or streamline the requirement rather than remove it.
Response.
We thank commenters for their thoughtful feedback. We have not finalized our proposal to remove the quality management system certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(4) or the corresponding reference in § 170.550(g)(2).
After considering the comments we received, we believe § 170.315(g)(4) continues to serve an important function in the Certification Program by providing a consistent baseline assurance that developers of certified health IT identify and use a quality management system in the development, testing, implementation, and maintenance of certified health IT capabilities. We recognize that many developers of certified health IT already maintain quality management principles and processes as part of routine operations. However, we believe that maintaining a baseline certification requirement at this time is important to ensure continuity of safety and quality practices and to promote consistent expectations across the market, including for new entrants. We recognize that quality management expectations may continue to evolve as part of broader health IT modernization efforts and that the QMS certification criterion continues to support providers and purchasers that rely on certification as a meaningful signal of developer quality management practices. Our decision to retain § 170.315(g)(4) also supports consistency with the Certification Program's broader approach to transparency and public reporting regarding the quality management processes used by developers for certified health IT.
Comments.
Some commenters who opposed removal of the QMS certification criterion expressed concerns about coordination with CMS program timelines and recommended delaying removal of the certification criterion to align with CMS program requirements and reduce potential provider compliance risks.
Response.
We acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding coordination with CMS program timelines and related provider compliance activities. However, while the QMS certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(4) impacts certified health IT used by health care providers for compliance with CMS programs, we are not aware of any direct requirements for adoption or use of certified health IT certified to the QMS certification criterion. For instance, with respect to the Promoting Interoperability program and the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, CMS has not specified the criterion in § 170.315(g)(4) as required to support any of the current measures in the program as part of the definitions of CEHRT in
42 CFR 495.4
or
42 CFR 414.1305
. Our decision not to finalize
(
printed page 67961)
removal of § 170.315(g)(4) is not based on CMS program dependency, but rather that this certification criterion continues to serve an important role within the Certification Program as a baseline quality management and assurance expectation, as well as to support transparency and maintain consistent adoption of QMS practices over time. Therefore, we have not finalized our proposal to remove the quality management system certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(4) or the corresponding reference in § 170.550(g)(2).
e. Accessibility-Centered Design
In the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60997
), we proposed to remove the “accessibility-centered design” (ACD) certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(5) and the corresponding reference to this certification criterion in § 170.550(g)(3) as of the effective date of this final rule. This certification criterion requires that all developers of Health IT Modules identify and use a health IT accessibility-centered design standard or law in the development, testing, implementation, and maintenance of each capability for which certification is sought. We stated that, if finalized, removal of this certification criterion would not exempt health IT developers and providers from their independent obligations under applicable Federal civil rights laws, including Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Comments.
Most commenters were not supportive of the removal of the ACD certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(5). These commenters expressed concerns that removal of this certification criterion could reduce accessibility and equitable access to certified health IT for individuals with disabilities and weaken a measurable certification baseline for accountability. One of these commenters emphasized that accessibility is not static and requires ongoing monitoring, updates, and testing as platforms evolve. Another commenter remarked that the impact of this certification criterion has not diminished and stated that there is no guarantee that health IT developers will ensure accessibility-centered design practices continue if the ACD certification criterion is removed.
Many commenters who opposed our proposal also expressed concerns that removal of the ACD certification criterion could reduce transparency and incentives to maintain accessibility-centered design practices, leading to uneven adoption, particularly among new market entrants, and widening gaps in digital participation. A few commenters also emphasized that accessibility-centered design requirements support standardized, interoperable access to health information and expressed concern that removal of this certification criterion could undermine accessibility in API-based and SI-enabled environments. Multiple commenters cautioned that reducing accessibility and usability requirements could increase the risk of inefficient workflows and could lead to an increase in clinician workload and cognitive burden. Many of these commenters expressed concerns that removal of § 170.315(g)(5) would shift costs, usability barriers, and responsibility for ensuring accessibility to providers, patients, and caregivers, including the potential for developers to charge additional fees for accessibility features previously included as part of certified health IT. Some commenters recommended that, if we were to remove § 170.315(g)(5), we should adopt a replacement accountability mechanism and provide transition guidance.
Several commenters who opposed removal of this certification criterion stated that applicable Federal civil rights laws do not serve the same function or provide the same measurable accountability as a Certification Program requirement. A few other commenters argued that removing the ACD certification criterion would not meaningfully reduce burden because some developers would maintain accessibility practices regardless of the certification requirement.
Response.
We thank commenters for their thoughtful feedback. We have not finalized our proposal to remove the ACD certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(5) or the corresponding reference in § 170.550(g)(3).
We continue to recognize that accessibility-centered design practices are broadly used across industry. However, we determined that this widespread use of accessibility-centered design practices supports retaining, rather than removing, the ACD certification criterion at this time. We have concluded that § 170.315(g)(5) continues to serve an important function in the Certification Program by maintaining a transparent, measurable baseline regarding the use of accessibility-centered design standards or laws by developers for certified health IT capabilities. We also believe that accessibility is not static and that continued certification transparency and accountability remain important.
The requirements in § 170.315(g)(5) support consistency with the Certification Program's broader approach to transparency and public reporting regarding the accessibility-centered design standards or laws used in the development of certified health IT. Additionally, retaining § 170.315(g)(5) helps to reduce the risk of uneven adoption or maintenance of accessibility-centered design practices over time, including among new market entrants. Therefore, we have not finalized our proposal to remove the ACD certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(5) or the corresponding reference in § 170.550(g)(3).
Comments.
A small number of commenters expressed support for or did not object to the removal of this certification criterion. Most of these commenters stated that this certification requirement is redundant given that accessibility requirements continue to apply under applicable Federal civil rights laws. Additionally, these commenters noted that removal of an attestation-based certification criterion would not meaningfully reduce burden or impact the Certification Program and that the current certification criterion is overly broad or limited in practical utility. A commenter noted that removal of the ACD certification criterion is a simplification measure for the Certification Program. Another commenter stated that accessibility-centered design features should be decided by markets. Several commenters recommended, if § 170.315(g)(5) was removed, that we explicitly clarify in the subsequent final rule that accessibility expectations for developers and healthcare organizations would remain subject to Federal civil rights laws.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback and continue to believe that § 170.315(g)(5) plays an important role in the Certification Program by providing a transparent and measurable baseline for how health IT developers apply accessibility-centered design standards or laws to certified health IT capabilities. We have not finalized our proposal to remove the ACD certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(5) or the corresponding reference in § 170.550(g)(3).
f. Consolidated CDA Creation Performance
In the Proposed Rule (
90 FR 60997
), we proposed to remove and reserve the “Consolidated CDA creation performance” certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(6). We also proposed to remove § 170.550(g)(4) which references the certification criterion. We stated that
(
printed page 67962)
the certification criterion helps to ensure the proper conformance of Consolidated CDAs (C-CDAs) for transition of care and referral summaries that are sent to and received from external organizations, and that while C-CDA-based standards are still in use, the industry is shifting toward adoption of FHIR-based standards, which are designed to enable greater interoperability and innovation. We stated that we believe that maintaining the current level of support for this and other C-CDA-based criteria, including putting effort and resources toward testing and certification, can detract from industry efforts to move toward FHIR-based solutions, and that removing the certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(6) would contribute to reducing the effort health IT developers and health care providers are focusing on C-CDA support and allow for redirection of efforts toward greater use of FHIR-based standards in health IT. We proposed to remove the Consolidated CDA creation performance certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(6) as of the effective date of this final rule.
Comments.
Of the commenters that specifically commented on this proposal, the majority of commenters were not supportive of removing the Consolidated CDA creation performance certification criterion, primarily because they believed that FHIR-based alternatives were not yet mature, finalized, or adopted at scale and that no equivalent FHIR-based replacement had been clearly identified, adopted, or deployed. Many commenters stressed that the current exchange environment remains hybrid, and C-CDA-based document exchange is still foundational, predominant, or widely used, particularly in under-resourced settings. Multiple commenters noted specific use cases that depend on C-CDA-based document exchange, including Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set (HEDIS), risk adjustment, care management, clinical registries and quality measurement, referrals, transitions of care, longitudinal aggregation, encounter notifications, public health, legacy EHR interoperability, patient event notifications, and certain legal documentation. Several commenters stated that C-CDA-based document exchange is better for patients, caregivers, and complete record sharing. Some commenters stressed that C-CDA-based document exchange helps bridge the transition to FHIR by supporting hybrid exchange, mappings, and longitudinal records. A number of commenters were concerned that removal of C-CDA-based requirements before a FHIR alternative was in place would create a gap and impact interoperability as well as reduce data quality, consistency, predictability, and usability. Several comments warned that removal of C-CDA-based requirements before FHIR-based alternatives are mature and widely adopted could lead to fragmented workflows and increased costs or data exchange burdens for providers.
Response.
We thank commenters for these comments regarding FHIR readiness and the removal of the current C-CDA-based certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(6) prior to having a FHIR alternative in place. We appreciate the concerns expressed by commenters that C-CDA-based document exchange is widely used and there is not a mature FHIR-based alternative available at this time. However, we note that the Consolidated CDA creation performance certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(6) has been a conditional, secondary C-CDA implementation requirement applied to health IT for which certification to a primary C-CDA-based certification criterion is sought. For instance, the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1) includes C-CDA-based requirements, and each product presented for certification to § 170.315(b)(1) would also need to be certified to § 170.315(g)(6) per its additional conformance requirements. It was this second layer of burden we proposed to remove, and we are finalizing the removal of § 170.315(g)(6). Additionally, as discussed earlier in section III.A.2.a, we have extended the timeline for removing the C-CDA-based standards requirements in § 170.315(b)(1) until January 1, 2030. We believe this addresses commenter concerns regarding the immediate removal of C-CDA-based standards requirements from the Certification Program without a viable FHIR alternative. As stated in section III.A.2.a, we explain that significant advances are occurring in the development and adoption of FHIR-based standards, and we anticipate substantial progress by January 1, 2030. Therefore, we do not believe it is necessary to retain this additional C-CDA-based certification requirement in § 170.315(g)(6) in order to ensure an appropriate transition from C-CDA-based standards to FHIR-based standards in the Certification Program. As such, we have finalized the proposal to remove the Consolidated CDA creation performance criterion in § 170.315(g)(6) as of the effective date of this final rule. We have also finalized the proposal to remove § 170.550(g)(4) as discussed in more detail in section III.E.2.
Comments.
Several commenters expressed concerns about patient safety, including concerns that removal of the certification criterion could disrupt continuity of care, care coordination, patient safety, or patient outcomes. Some commenters noted that certification to the criterion in § 170.315(g)(6) is an important safeguard, accountability mechanism, and testing floor.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns about patient safety, and we appreciate the importance of ensuring that health information is exchanged reliably during transitions of care and in referral summaries. However, as already noted, the certification criterion in § 170.315(g)(6) is not the only certification criterion in the Certification Program that requires use of C-CDA-based standards and that helps ensure reliable data exchange during transitions of care. As discussed in section III.A.2.a, we have extended the deadline for removal of C-CDA-based requirements in the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1). We believe this extension will provide enough time for certified health IT to move from C-CDA-based standards to FHIR-based standards without sacrificing patient safety. In addition, we reiterate that the removal of the certification criterion does not necessitate removal of the functionality from health IT systems for users who may have these functions implemented, nor does it prohibit continued use of the referenced standards in existing and new health IT implementation.
Comments.
A number of commenters expressed concerns about additional burden that the proposal could place on providers, stating that the removal of C-CDA-based exchange requirements could increase manual workflows, reconciliation, quality assurance, testing, normalization, and other administrative burden. Some commented that the proposal could disproportionately burden smaller, rural, safety-net, tribal, post-acute, behavioral health, and similar under-resourced settings. Another commenter stated that the proposal would not reduce developer burden because developers would still need to maintain C-CDA support for the foreseeable future.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns about burden, and in particular burden on under-resourced providers and settings. We
(
printed page 67963)
appreciate the importance of not imposing additional burden on providers by removing requirements related to C-CDA-based exchange. Again, it is important to understand the context associated with this specific certification criterion, which is secondarily applied to health IT certified to a C-CDA referencing criterion. C-CDA IGs have become more rigorous and less ambiguous, and existing test tools and industry experience with C-CDA is far greater now than when this certification criterion was first introduced. Thus, we believe that the continued need for this certification criterion in the Certification Program has concluded. Regarding the comment about the burden reducing impact of this proposal, we believe that even if a developer maintains C-CDA support, removal of this certification criterion would reduce maintenance efforts for developers, including effort and resources that would be put toward testing and certification to this criterion if the criterion remained part of the Certification Program.

Some commenters expressed disagreement with the general rationale that health IT developers would continue to support C-CDA-based exchange after removal of C-CDA-based exchange requirements in the Certification Program. These commenters were concerned that removal might result in developers charging extra for C-CDA-based exchange functionality once that functionality is no longer part of the certification requirements, and several commenters were concerned that fees to maintain C-CDA-based exchange would harm under-resourced providers and settings. Some commenters had concerns that new entrants to the market might omit core capabilities, implement them inconsistently, use proprietary alternatives, or lack the real-world knowledge needed to support C-CDA-based exchange.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing these concerns about developers, and in particular new entrants to the market, not providing support for C-CDA-based exchange. We appreciate the importance of ensuring that support for this functionality is continued during a transition to FHIR-based exchange, especially for under-resourced providers and settings. As stated above, other certification criteria in the Certification Program also require use of C-CDA-based standards for exchange and can help ensure support during a transition from C-CDA-based exchange to FHIR-based exchange. We have extended the deadline for removal of C-CDA-based requirements in the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1) until January 1, 2030. We believe this extension will provide enough time for certified health IT to move from C-CDA-based standards to FHIR-based standards without providers being subject to increased fees or reduced developer support for C-CDA-based exchange during the transition. As noted above, we reiterate that removing this certification criterion neither requires removal of the functionality from existing implementations nor prohibits continued use of the referenced standards in new or existing health IT.

As discussed in section III.A.2.a, we have finalized an extension of the deadline for removal of C-CDA-based requirements in the transitions of care certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1). We believe this extension provides a clear and workable timeline for certified health IT to move from C-CDA-based standards to FHIR-based standards. We note that we provide guidance and resources on all Certification Program requirements on our website at
healthit.gov
and anticipate that future guidance materials and resources will continue to focus as needed on transitioning from C-CDA-based exchange to FHIR-based exchange.

B. Standards and Implementation Specifications for Health Information Technology
1. Standards and Implementation Specifications
As discussed in the Proposed Rule, we proposed to remove or revise certain certification criteria in the Certification Program in an effort to reduce burden, offer flexibility to both developers and health care providers, as well as to support innovation. Included in certain certification criteria are references to standards. In those instances where we proposed to remove the criterion, we also generally proposed to remove the standard that is referenced from the CFR. Where the certification criterion is not removed as of the effective date of this final rule but allows time for transition until January 1, 2027, we generally proposed to also remove those referenced standards on January 1, 2027. Only in limited circumstances do we retain a standard that is referenced in a certification criterion proposed for removal. We also specifically requested comment on whether we should retain any of the standards and implementation specifications proposed for removal because the standard or implementation specification should be required for purposes of health IT alignment, for instance, when acquiring, implementing or upgrading health IT systems and products consistent with sections 13111 and 13112 of the HITECH Act. In certain instances, we did not propose to remove a standard even though we proposed to remove the certification criterion where the standard is referenced. As noted, under section 3004 of the PHSA, we may adopt standards independently of associated criteria in the Certification Program. Standards adopted in
45 CFR 170 subpart B
may be referenced by other HHS programs and policies besides the Certification Program. For example, standards adopted in
45 CFR 170 subpart B
, regardless of whether they are associated with health IT certification criteria, are also required for use under sections 13111 and 13112 of the HITECH Act when acquiring, implementing or upgrading health IT systems and products in certain instances.
We did not propose to remove the standard in § 170.205(o), data segmentation for privacy, because some developers still rely on these standards, which allow health care providers to tag healthcare documents with privacy metadata. We also did not propose to remove the Direct Project transport standard in § 170.202(a)(2) since we realize that the Direct Project standards are widely utilized in various use cases and emphasized that developers may still use these standards even if they are removed from certification criteria.
We proposed a minor revision to § 170.205(d)(2) to add the full name of the HL7 Messaging Standard Version 2.5.1 standard. Lastly, we requested comments on retaining the “Applicability Statement for Secure Health Transport” requirement found in § 170.315(h)(1)(i).

We thank commenters for their feedback on the proposed
(

compliance and transition dates. Comments.
The majority of commenters supported our proposed conforming edits and streamlining of the API Conditions and Maintenance of Certification requirements, stating that they would have the benefit of reducing unnecessary burden while focusing on currently relevant, standards-based APIs and a limited set of meaningful interoperability signals.

Response.
We thank commenters for their support of our proposals to make conforming revisions in § 170.404. We also appreciate the concerns raised by commenters regarding continued API transparency, availability, documentation, and accountability. The revisions we have finalized in § 170.404 remove expired transition provisions and obsolete cross-references; they do not reduce or otherwise alter the substantive requirements in § 170.404(a) or the continuing Maintenance of Certification requirements in § 170.404(b)(1) and (2).
We disagree with the commenter who urged us not to retain the public service base URL publication requirement. We did not propose to eliminate the requirement in § 170.404(b)(2). We recognize that publication of service base URLs and related organization details may reveal customer relationships and permit inferences about a developer's market presence. Nevertheless, public endpoint information enables patients and applications to identify the appropriate deployed API and connect without special effort. The requirement is limited to the service base URLs and related organization details specified in § 170.404(b)(2). The patient access, transparency, and interoperability benefits of endpoint publication outweigh the competitive concerns identified by the commenter, and we, therefore, retain the requirement.
We also disagree that the conforming revision to the definition of “Certified API technology” in § 170.404(c) eliminates or requires discontinuation of the functionality associated with former § 170.315(g)(7) and (g)(9). The revision aligns the definition with the certification criteria that remain in the CFR; it does not independently remove functionality. We agree with the commenter that stated that third-party application developers should not face practices that impermissibly impede access to or use of certified API technology. We disagree, however, that the conforming revisions finalized in § 170.404 weaken the API Condition and Maintenance of Certification requirements in practice.
Accordingly, we have finalized these proposals as proposed. Because the transition dates in § 170.404(b)(2), (3), and (4) have passed, we have finalized a revision to the Maintenance of Certification requirements in § 170.404(b). We have finalized a revision in § 170.404(b)(2) to remove the date, and we have finalized the removal of paragraphs (b)(3) and (b)(4) entirely as they are outdated and, in the case of (b)(4) because it refers to certification criteria that we have removed. We also finalized a revision in § 170.404(c) to update certification criteria referenced in the “Certified API technology” definition. We have finalized the removal of the reference to “§ 170.315(g)(7) through” and only keep the reference to § 170.315(g)(10) in the “Certified API technology” definition because we have finalized the removal of § 170.315(g)(7) through (9).

Removal of RWT Plan Submission and Reduced RWT Results Reporting
Comments.
Several commenters supported our proposal to remove the RWT plan submissions and reduce RWT results reporting, particularly by narrowing reporting obligations to FHIR-based API criteria. These commenters generally argued that the current RWT framework imposes significant administrative and compliance burdens while providing limited practical value. Commenters described the annual testing plans as largely formulistic endeavors that consume resources without meaningfully improving interoperability outcomes. These commenters also emphasized that focusing RWT oversight on key API certification criteria—such as § 170.315(g)(10) and the “prior authorization” API criteria—better aligns with ONC's “FHIR-forward” strategy and concentrates on the interoperability functions most critical to real-world EHI exchange.
A majority of commenters opposed our proposal to remove the RWT plan submissions and reduce RWT results reporting. Commenters asserted that our proposals would weaken developer accountability, interoperability assurance, and patient safety protections (
e.g.
, identifying missing meds, incomplete data). Commenters stressed that publicly available RWT plans and results provide important transparency for healthcare organizations making purchasing and implementation decisions and help smaller providers, rural organizations, and public health agencies assess whether products will function effectively. Commenters argued that reducing RWT reporting to API criteria was premature because there is not yet a fully mature and stable FHIR-based ecosystem. Commenters also argued that the proposed approach could leave important interoperability gaps undetected, such as with public health reporting.
Response.
We thank commenters for expressing both their supporting and opposing viewpoints. We have finalized the removal of the RWT plan requirement and the reduced RWT results reporting as proposed. We agree with commenters who stated that the previously codified RWT plans and results reporting requirements created significant burden without meaningful results. An API-focused approach will align with our overall strategy for the Certification Program and support interoperability. Considering the
(
printed page 67971)
planned API and FHIR-forward future approach for the Certification Program, we believe that future results reporting will provide the transparency and interoperability assurance advocated for by commenters. For example, as we propose, and should we adopt, more API and FHIR-based certification criteria,
[
49
]
we anticipate that there would continue to be RWT results reporting for those criteria that can provide insights into the interoperability of certified health IT.
While we appreciate commenters' statements that RWT results may be used to inform decisions regarding the purchasing and licensing certified health IT, we believe that, based on our interactions with health care providers and their executives, it is only one of a multitude of factors that they consider. Further, we believe that the current RWT results reporting and anticipated future RWT results reporting related to APIs will provide information that health care providers may find useful in making certified health IT purchasing and licensing decisions.
We also believe that the Certification Program, through conformance testing, ONC-ACB surveillance and corrective action, and ONC direct review, provides the requisite developer accountability and program oversight to provide assurances to consumers and users of certified health IT. These same processes also support patient safety, including through retention of the revised safety-enhanced designed certification criterion (§ 170.315(g)(3)).
SVAP
Comments.
We received significant support from commenters for our proposal to streamline the SVAP reporting process, with only a few commenters expressing indirect opposition to the proposal based on their belief that our proposals would reduce overall oversight of the Certification Program. Commenters requested clarification on when SVAP standards must be reported in RWT results reports for non-API criteria, including whether reporting applies to all SVAP standards on the CHPL listing, only those implemented during the applicable calendar year, or only newly added SVAP standards not previously reported. Another commenter questioned the burden of requiring RWT Results Reports solely to restate SVAP information already available on CHPL. A few commenters requested that we provide clear expectations and transition guidance if RWT requirements change during the 2026-2027 implementation period.
Response.
We have finalized with modification our proposed revisions of SVAP. SVAP is a voluntary process that requires affirmative actions by developers to adopt and certify their health IT to a newer version of a standard or implementation specification that is included in certification criteria that are specified in RWT under § 170.405(a). Ultimately, through attestations under
45 CFR 170.406
, a developer attests that their certified health IT is conformant to the “SVAP” version of the standard or implementation specification as part of their overall attestation to compliance with
45 CFR 170.405
.
Except as follows, we have finalized as proposed our proposed modifications to SVAP. In consideration of the regulatory version updating and attestation processes outlined above and public comment noting that SVAP standards are identified via the CHPL for certified health IT, we have not finalized our proposal to require, as part of RWT results reporting, the identification of any SVAP updates to health IT certified to the non-API RWT certification criteria identified in § 170.405(a) (the non-(g) certification criteria). We believe sufficient assurances and transparency will be provided by the aforementioned attestation and CHPL listings. As a result, there is no need for developers to identify in their RWT results their voluntary updates (health IT products, certification criteria, and standards/implementation specifications). This approach avoids redundancies and further reduces burden. We have, however, finalized our proposal that the RWT SVAP reporting requirements would not change for API-focused certification criteria identified as (g) criteria in § 170.405(a). This is because we proposed that all provisions under § 170.405(b) would still apply to health IT certified to API-focused certification criteria, and we expect such RWT and reporting to occur, including with SVAP versions of standards and implementation specifications, as applicable. For clarity, we have still finalized the proposed revision to § 170.405(b)(8) to cross-reference paragraph (a) of § 170.405 instead of paragraph (b). This will provide the availability of SVAP for all health IT certified to certification criteria identified in § 170.405(a), which supports advancing interoperability. Comments.
We received a number of comments that were supportive of our proposal to remove six of the Insights measures. Commenters stated that the preparations for compliance with the reporting requirements for the Insights measures would have been a significant investment burden for eligible health IT developers. A commenter also asserted that there is no clear connection between the accumulation of data and marketplace improvement. Another commenter expressed support for our approach in the selection of measures for removal in comparison to those we did not propose to remove. Specifically, the commenter noted that data from the “use of FHIR in apps” measure, which we did not propose to remove, could be collected directly by health IT developers for reporting the measure and could therefore create less burden than the other Insights measures.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback on our proposal to remove six Insights measures. We agree with commenters' perspective that some of the Insights measures would impose significant costs and burden to health IT developers. As we stated in the Proposed Rule, our proposals would ensure that the Insights Condition is aligned with other proposed policies and changes to the Certification Program that prioritize exchange using FHIR-based APIs (
90 FR 61004
). For the reasons described above regarding the burden to health IT developers and our policies to prioritize exchange using FHIR-based APIs, we have finalized the removal of the following measures as proposed: § 170.407(a)(3)(i) “the individuals' access to electronic health information,” § 170.407(a)(3)(ii) “consolidated clinical document architecture (C-CDA) problems, medications, and allergies reconciliation and incorporation,” § 170.407(a)(3)(iii) “applications supported,” § 170.407(a)(3)(vi) “immunization administrations electronically submitted to immunization information systems,”
(
printed page 67973)
and § 170.407(a)(3)(vii) “immunization history and forecasts.”
As we discuss hereafter, we have decided not to finalize the removal of the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(v) as proposed because we believe that retaining the measure aligns with our FHIR-forward future strategy and our other changes finalized in this rule to prioritize exchange using FHIR-based APIs in the Certification Program. We believe that “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure will provide valuable insights related to the implementation and use of FHIR that will not be captured by the “use of FHIR in apps” measure alone (which, as noted, we did not propose to remove). While we did not finalize the removal of the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure, we have finalized revisions to § 170.407(b)(1)(i)(B) and (C) to provide more time before reporting of this measure is required. Specifically, we are moving the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure (previously paragraph (a)(3)(v); paragraph (a)(3)(ii) as finalized in this final rule) from § 170.407(b)(1)(i)(B) to (C). In practice, this means health IT developers will have additional time and will now be required to begin reporting responses for the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure in July 2029, rather than in July 2028. Developers must collect the required reporting data annually during the preceding year and develop and deploy the technology needed to support data collection in client settings. Considering the timing of the publication of this final rule, there would not be sufficient time for health IT developers to complete these activities in preparation for reporting. Accordingly, moving the reporting start date from July 2028 to July 2029 is appropriate to provide sufficient notice and time for health IT developers to prepare for reporting.
We have finalized conforming edits to the list structure in § 170.407(a)(3) to revise the “use of FHIR in apps through certified health IT” as paragraph (i) instead of (iv) and revise the “use of FHIR bulk data access through certified health IT” as paragraph (ii) instead of (v). We have also finalized conforming edits to § 170.407(a)(1)(ii)(B) and (C) to remove references to the measures that we are removing from § 170.407(a)(3) as well.
Additionally, we have finalized a revision, as proposed, to the name of § 170.407 (Insights Condition and Maintenance of Certification) to simply “Insights” to ensure consistency and uniformity across all the Conditions and Maintenance of Certification in subpart D of
45 CFR part 170
.
Comments.
We received several comments regarding our proposal to remove the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(v). These commenters stated the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure is necessary for the measurement of large-scale analytics of app traffic. Commenters also emphasized that the data obtained from the “use of FHIR in apps” measure would be an insufficient substitute for the data that would be obtained from the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure. Another commenter stated that the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure would require less effort because it requires tracking minimal data. The commenter also noted that the measure would provide information on the inconsistent implementation of bulk access capabilities. Commenters recommended that ONC retain the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure to preserve access to information on large-scale data interoperability.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback regarding our proposal to remove the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(v). As discussed above, we have decided to retain the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(v) (which we have moved to § 170.407(a)(3)(ii)) and have not finalized the removal of the measure as proposed. We agree with commenters that the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure should be retained to address gaps in measurement and provide transparency on the use of certified health IT not captured by “the use of FHIR in apps” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(iv). We adopted the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure to address gaps in measurement and provide transparency on the use of certified health IT not captured by the “use of FHIR in apps” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(iv) (
88 FR 23840
through
23841
). There are a number of reports that the performance of FHIR bulk data access is suboptimal, which could be a result of health IT developers' implementation of the standard.
[
52 53 54
]
Retaining the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(v) will allow us to monitor issues that may be limiting the performance of Bulk FHIR data access by providing insights related to implementation and use of the FHIR standard in large-scale app traffic that Bulk FHIR data access supports. This insight is particularly important as innovators throughout the industry continue to advance bulk data use cases for quality measurement, public health reporting, and clinical research purposes. Retaining the “use of FHIR bulk data access” measure also aligns with our other finalized changes in this rule to prioritize exchange using FHIR-based APIs in the Certification Program by providing insights into the implementation and use of FHIR that will not be captured by the “use of FHIR in apps” measure alone.
Comments.
We received a number of comments that broadly opposed our proposal to remove the six identified Insights measures. Commenters stated that the Insights measures would have provided transparency regarding interoperability and FHIR capabilities across health IT products and the health IT industry as a whole. Many commenters emphasized that the data that would have been provided by the Insights measures would be an important tool for accountability in the marketplace for Health IT Modules. Some commenters also suggested that ONC adopt alternative reporting measures that are less burdensome to replace the Insights measures if we finalize the removal of six of the seven Insights measures as proposed.
Response.
We appreciate the comments that we received about our proposal to remove the six identified Insights measures. We understand commenters' concerns about losing access to the data that would have been obtained from the Insights measures that we proposed to remove, but we respectfully disagree with this perspective. We believe that the investment necessary to implement many of the current Insights measures would impose a significant burden on health IT developers that outweighs the benefit we would expect from the data that would have been obtained from the Insights measures for which we have finalized the removal. We clarify that we have not removed the Insights Condition of Certification in its entirety as discussed in detail above. In response to the suggestion that we adopt alternative measures, we will continue to evaluate the Insights measures.

printed page 67974)
Comments.

Comments.
We received a number of comments specific to our proposals to remove the “immunization administrations electronically submitted to immunization information systems through certified health IT” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(vi) and the “immunization history and forecasts through certified health IT” measure in § 170.407(a)(3)(vii). Some commenters recommended that ONC retain these measures. Commenters emphasized the significant role that immunization information systems play in public health systems and stated that health care providers and patients would benefit from the two measures providing data on utilization of immunization data exchange and access to immunization data exchange. One commenter asserted that the data that would be obtained from the “immunization administrations electronically submitted to immunization information systems through certified health IT” and the “immunization history and forecasts through certified health IT” measures could be used by public health agencies to improve their awareness of and response to public health threats.
Response.
We thank commenters for their feedback. We respectfully disagree with the perspective of the commenters regarding our proposal to remove the “immunization administrations electronically submitted to immunization information systems” measure and “immunization history and forecasts” measure. As we stated in the Proposed Rule, we believe that removing these Insights measures will reduce cost and burden to the public, and we want to ensure that the Insights Condition is aligned with other policies and changes to the Certification Program that prioritize exchange using FHIR-based APIs (

For these reasons and those stated above, we have finalized the removal of the measures in § 170.407(a)(3)(vi) and § 170.407(a)(3)(vii) as proposed.

(

1. Regulatory Planning and Review Analysis
This rule is consistent with the policies outlined in EOs 12866, 13563, and 14192.
E.O. 12866
and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, and distributive impacts).
E.O. 14192
, as noted above, focuses on deregulatory actions and cost savings associated with deregulatory actions. This rulemaking is significant under Section 3(f)(1) of
E.O. 12866
, and we have prepared an RIA.
a. Costs and Benefits
These finalized deregulatory actions provide substantial relief for developers of certified health IT and significant cost savings realized from the revision and removal of certain program requirements. For the purpose of estimating the cost savings of this rulemaking, we have determined that these policies would continue absent this regulatory action. The cost savings have been estimated using the best available data and modeled on the costs estimated and finalized in prior ONC rulemakings. As articulated in the preamble, these deregulatory actions reduce the effort of developers of certified health IT to meet ongoing program requirements and reduce barriers to entry for new program participants. The actions, importantly, return effort back to developers of certified health IT to innovate their technology and focus on the needs of their clients and end users.
Comments.
Multiple commenters argue that the RIA underestimates or overlooks significant downstream costs that may shift to providers, health information exchanges, networks, and patients when certification criteria are removed. They warn that eliminating requirements—particularly in privacy, security, and interoperability—could increase variability, reduce auditability, and force providers to independently validate or maintain capabilities previously ensured through certification. Safety net and resource—constrained organizations expressed concern that weakened Federal baselines may expose them to security risks, added vendor fees, contractual burdens, and additional operational responsibilities they are not equipped to absorb. Several commenters emphasized that these unintended consequences may widen inequities, especially for small clinics and rural providers, unless ONC fully evaluates downstream impacts and implements post-final monitoring to mitigate burden shifting. Collectively, commenters urged ONC to account for patient harms, civil rights risks, and the ongoing need for reliable, standards-based functionality within its cost-benefit analysis.
Response.
This rulemaking and impact analysis examines the continued value of maintaining program requirements weighed against the ongoing cost of that compliance. Our original analysis and public comments helped shape final decisions and economic analyses presented in this finalized impact analysis. The finalized revisions to the Certification Program carefully considered public comments, and, in particular, we have decided not to finalize proposals to remove criteria that enable secure and confidential access and use of patient health information and certain information exchange capabilities. Finalized revisions to the Certification Program largely encompass reductions in the frequency and scope of data reporting and documentation that developers are required to provide to comply with certification, specifically—narrowing requirements for the Real World Testing and Insights Conditions of Certification and removing annual reporting of source attributes for the “decision support interventions” criterion. We proposed to remove 34 criteria and have, instead, finalized the removal of 14 criteria, with some criteria, previously proposed to be removed, revised instead with a narrower scope, retaining essential functionality and standard references to ensure a necessary floor of technical capability are available to all certified health IT users. The decreased regulatory burdens and estimated cost savings presented in this impact analysis relate to the compliance costs associated with testing and certification and do not fully encompass the total costs of implementing the technology by end-users.
We considered the effects of revisions to the Certification Program on end-users as part of our calculus; however, we have limited data on how revisions to program requirements may affect the availability or functionality of certified health IT to these end-users. It is difficult to estimate the wide variation in how certified health IT is ultimately deployed and implemented by end-users, as well as evaluate how those choices are tied to Certification Program requirements or the requirements and specifications of other programs that adopt certified health IT. For example, we finalized removal of the “direct project” criterion in § 170.315(h)(1) but have retained reference to the Direct Messaging standard in § 170.202(a)(2). Survey data from 2025 show that a majority of hospitals often use the Direct Messaging standard to send and receive information with outside organizations.
[

]
However, other electronic exchange methods complement or substitute for this messaging protocol, like those used for network-based exchange via State, national, and qualified health information networks, and use of those methods by hospitals now exceed use of Direct Messaging. This change occurred despite the broad certification of Health IT Modules to the criterion and ubiquitous adoption of certified health IT by hospitals.

We would not anticipate removal of the criterion from the Certification Program to alone affect future use of the standard or the messaging functionality, as health information exchange is multi-faceted and can be driven by compliance with Federal requirements, the needs of the marketplace, and changing norms and behaviors among healthcare organizations.
Other finalized revisions, like the removals of the “family health history” in § 170.315(a)(12) and “care plan” in § 170.315(b)(9) reflect policy shifts from

Finalized removals, like those mentioned above, are consistent with this policy shift, ensuring that data made available and accessible for exchange conform to the standards adopted as part of USCDI. In this final rule, and other finalized rulemakings, we acknowledge that regulatory costs incurred by developers of certified health IT may be passed on to end users of certified health IT in the form of increased fees and other costs.
[

We anticipate that these finalized deregulatory actions will provide immediate relief and reduce ongoing burden on developers of certified health IT, which may result in reduced marginal costs or other cost savings for end users. The monitoring and evaluation of Certification Program requirements and the deployment of certified health IT in real-world settings is a cornerstone of ONC practice. ONC makes nearly all Certification Program data publicly available and searchable via its public website, permitting full transparency about the types of health IT tested and certified by the Certification Program and how that health IT meets specific program requirements. ONC also leads the collection of data via surveys and other instruments about the real-world experiences of health care providers, patients, networks, and digital health companies using or gaining access to certified health IT. This data is also made publicly available and ONC reports extensively on findings in peer-reviewed journals, via its public website, and other venues. ONC's research informed both deregulatory decision-making and the estimated cost savings presented here. ONC will continue to study and evaluate the development and use of certified health IT, as well as the real-world impact of the Certification Program on providers, networks, and patients.
Comments:
Commenters argued that the projected cost savings in the proposed rulemaking are significantly overstated because most certifications involve routine maintenance rather than new development. They note that many features are already implemented, so large claimed savings—such as millions of hours or over a billion dollars—lack evidentiary support. Overall, they believe the RIA misrepresents the true scale of savings by not accounting for the limited effort required to maintain existing capabilities.
Response:
We thank commenters for their input. We agree with the commenters' assessment that most certifications are recertifications that require annual maintenance costs rather than new development or integration costs. This impact analysis took a variety of approaches to estimate cost savings, based on the type of deregulatory action. In all cases, our approach to estimating cost savings calculated maintenance costs as a fraction of new development costs finalized in prior ONC rulemakings to estimate cost savings for the revision or removal of a program requirement. For example, in Table R-1: Panel A “Estimates of Annual Labor Hours Saved for the Removal of Certification Criteria,” average maintenance costs across all removals was 15% with a maximum maintenance cost of 27% of new development costs. As described in our methodology for removed criteria, we leveraged data and information collected from the developer community, as part of the Department's request for public comment on deregulatory actions. The public feedback and discussions with developers and other interested parties provided additional context on the ongoing costs of meeting certain Certification Program requirements, in addition to the overall value of this compliance on end-users and other entities. This data, and information informed methodologies discussed in detail in the following analyses, provide concrete evidentiary support for estimated cost savings from these deregulatory actions. It is worth noting that the majority of estimated cost savings are derived from the revision of three Certification Program requirements: safety-enhanced design, decision support interventions, and real world testing. All three requirements involve regular, typically annual effort for developers to test updated or new modules, provide data and documentation on predictive super intelligence models, and plan, measure, and report on metrics for dozens of certification criteria. These cost savings are also in aggregate across all developers of certified health IT. As of April 1, 2026, there are over 450 developers who participated in the Certification Program. Cost savings are calculated for individual criteria and reporting requirements and reflect the current number of developers and products that adopt the criteria or must comply with a reporting requirement. Therefore, more cost savings may flow to certain developers who currently have Health IT Modules certified to more criteria that will be removed from the Certification Program or who are subject to more extensive reporting requirements that this rule revises. On average, we project that a developer of certified health IT may realize $300,000 to $400,000 in undiscounted savings annually or roughly the equivalent of two data engineer FTEs. Where applicable, we describe estimation methodologies in more detail for individual policy changes.

We developed a common model for estimating cost savings associated with the removal of all certification criteria, described below.
Table R-1, below, provides criterion-level results of our model for the finalized criteria removals. For each certification criterion we identified the original costs to certify to the functionality from prior rules (the lower and upper bounds of “Total Hours” in Table R-1.)

We are not aware of any published evidence that would directly inform this calculation, and, therefore, developed a novel approach using various information sources. We defined this fraction (“Final Effort Multiplier” in Table R-1) based on five factors: (1) “Test”: the criterion's certification conformance method, assuming that criteria with a test procedure had additional maintenance costs while those with a conformance method of attestation had no additional cost beyond what was initially incurred; (2) “Stakeholder feedback”: stakeholder feedback received by ONC through meetings, informal conversations, and letters from impacted parties on effort involved in certifying and updating the specific certification criterion; (3) “Complexity of standard”: whether the criterion referenced a standard and an assessment of the complexity involved in maintaining and updating conformance to that standard over time; (4) “Complexity of test procedure”: an assessment of the complexity of the test procedure or evaluative work to support attestation when it was necessary to undertake the certification process; and (5) “General complexity”: an overall assessment of the complexity of maintaining the certification criterion and underlying functionality.

We then estimated the lower and upper bounds of “Hours saved” by multiplying the “Annual” hours by the number of products that certify each criterion. 2. Revisions
2.1 Revision of Certification Criteria
We have finalized the revision of 5 certification criteria, 2 of which were proposed for removal. For each revised certification criterion, we have estimated the annual savings generated by the finalized revisions.
2.1.1 § 170.315(b)(1) Transitions of Care
We have finalized revisions to the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(1) to reduce burden on developers of health IT by removing the “send and receive via edge protocol” C-CDA requirement and “create” C-CDA requirement in the criterion and by simplifying the remaining criterion requirements to focus solely on validating receipt of C-CDA documents. We originally proposed to revise the certification criterion with an effective date of January 1, 2027. We have finalized the criterion revisions to be effective as of January 1, 2030. We believe that these revisions remove a substantial proportion of the ongoing effort required to maintain and update the functional requirement of the certification criterion, but we acknowledge that it does not remove requirements to support the C-CDA standard or to update functionality to receive C-CDA documents. We assume that this reduces the overall ongoing cost for this certification criterion by 60%. Following the methodology described for removed criterion, we considered annual maintenance of § 170.315(b)(1) to represent high complexity equivalent to 15% of the initial development costs annually. We note from an analysis of current Certification Program data that 254 developers have certified 294 products to § 170.315(b)(1) and that the initial developer hours estimated to implement the criterion had a lower bound of 3,000 hours and an upper bound of 4,000 hours in the 2015 Edition Final Rule (
80 FR 62602
).

We therefore estimate that the revision of this criterion will reduce effort to maintain the criterion annually by 9% annually or between 270 and 360 hours per product and 79,380 to 105,840 hours across all products. We estimate the total undiscounted annual cost savings to range from $11,033,820 to $14,711,760, beginning in 2030.
2.1.2 § 170.315(b)(2) Clinical Information Reconciliation and Incorporation
We proposed to remove the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2). We have not finalized as proposed, and, instead, have revised the certification criterion in § 170.315(b)(2) to reduce burden on developers of health IT by removing the standards-based requirements while maintaining the capability to reconcile and incorporate patient health information electronically. Following the methodology described for removed criterion, we consider § 170.315(b)(2) to represent high complexity equivalent to 28% of the initial development costs annually, of which 8% of this maintenance effort is attributable to the complexity of the test procedure and 10% is attributable to the complexity of the referenced standard. The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small businesses if a rule has a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities. The Small Business Administration (SBA) establishes the size of small businesses for Federal Government programs based on average annual receipts or the average employment of a firm.

With the exception of rule review costs, this finalized rulemaking is deregulatory and does not create new requirements on developers of certified health IT, including small businesses. We believe the finalized deregulatory actions will create net cost savings for developers and would create a significant positive economic impact on small entities who participate directly in the Certification Program as a developer of certified health IT or as an entity who interoperates with certified health IT. Finalized revisions reduce burdens on small developers to meet ongoing reporting and documentation requirements, as well as support for redundant standards and functionalities—which can weigh heavier on smaller developers with smaller developer and engineering teams. As the finalized revisions largely reflect reduced effort to meet annual reporting, other recurring program requirements, and ongoing maintenance of Health IT Modules, we assume the projected cost savings in this final rule may be shared equally across developers, both small and large.
