E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule that imposes unfunded mandates on State, local, and Tribal governments or the private sector requiring spending in any one year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. The current inflation-adjusted statutory threshold is approximately $187 million in 2025. This finalized rule is deregulatory, and, therefore, the estimated potential cost effects of this finalized rule do not reach the statutory threshold. This finalized rule does not impose unfunded mandates on State, local, and Tribal governments, or the private sector.
Comments.
Multiple commenters expressed concern that our proposals impose unfunded mandates on State, local, and tribal governments and the private sector. Commenters were concerned that de-regulation shifts the burden of assessing health IT functionality and standards adoption to end users. Two commenters expressed their concerns specifically with the downstream effects of our public health-related proposals (§ 170.315(f)(4), § 170.315(f)(5), § 170.315(f)(6) and § 170.315(f)(7)) which sought to remove the standards-based requirements for electronic case reporting and antimicrobial use and resistance reporting and remove the requirements to support cancer registry reporting and creation of health care survey information.
Response.
We thank commenters for their input. The changes in § 170.315(f)(4), § 170.315(f)(5), and § 170.315(f)(7) have not been finalized as proposed—we are maintaining requirements to support cancer registry reporting and creation of health care survey information and keeping electronic case reporting as a standards-based criterion. We have finalized as proposed the removal of standards-based requirements in § 170.315(f)(6), which have not kept pace with reporting requirements and therefore we believe this change will not impose downstream costs on end-users to submit AUR data NHSN. Given these final decisions, we do not anticipate any significant downstream costs or burdens to be shifted on public health entities. In response to broader concerns that our proposals impose unfunded mandates or that de-regulation shifts the burden of assessing health IT and standards adoption to end users, we have chosen to finalize 14 of 34 criteria proposed for removal from the CFR, with many of those removals consisting of criteria with low adoption rates overall. Furthermore, the reduced scope of conditions and maintenance of certification reflect the prioritization of reporting and documentation requirements to focus developer efforts on API criteria and associated requirements, as these are less mature and evolving requirements which necessitate focused developer efforts to monitor and evaluate these functionalities in real world settings. These are necessary program improvements that will enhance the overall performance of the Certification Program and allow it to evolve to meet emerging needs that will benefit the nation as a whole.

International Trade Commission
[Investigation No. 337-TA-1439]
AGENCY:
U.S. International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that the U.S. International Trade Commission (“Commission”) has determined to review in part a final initial determination (“FID”) of the presiding administrative law judge (“ALJ”). The Commission requests written submissions from the parties on the issues under review and submissions from the parties, interested government agencies, and other interested persons on the issues of remedy, the public interest, and bonding, under the schedule set forth below.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Noah Priluck, Esq., Office of the General
(
printed page 67853)
Counsel, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, telephone (202) 205-3107. Copies of non-confidential documents filed in connection with this investigation may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov
.
For help accessing EDIS, please email
EDIS3Help@usitc.gov
.
General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server at
https://www.usitc.gov
.
Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information on this matter can be obtained by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on (202) 205-1810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission instituted this investigation on February 21, 2025, based on a complaint filed by Syensqo SA of Brussels, Belgium; Solvay Specialty Polymers, USA LLC of Alpharetta, Georgia; and Solvay Specialty Polymers Italy S.P.A. of Bollate, Italy (collectively, “Complainants”).
90 FR 10082-83
(Feb. 21, 2025). The complaint, as supplemented, alleges violations of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended,
19 U.S.C. 1337
, in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, or the sale within the United States after importation of certain polyvinylidene fluoride resins by reason of infringement of claims 1-7, 10, and 12 of U.S. Patent No. 8,337,725 (“the '725 patent”).
Id.
The complaint further alleges that a domestic industry exists or is in the process of being established.
Id.
The Commission's notice of investigation named as respondents: (1) Inner Mongolia 3F Wanhao Fluorochemical Industry Co. Ltd. of Fengzhen, China (“3F”); (2) Zhejiang Juhua Co., Ltd. of Quzhou City, China (“Juhua”); (3) Zhejiang Fluorine Chemical New Material Co. Ltd. of Shaoxing, China; and Hubei Fluorine New Materials Co., Ltd. of Dongtan Village, China (collectively, “Fluorine”); and (4) Sinochem Lantian Co., Ltd. (“Sinochem”) of Hangzhou, China.
Id.
The Office of Unfair Import Investigations is not participating in the investigation.
Id.
On July 14, 2025, the Commission amended the complaint and notice of investigation to include allegations asserting infringement of claims 8 and 9 of the '725 patent. Order No. 9 (June 23, 2025),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (July 14, 2025),
90 FR 33394-95
(July 17, 2025). The Commission also amended the complaint and notice of investigation to change the name of two complainants from Solvay Specialty Polymers, USA LLC to Syensqo Specialty Polymers, USA LLC, and Solvay Specialty Polymers Italy S.P.A. to Syensqo Specialty Polymers Italy S.P.A. to reflect corporate name changes. Order No. 19 (Nov. 19, 2025),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (Dec. 9, 2025),
90 FR 57485
(Dec. 11, 2025).
The Commission previously terminated the investigation with respect to 3F. Order No. 8 (Mar. 28, 2025),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (Apr. 21, 2025). The Commission also previously terminated the investigation with respect to claim 7 of the '725 patent. Order No. 24 (Dec. 4, 2024),
unreviewed by
Comm'n Notice (Jan. 5, 2026).
On September 29, 2025, the ALJ granted Respondents' motion for summary determination of no importation or sale for importation as to Juhua, but not as to Fluorine or Sinochem. Order No. 16 (Sept. 29, 2025). On November 24, 2025, the ALJ granted Juhua's motion to terminate itself from the investigation based on Order No. 16. Order No. 20 (Nov. 24, 2025).
From December 8-12, 2025, the ALJ held an evidentiary hearing involving Complainants and Respondents Fluorine and Sinochem.
On February 11, 2026, the Commission determined to review and, on review, reverse Order Nos. 16 and 20, thus reinstating Juhua as a party. Comm'n Notice (Feb. 11, 2026).
The ALJ held a supplementary evidentiary hearing on May 6, 2026.
On August 7, 2026, the ALJ issued the FID finding a violation of section 337 based on: (1) Complainants proving infringement of claims 1, 3, 6, 8, and 9 of the '725 patent with respect to all of the accused products; (2) Complainants proving importation of one accused product by respondent Fluorine but no importation of any other accused product;
[
1
]
(3) Respondents failing to prove any asserted claims invalid; (4) Complainants satisfying the technical prong of the domestic industry requirement with respect to claims 1, 3, and 6 of the '725 patent; and (5) Complainants proving that an economic domestic industry is in the process of being established as required by section 337(a)(2). The FID also includes the ALJ's Recommended Determination should the Commission find a violation, recommending issuance of a limited exclusion order with a standard certification provision. The ALJ also recommended that the Commission set a bond of 4.5 percent bond of the value of infringing imports during the period of Presidential review.
On August 21, 2026, Complainants and the named respondents filed petitions for review of the FID, with responses filed on August 31, 2026.
On September 8, 2026, Complainants filed a public interest submission pursuant to Commission Rule 210.50(a)(4)(i),
19 CFR 210.50(a)(4)(i)
. No submissions were filed in response to the Commission notice published in the
Federal Register
requesting submissions on the public interest from the public should the Commission find a section 337 violation.
91 FR 52711-12
(Aug. 14, 2026).
Having reviewed the record of the investigation, including the FID and the parties' submissions to the ALJ and to the Commission, the Commission has determined to review the FID in part. Specifically, the Commission has determined to review the FID's finding that the asserted claims of the '725 patent are not invalid for indefiniteness and for failure to satisfy the written description requirement. The Commission has also determined to review the FID's findings as to whether Complainants have established importation or sale for importation with respect to Juhua, Sinochem, and Fluorine. The Commission has determined not to review the remainder of the FID's findings.
In connection with its review, the Commission requests responses to the following questions. The parties are requested to brief their positions with reference to the applicable law and the existing evidentiary record.
1. Explain whether the term “sale for importation” requires knowledge (actual or constructive) of the importation. Did Congress intend to prevent the Commission from excluding infringing imports in the absence of such knowledge? Provide support with reference to the statute (including the provisions regarding violation and remedy establishing the Commission's statutory authority over the imported articles), the legislative history, and/or applicable precedent. If some kind of knowledge is required, what evidence should be considered in determining whether the sale for importation is satisfied?
2. Address whether the asserted claims of the '725 patent are invalid for indefiniteness under
35 U.S.C. 112
taking into account the parties' electrode-based and acetone-based arguments, and, in particular whether the FID correctly focuses on the global maximum rate of change, rather than the
(
printed page 67854)
local maximum rates of change in analyzing the relevant titrations.
The parties are invited to brief only the discrete issues requested above. The parties are not to brief other issues on review, which are adequately presented in the parties' existing filings.
In connection with the final disposition of this investigation, the statute authorizes issuance of,
inter alia,
(1) an exclusion order that could result in the exclusion of the subject articles from entry into the United States; and/or (2) cease and desist orders that could result in the respondents being required to cease and desist from engaging in unfair acts in the importation and sale of such articles. Accordingly, the Commission is interested in receiving written submissions that address the form of remedy, if any, that should be ordered. If a party seeks exclusion of an article from entry into the United States for purposes other than entry for consumption, the party should so indicate and provide information establishing that activities involving other types of entry either are adversely affecting it or likely to do so. For background, see
Certain Devices for Connecting Computers via Telephone Lines,
Inv. No. 337-TA-360, USITC Pub. No. 2843, Comm'n Op. at 7-10 (Dec. 1994).
The statute requires the Commission to consider the effects of that remedy upon the public interest. The public interest factors the Commission will consider include the effect that an exclusion order would have on: (1) the public health and welfare, (2) competitive conditions in the U.S. economy, (3) U.S. production of articles that are like or directly competitive with those that are subject to investigation, and (4) U.S. consumers. The Commission is therefore interested in receiving written submissions that address the aforementioned public interest factors in the context of this investigation.
If the Commission orders some form of remedy, the U.S. Trade Representative, as delegated by the President, has 60 days to approve, disapprove, or take no action on the Commission's determination.
See
Presidential Memorandum of July 21, 2005,
70 FR 43251
(July 26, 2005). During this period, the subject articles would be entitled to enter the United States under bond, in an amount determined by the Commission and prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury. The Commission is therefore interested in receiving submissions concerning the amount of the bond that should be imposed if a remedy is ordered.
Written Submissions:
The parties to the investigation are requested to file written submissions on the issues identified in this notice. Parties to the investigation, interested government agencies, and any other interested parties are encouraged to file written submissions on the issues of remedy, the public interest, and bonding. Such submissions should address the recommended determination by the ALJ on remedy and bonding.
In its initial submission, Complainants are also requested to identify the remedy sought and to submit proposed remedial orders for the Commission's consideration. Complainants are further requested to provide the HTSUS subheadings under which the accused products are imported, and to supply the identification information for all known importers of the products at issue in this investigation. All initial written submissions, from the parties and/or third parties/interested government agencies, and proposed remedial orders from the parties must be filed no later than the close of business on November 6, 2026. All reply submissions must be filed no later than the close of business on November 13, 2026. Opening submissions from the parties are limited to 25 pages. Reply submissions from the parties are limited to 15 pages. All submissions from third parties and/or interested government agencies are limited to 10 pages. No further submissions on any of these issues will be permitted unless otherwise ordered by the Commission.
Persons filing written submissions must file the original document electronically on or before the deadlines stated above pursuant to
19 CFR 210.4(f)
. Submissions should refer to the investigation number (Inv. No. 337-TA-1439) in a prominent place on the cover page and/or the first page. (
See
Handbook for Electronic Filing Procedures,
https://www.usitc.gov/​secretary/​documents/​handbook_​on_​filing_​procedures.pdf
). Persons with questions regarding filing should contact the Secretary, (202) 205-2000.
Any person desiring to submit a document to the Commission in confidence must request confidential treatment by marking each document with a header indicating that the document contains confidential information. This marking will be deemed to satisfy the request procedure set forth in Rules 201.6(b) and 210.5(e)(2) (
19 CFR 201.6(b)
& 210.5(e)(2)). Documents for which confidential treatment by the Commission is properly sought will be treated accordingly. Any non-party wishing to submit comments containing confidential information must serve those comments on the parties to the investigation pursuant to the applicable Administrative Protective Order. A redacted non-confidential version of the document must also be filed with the Commission and served on any parties to the investigation within two business days of any confidential filing. All information, including confidential business information and documents for which confidential treatment is properly sought, submitted to the Commission for purposes of this investigation may be disclosed to and used: (i) by the Commission, its employees and Offices, and contract personnel (a) for developing or maintaining the records of this or a related proceeding, or (b) in internal investigations, audits, reviews, and evaluations relating to the programs, personnel, and operations of the Commission including under 5 U.S.C. Appendix 3; or (ii) by U.S. government employees and contract personnel, solely for cybersecurity purposes. All contract personnel will sign appropriate nondisclosure agreements. All nonconfidential written submissions will be available for public inspection on EDIS.
The Commission vote for this determination took place on October 23, 2026.
The authority for the Commission's determination is contained in section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (
19 U.S.C. 1337
), and in Part 210 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (
19 CFR part 210
).
By order of the Commission.
Issued: October 23, 2026.
Sharon Bellamy,
Supervisory Hearings and Information Officer.

                         Although the FID does not state so specifically, because the FID does not find importation by Juhua or Sinochem, the FID does not find a violation with respect to those respondents.

[Docket ID: FEMA-2026-0232; OMB No. 1660-0004]
AGENCY:
Federal Emergency Management Agency, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
30-Day notice of extension and request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) will submit the information collection abstracted below to the Office of Management and Budget for review and clearance in accordance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. FEMA invites the general public to take this opportunity to comment on an extension of a currently approved information collection. In accordance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, this notice seeks comments concerning the collection of information under which communities submit information to FEMA for application and continued participation in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP).
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before November 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Requests for additional information or copies of the information collection should be made to Director, Information Management Division, 500 C Street SW, Washington, DC 20472, email address
FEMA-Information-Collections-Management@fema.dhs.gov
or Charles Baker, Program Analyst, Floodplain Management Division at
charles.baker@fema.dhs.gov
or (202) 600-1885.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The NFIP, codified at
42 U.S.C. 4001
et seq.,
requires all flood-prone communities throughout the country to apply for participation in the NFIP one year after their flood-prone status is identified or submit to the prohibition of certain types of federal and federally related financial assistance for use in their floodplains.
44 CFR 59.2
authorizes previously unavailable flood insurance protection to property owners in flood-prone areas and identifies the information that communities are required to submit to FEMA for application into the NFIP.
44 CFR 59.22
and
59.24
identify the information a community is required to submit to FEMA for continued participation in the program. This collection also accounts for the burden hours associated with the applicant's time to collect information
(
printed page 67849)
as part of the community development permit process. To qualify for the NFIP, a participating community must adopt certain minimum standards in accordance with FEMA's regulations at
44 CFR 60.3
,
60.4
, and
60.5
. To verify whether communities maintain such standards, the NFIP requires participating communities to retain documentation on development taking place in the flood hazard areas within the community. See
44 CFR 59.22
. Such information will be made available to FEMA upon request. This information assists FEMA in evaluating the effectiveness of a community's floodplain management program and participating property owners' eligibility for flood insurance. The “Application for Participation in the NFIP” and the “NFIP and the Community Development Permit Process” are separate actions documented under the same collection.
This proposed information collection previously published in the
Federal Register
on July 30, 2026, at
91 FR 48400
with a 60-day public comment period. Two public comments were received. One public comment suggested a ceiling on the value of properties eligible for flood insurance, and the other was supportive of this information collection. One comment is not relevant to this information collection, and the other is supportive of its renewal. The purpose of this notice is to notify the public that FEMA will submit the information collection abstracted below to the Office of Management and Budget for review and clearance.
Collection of Information
Title:
Application for Participation in the National Flood Insurance Program.
Type of Information Collection:
Extension, without change, of a currently approved information collection.
OMB Number:
1660-0004.

Library of Congress
Copyright Office
37 CFR Part 201
[Docket No. 2026-4]
AGENCY:
U.S. Copyright Office, Library of Congress.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
The United States Copyright Office is conducting the tenth triennial rulemaking proceeding under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (“DMCA”), concerning temporary exemptions to the DMCA's prohibition against circumvention of technological measures that control access to copyrighted works. Having carefully considered the petitions for new and renewal exemptions and comments received in response to the June 9, 2026 Notification of Inquiry, the Office announces the Register's intention to recommend all but one of the existing exemptions for renewal, and initiates three rounds of public comment on newly proposed exemptions. Comments submitted may not exceed twenty-five pages per class, excluding documentary evidence.
DATES:
Initial written comments, along with any documentary or multimedia evidence, from proponents and other members of the public who support the adoption of a proposed exemption, as well as those that neither support nor oppose an exemption but seek to share pertinent information, are due December 7, 2026. Written response comments, along with any documentary or multimedia evidence, from those who oppose the adoption of a proposed exemption are due February 22, 2027. Written reply comments from supporters of a proposal and parties that neither support nor oppose a proposal are due March 22, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
The Copyright Office is using the
regulations.gov
system for the submission and posting of comments in this proceeding. All comments are to be submitted electronically through
regulations.gov.
The Office is accepting two types of comments. First, commenters who wish briefly to express general support for or opposition to a proposed exemption may submit such comments electronically by typing into the comment field on
regulations.gov.
Second, commenters who wish to provide a fuller legal and evidentiary basis for their position may upload a Word or PDF document, but such longer submissions must be completed using the long comment form provided on the Office's website at
https://www.copyright.gov/​1201/​2027
.
Specific instructions for submitting comments, including multimedia evidence that cannot be uploaded through
regulations.gov,
are available at
https://www.copyright.gov/​1201/​2027/​comment-submission/​
.
If a commenter cannot meet a particular submission requirement, please contact the Office using the contact information below for special instructions.

Rhea Efthimiadis, Assistant to the General Counsel, by email at
USCOGeneralCounsel@copyright.gov
or by telephone at (202) 707-8350.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On June 9, 2026, the U.S. Copyright Office (“Office”) initiated the tenth triennial section 1201 rulemaking by publishing a Notification of Inquiry (“NOI”) and requesting petitions to renew current exemptions, comments responding to the renewal petitions, and petitions for newly proposed exemptions.
[
1
]
In response, the Office received 43 renewal petitions, three comments supporting renewal of an exemption, and eight comments opposing renewal of an exemption.
[
2
]
In addition, the Office received 25 petitions for new exemptions or for expansion of current exemptions.
This Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) summarizes the renewal petitions and states which exemptions the Register of Copyrights (“Register”) intends to recommend for renewal without requiring petitioners to further develop the administrative record. Separately, this NPRM outlines the proposed classes for new exemptions for which the Office is initiating three rounds of public comment, including the one meaningfully opposed renewal petition that the Office will consider as a new petition.
I. Standard for Evaluating Proposed Exemptions
As the NOI explained, before the Register can recommend a temporary
(
printed page 67789)
exemption from the prohibition on circumvention, the record must establish that “persons who are users of a copyrighted work are, or are likely to be in the succeeding 3-year period, adversely affected by the [anti-circumvention] prohibition . . . in their ability to make noninfringing uses under [title 17] of a particular class of copyrighted works.”
[
3
]
When defining a “class of copyrighted works,” the Office generally uses the categories of works in
17 U.S.C. 102
as a starting point and then refines the class by other criteria, such as the technological protection measures (“TPMs”) used, distribution platforms, and types of uses or users.
[
4
]
In evaluating the evidence, the Register weighs the statutory factors in section 1201(a)(1)(C): “(i) the availability for use of copyrighted works; (ii) the availability for use of works for nonprofit archival, preservation, and educational purposes; (iii) the impact that the prohibition on the circumvention of technological measures applied to copyrighted works has on criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, or research; (iv) the effect of circumvention of technological measures on the market for or value of copyrighted works; and (v) such other factors as the [Register] considers appropriate.”
[
5
]
After the Office develops a comprehensive administrative record, the Register makes a recommendation to the Librarian of Congress (“Librarian”) concerning whether exemptions are warranted based on that record.
In considering whether to recommend an exemption consistent with the statutory text, the Register considers the question: “
Are users of a copyrighted work adversely affected by the prohibition on circumvention in their ability to make noninfringing uses of a class of copyrighted works, or are users likely to be so adversely affected in the next three years?
”
[
6
]
This inquiry breaks down into the following elements:
Does the proposed class include at least some works protected by copyright?
Are the uses at issue likely noninfringing under title 17?
Are users currently, or likely to be, adversely affected in their ability to make such noninfringing uses during the next three years?
[
7
]
Is the statutory prohibition on circumventing access controls the cause of the adverse effects?
[
8
]
To determine whether a proposed use is likely to be noninfringing, the Register considers the Copyright Act and relevant judicial precedents.
[
9
]
When considering whether such uses are being adversely impacted by the prohibition on circumvention, the rulemaking focuses on “distinct, verifiable, and measurable impacts” compared to “
de minimis
impacts.”
[
10
]
The Register examines the administrative record as a whole to consider whether the preponderance of the evidence shows that the conditions for granting an exemption have been met.
[
11
]
II. Review of Petitions To Renew Existing Exemptions
In this proceeding, the Office is again using the streamlined process, first adopted in the seventh triennial rulemaking, for the Register's recommendations of renewal of exemptions previously issued by the Librarian.
[
12
]
As the Office explained in its 2017 policy study, the “Register must apply the same evidentiary standards in recommending the renewal of exemptions as for first-time exemption requests,” and the statute requires that “a determination must be made specifically for each triennial period.”
[
13
]
The Office further determined that “the statutory language appears to be broad enough to permit determinations to be based upon evidence drawn from prior proceedings, but only upon a conclusion that this evidence remains reliable to support granting an exemption in the current proceeding.”
[
14
]
The Office has employed this process in each subsequent triennial rulemaking.
Renewal petitions must request readoption of exemptions as currently formulated, without modification. Petitions should support a determination by the Register that, due to a lack of legal, marketplace, or technological changes, the factors that led her to recommend adoption of the exemption in the prior rulemaking remain a reliable basis for the adoption of the exemption.
[
15
]
To the extent that a renewal petition proposes uses beyond the current exemption or language that varies from the exemption as currently enacted, the Office disregards those portions of the petition for purposes of considering the renewal of the exemption, and asks only whether the petition provides sufficient information
(
printed page 67790)
to warrant renewal of the exemption in its current form.
In response to its current NOI, the Office received petitions to renew every existing exemption. Each of the forty-three renewal petitions included a summary of the basis for the continuing need and justification for the exemption. Each petitioner also signed a declaration stating that, to the best of their personal knowledge, there has not been any material change in the facts, law, or other circumstances set forth in the prior rulemaking record such that renewal of the exemption would not be justified. This sworn declaration also includes a statement that, based on their personal knowledge and experience, petitioners believe that if the exemption were not renewed, users would be diminished in their ability to make use of the works at issue.
[
16
]
The Office received eleven comments in response to the renewal petitions, three of which support renewal of specific exemptions. Eight comments oppose certain aspects of the renewal petitions.
[
17
]
As detailed below, after reviewing the petitions for renewal and comments in response, the Office finds that it has received a sufficient petition for each of the existing exemptions. The Office finds meaningful opposition to renewal of one exemption (the current medical device repair exemption); it will not grant this exemption through the streamlined renewal process but will instead allow interested parties to develop the record further so that it can be considered as a new proposed exemption in the regular rulemaking process. The Register intends to recommend readoption of each of the other existing exemptions in their current forms.
A. Audiovisual Works—Criticism and Comment—Filmmaking
International Documentary Association and Kartemquin Educational Films (collectively “Joint Filmmakers”) jointly petition to renew the exemption for motion pictures
[
18
]
for uses in documentary films or other films where the use is a parody or for a biographical or historically significant nature (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(1)(i)(A)
).
[
19
]
No comments were filed opposing renewal.
Joint Filmmakers represent thousands of independent filmmakers across the nation and have participated in every triennial rulemaking since 2008. They state that TPMs such as encryption continue to prevent filmmakers from accessing needed material, and that this is “especially true for the kind of high fidelity motion picture material filmmakers need to satisfy both distributors and viewers.”
[
20
]
Petitioners state their firsthand knowledge that filmmakers have found it necessary to rely on this exemption and will continue to do so.
[
21
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
B. Audiovisual Works—Criticism and Comment—Noncommercial Videos
The Organization for Transformative Works (“OTW”) petitions to renew the exemption for motion pictures for use in noncommercial videos (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(1)(i)(B)
).
[
22
]
OTW, which has advocated for the noncommercial video exemption in past triennial rulemakings, states it has heard from “a number of noncommercial remix artists” who have used the exemption in the past and anticipate needing to use it in the future as well as the increasing cultural and political importance of “fan edits.”
[
23
]
OTW states that “creators continue to make video remixes using DVD and Blu-Ray source[s]” for several reasons, such as engaging in “valuable commentary” and that the “fundamental conditions surrounding video remix have not changed” in the preceding three-year period.
[
24
]
No comments were filed opposing renewal of the exemption as currently formulated.
The Office did, however, receive opposition to OTW's renewal petition to the extent it seeks to modify the regulatory language of this exemption. As in the previous proceeding, OTW's renewal petition proposes the Office “us[e] the relatively simple language defining the exempted class from the 2008 rulemaking,” rather than the exact language in the current exemption, which was adopted in the 2021 rulemaking.
[
25
]
The Entertainment Software Association, Motion Picture Association, and Recording Industry Association of America (collectively “Joint Creators”) jointly oppose OTW's petition to the extent that it requests modification of the exemption's language, arguing the request constitutes an expansion and should therefore be properly submitted as a petition for a new exemption.
[
26
]
The Office agrees. Such a modification cannot be granted via the streamlined exemption renewal procedure and must instead be petitioned for as a new exemption.
[
27
]
OTW did not submit a separate new exemption petition for its proposed modifications. Therefore, OTW's renewal petition will be considered only to the extent that it requests readoption of the current exemption; its proposed modifications cannot be considered in this triennial proceeding.
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of meaningful opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
C. Audiovisual Works—Criticism and Comment—Multimedia E-Books
Authors Alliance and independent film producer and author, Bobette Buster, filed a joint petition to renew the exemption for the use of motion picture excerpts in nonfiction multimedia e-books (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(1)(i)(C)
).
[
28
]
No comments were filed opposing renewal.
Petitioners point to Professor Buster's continuing work authoring film education e-books, which rely on the “essential” use of high-resolution video that would not be available “without the circumvention of technological protection measures.”
[
29
]
In addition to the e-book series titled “Deconstructing Master Filmmakers” discussed in previous rulemakings, Professor Buster
(
printed page 67791)
newly references her lecture series titled “How to Tell Your Story Well,” “What's the Big Idea,” and “Satire and the Shaping of American Culture” and states that she uses the lectures' source material—“particularly film clips that are the subject of this exemption”—in e-book projects that are part of this “broader work in deconstructing feature-length films in-depth.”
[
30
]
Such contemporary evidence of the ongoing need for the exemption combined with petitioners' participation in the last four triennial rulemakings, provide a sufficient basis for renewal of the current exemption.
[
31
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
D. Audiovisual Works—Criticism and Comment—Universities and K-12 Educational Institutions
Peter Decherney, John Jackson, Sarah Banet-Weiser, Library Copyright Alliance (“LCA”), and Society for Cinema and Media Studies (“SCMS”) (collectively “Joint Educators”) jointly petition to renew the exemption for the use of motion picture excerpts for educational purposes by college and university faculty, students, or employees, or K-12 educators and students (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(1)(ii)(A)
).
[
32
]
Brigham Young University-Idaho (“BYU-Idaho”) filed a comment in support of renewal,
[
33
]
and no comments opposing renewal were filed.
Joint Educators provide several contemporary examples of educators and students using film clips for educational purposes including class presentations and coursework. Co-petitioner Decherney declares that he “continues to teach courses every semester that require[s] students to create video essay[s],” which are “piece[s] of video-based criticism or scholarship that makes an argument through the audiovisual medium itself” that are subsequently presented for comment and discussion.
[
34
]
Joint Educators also point to an increase of multimedia criticism in the classroom, with educators “treating film clips and other media not as illustrations of a written argument but as evidence and analytic tools in their own right,” and “build[ing] a lecture or seminar around close analysis of scenes from documentaries, news footage, or television dramas.”
[
35
]
In this rulemaking and through their participation in previous triennial rulemakings, petitioners have represented thousands of digital and literacy educators and/or members supporting educators and students. Joint Educators again suggest that the “entire field” of video essays or multimedia criticism “could not have existed in the United States without fair use and the 1201 educational exemption.”
[
36
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
E. Audiovisual Works—Criticism and Comment—Massive Open Online Courses (“MOOCs”)
Joint Educators also petition to renew the exemption for motion pictures for educational uses in MOOCs (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(1)(ii)(B)
).
[
37
]
No comments opposing renewal were filed, and BYU-Idaho filed a comment in support of renewal.
[
38
]
The petition states that instructors continue to rely on the exemption to “develop, provide, and improve MOOCs,” as well as increase the number of (and therefore access to) MOOCs, particularly in the field of film and media studies.
[
39
]
Joint Educators note the impact of Professor Decherney's History of Hollywood class, which “offers close readings of Hollywood classics like”
King Kong
and
Casablanca
and “analyzes digital special effects, sound design, and other elements of filmmaking”—reaching almost 80,000 students.
[
40
]
The petition also states that the exemption's relevance and use has flourished since the COVID-19 pandemic and the “universal continuing shift of our education systems to online learning,” which has resulted in increased MOOCs offerings and enrollment.
[
41
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
F. Audiovisual Works—Criticism and Comment—Digital and Media Literacy Programs
LCA petitions to renew the exemption for motion pictures for educational uses in nonprofit digital and media literacy programs offered by libraries, museums, and other nonprofits (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(1)(ii)(C)
).
[
42
]
No comments opposing renewal were filed, and BYU-Idaho filed a comment in support of renewal.
[
43
]
LCA, whose member associations comprise “over 100,000 libraries in the United States,” states in its petition that librarians, museums, and other nonprofit entities across the country have relied on the current exemption and will continue to do so for their digital and media literacy programs.
[
44
]
Noting that LCA has participated in every previous triennial rulemaking, including several related to this particular exemption, the petition states that LCA has a high degree of familiarity with the relevant standards.
[
45
]
It states that libraries, museums, and other nonprofit entities “will continue to need to circumvent technological protections so as to enable noninfringing uses of motion pictures in their digital and literacy programs.”
[
46
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
(
printed page 67792)
G. Audiovisual Works—Captioning and Audio Description
The Association on Higher Education and Disability (“AHEAD”), LCA, and KeriAnn Hollerud jointly petition to renew the exemption for motion pictures for the provision of captioning and/or audio description by disability services offices or similar units at educational institutions for students, faculty, or staff with disabilities (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(2)
).
[
47
]
No comments were filed opposing renewal.
Petitioners assert that students with disabilities continue to rely on the exemption, stating that disability services professionals and supporting entities, such as libraries, “have used the exemption to address the requests and concerns of students with disabilities in attendance at their respective educational institutions to create equitable educational experiences,” “ensur[ing] that students with disabilities have access to the same advantages as their peers in the pursuit of education.”
[
48
]
“Based on their regular interaction with those affected by the exemption,” petitioners believe that the circumstances justifying the exemption currently exist and will persist for the next three years.
[
49
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
H. Audiovisual Works—Preservation or Replacement—Library, Archives, and Museum
LCA petitions to renew the exemption for motion pictures for preservation or the creation of a replacement copy by an eligible library, archives, or museum (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(3)
).
[
50
]
No comments were filed opposing renewal.
LCA, which participated in the triennial rulemakings that granted the initial and renewal exemptions, states in its petition that “[c]ultural heritage institutions across the country have relied on the exemption . . . to make preservation and replacement copies of the motion pictures in their collections stored on DVDs and Blu-ray discs.”
[
51
]
The petition further notes that many motion pictures in its over 100,000 member libraries' collections “are unavailable for purchase or streaming” or “continue to deteriorate,” demonstrating the need to engage in such preservation efforts.
[
52
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
I. Audiovisual Works—Text and Data Mining—Scholarly Research and Teaching
Authors Alliance and LCA jointly petition to renew the exemption for text and data mining (“TDM”) of motion pictures by researchers affiliated with a nonprofit institution of higher education, or at the direction of such researchers, for the purpose of scholarly research and teaching (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(4)
).
[
53
]
No comments were filed opposing renewal.
The petition reports that this “exemption has enabled ambitious research agendas that have resulted in published scholarship,” citing a study published in
PNAS
analyzing diversity in Hollywood and other ongoing projects.
[
54
]
“Many researchers are now actively relying on” the exemption for their research, including those at “large research-intensive institutions, such as Stanford University, UC Berkeley, the University of Chicago, [and] Dartmouth.”
[
55
]
Authors Alliance and LCA claim “an increasingly broad group of researchers from smaller and less research-intensive institutions” like Haverford College and Hofstra University “have expressed interest in using the new exemption.”
[
56
]
According to the petition, “academic researchers need to assemble and annotate their own research corpora,” and will continue to need to do so.
[
57
]
The petition further states that the relevant case law has not changed and although “[c]ommercially licensed text and data mining products continue to be made available to research institutions,” such products “do not allow researchers to license the full array of films needed to engage in the research they seek to do, and those works remain protected from copying by” TPMs.
[
58
]
Finally, the petition notes that the exemption excludes compilations licensed for institutional TDM research.
[
59
]
Based on the information provided in the renewal petition and the lack of opposition, the Office concludes that the conditions that led to the adoption of this exemption are likely to continue during the next triennial period. Accordingly, the Register intends to recommend renewal.
J. Literary Works—Text and Data Mining—Scholarly Research and Teaching
Authors Alliance and LCA also jointly petition to renew the exemption for text and data mining of literary works distributed electronically, conducted by researchers affiliated with a nonprofit institution of higher education, for the purpose of scholarly research and teaching (codified at
37 CFR 201.40(b)(5)
).
[
60
]
The Association of American Publishers (“AAP”) submitted a comment in opposition.
This petition parallels the petition for text and data mining of audiovisual works, submitted by the same joint petitioners. Petitioners, who have communicated with “well over a thousand researchers, librarians, and other academic faculty” as part of their outreach to digital humanities research communities, state these researchers are “now actively relying on the TDM exemption in their research.”
[
61
]
Petitioners assert “[t]he exemption has contributed to the growing field of the digital humanities . . . [and] has enabled discrete research projects as well as the development of new research methods.”
[
62
]
Acknowledging that “[c]ommercially licensed [TDM] products continue to be made available to research institutions,” petitioners nonetheless state that these products do not provide researchers access to the “full array of texts needed” to conduct their research.
[
63
]
Because researchers actively rely on the current exemption, and because “there are no material changes in facts, law, technology, or other circumstances that would justify failing to renew it,” petitioners seek to renew the exemption in this cycle.
[
64
]
AAP's comment opposing renewal contends that the previous rulemaking
(
printed page 67793)
record has become unreliable due to factual developments.
[
65
]
AAP first argues that market solutions for researchers to access large corpora of rights-cleared works have emerged in recent years, obviating the need for circumvention and undermining the finding in past rulemakings that researchers lack alternatives to circumvention.
[
66
]
AAP lists several services through which publishers offer their works for use in TDM research, stating that a “wide array of prominent nonprofit research institutions of higher education have already adopted [these services] as a library service to facilitate TDM research, including Columbia University, University of Washington, University of Chicago, Brown University, and University of Oxford.”
[
67
]
AAP also argues that the exemption has had the unintended consequence of contributing to the use of unlawfully acquired works for TDM, asserting that some researchers have scraped pirate sites for TDM research, and that “concerns that unprotected corpora created under the exemption will be siphoned off to train generative [artificial intelligence (`]AI[')] models” have been heightened.
[
68
]
The growth in licensed options for text and data mining that AAP describes is an important consideration to the extent that it obviates the need for the exemption.
[
69
]
While petitioners and opponents agree that such growth has occurred since the last triennial rulemaking proceeding, the evidence AAP provides relates only to a small subset of the works used for TDM research. Even with access to the new options AAP describes, researchers would not have access to the full array of works currently covered by the exemption in the absence of renewal. Accordingly, these developments do not show that the prior rulemaking record no longer reliably supports renewal. For instance, the record does not show that contemporary, in-copyright literary works (like mass market fiction) are now available for licensed TDM use. In 2021, the Register found that the research and teaching the TDM exemption supports can require this type of works: “But for the prohibition on circumvention, researchers would be able to perform TDM techniques on contemporary literary works . . . and teach those techniques in their courses.”
[
70
]
Proponents explained that TDM research on literary works had “typically only been done on works that are in the public domain,”
[
71
]
and that the inability to conduct TDM apart from public domain texts contributed to existing biases within the field.
[
72
]
The Register also found that the offerings of digital libraries like HathiTrust “are insufficient to allow researchers to conduct [this] type of research” in part because of “substantial gaps in its collection,” which “contains a greater proportion of academic monographs than mass-market fiction.”
[
73
]
The inability to use contemporary literary works to teach engaging lessons on TDM was an issue that many academics raised.
[
74
]
The Register found that the new exemption would “enable professors to teach TDM techniques to students using contemporary, diverse, and inclusive works.”
[
75
]
In 2024, the Register found that the Copyright Clearance Center's RightFind service, which licenses journal articles for text and data mining, was not a “serious alternative to circumvention . . . due to the relatively limited scope of the materials it licenses.”
[
76
]
AAP does not identify the works that the publisher and platform offerings it cites make available for TDM research. The services it describes—API access from Wiley, Springer Nature, and Elsevier—are offered by scholarly and scientific publishers. Their offerings are of the same nature as the journal article licensing the Register found inadequate for these TDM research uses in 2024,
[
77
]
although no doubt enormously powerful for mining the scientific, technical, and medical literature those publishers produce. The collection AAP describes most specifically, the twenty-five million pages of historical archival materials in History Vault that ProQuest recently added to its TDM Studio product,
[
78
]
does not supply what the prior record documented researchers could not obtain. The valuable addition of vast amounts of archival materials to the scholarly and scientific platforms detailed by AAP still do not make these platforms adequate alternatives for large swaths of the research being conducted under this exemption.
[
79
]
AAP's other arguments raise concerns about conduct that is outside of the scope of the exemption. While the Office understands the seriousness of unlawful acquisition and use of copyrighted works—and shares in AAP's concern about such risks—the exemption is written to specifically exclude such conduct. To the extent there is any doubt, we reaffirm here that the exception does not permit or sanction these types of acts.
AAP's comment does not provide support for its contention that the exemption is “providing inadvertent cover” for the use of unlawfully acquired literary works.
[
80
]

As stated in the NOI, the Office will not at the NPRM phase “reject any petitioned-for exemption unless it fails to meet the threshold requirements of section 1201(a).”

]
After reviewing the petitions that seek new exemptions, the Office observes that two petitions cannot be granted as a matter of law, as they fail to allege “a particular class of works” or “distinct, verifiable and measurable impacts” on noninfringing uses.
[

]
The first petition proposes that “researchers, journalists, educators, students, investigators, legal professionals, archivists, nonprofit workers, and individuals” be permitted to circumvent “online audiovisual works, web pages, images, PDFs, and related metadata” for “documentation, research, evidence preservation, citation, accessibility, archival review, journalism, education, legal investigation, or personal recordkeeping” purposes.
[
283
]
The relevant barriers to access include TPMs and “streaming-only delivery, expiring URLs, platform restrictions, embedded players, account-gated access, anti-download controls, disappearing or modified online content, and formats that prevent users from saving evidence-quality local copies of materials they can lawfully view.”
[
284
]
The second petition proposes “a class-wide remedy for motion pictures on protected consumer optical discs” where users, “[un]limit[ed] . . . by ownership or occupation,” can circumvent the works for unrestricted purposes, including “private disc-present playback without a fixed copy; private-home filtering under [section] 110(11); criticism or comment using short portions; disability access; public-domain-only use; qualifying replacement or preservation; and restoration of a specifically promised bundled copy.”
[
285
]
The relevant barriers to access include CSS on DVDs, AACS on HD DVD and standard Blu-ray discs, and AACS2 on Ultra HD Blu-ray discs.
[

]
These proposed exemptions are beyond the Librarian's authority to adopt because they do not meet the statutory requirements of an exemption authorized by section 1201. As previously discussed, section 1201 requires that any exemption adopted as part of the triennial rulemaking be limited to “a particular class of copyrighted works.”
[
287
]
Legislative history explains that Congress intended the phrase to encompass “a narrow and focused subset of the broad categories of works . . . identified in [s]ection 102 of the Copyright Act.”
[
288
]
Therefore, the Office uses the section 102 categories as a starting point and refines the proposed classes by other criteria, such as the types of TPMs used or the types of uses. As Congress explained, while the category of “literary works” under section 102(a)(1) “embraces both prose creations such as journals, periodicals or books, and computer programs of all kinds,” “[i]t is exceedingly unlikely that the impact of the prohibition on circumvention of access control technologies will be the same for scientific journals as it is for computer operating systems.”
[
289
]
Congress concluded the “two categories of works . . . do not constitute a single `particular class' for purposes of” section 1201(a)(1).
[
290
]
Neither the first petition (which proposes an exemption for all or nearly all works available online) nor the second petition (which proposes an exemption for all motion pictures with an express lack of limits as to users and uses)
[
291
]
propose an exemption for a single particular class for the purposes of section 1201.
“Determining the appropriate scope of a `class of works' for an exemption may also involve consideration of the adverse effects an exemption may have on the market for or value of copyrighted works.”
[
292
]
Adverse effects may be shown by demonstrating “distinct, verifiable and measurable impacts” on noninfringing uses.
[
293
]
The second petition contains multiple undefined uses that lack any clear bounds and is premised on the concept that they should not have to show adverse effects use-by-use. The Register and the Librarian are unable to analyze the adverse effects of unbounded uses in order to determine whether an exemption could be granted.
[
294
]
The Office's determination not to offer this petition for comment does not foreclose consideration of any of the listed uses: the petition itself states that “each narrower alternative can stand alone,”
[
295
]
and each of those uses were filed by the same petitioner as separate petitions for new exemptions, which the Office has put forth for consideration above.
[
296
]
Because these two petitions fall outside the scope of exemptions that the Register can recommend and the Librarian can adopt under section 1201, the Office declines to put these petitions forward for public comment.
(
printed page 67807)
IV. Phases of the Tenth Triennial Rulemaking
A comprehensive administrative record for the section 1201 triennial rulemaking is developed through written comments, public hearings, post-hearing questions, and
ex parte
meetings. The Register then makes her recommendation to the Librarian, who adopts a final rule. Each future phase of the administrative process is described below.
[
297
]
Late filed submissions in
any
phase of the rulemaking, including amendments or supplements thereto, will not be accepted without a showing of good cause, and their acceptance is subject to the Office's discretion.
[
298
]
Participants should timely file complete comments using the appropriate form. Informational guides explaining section 1201 and the rulemaking process can be found on the Office's section 1201 rulemaking web page at
https://www.copyright.gov/​1201
.
A. Public Comment Phase
This NPRM initiates the second phase of the triennial rulemaking: the public comment phase, which consists of three rounds of written public comments regarding the petitions for new exemptions and any meaningfully opposed renewal petitions. Commenters should present their complete legal and evidentiary case in support of or in opposition to the proposed exemption. In this proceeding, the Office is initiating a page limit requirement for each of the three rounds of written public comments.
1. Substance of Comments
Parties wishing to address proposed exemptions, including the one meaningfully opposed renewal petition, in written comments should familiarize themselves with the substantive legal and evidentiary standards for the granting of an exemption under section 1201(a)(1), as described in the
Addresses
section of this notice above. In addressing factual matters, commenters should be aware that the Office favors specific, real-world examples supported by evidence over hypothetical observations. Commenters should describe with specificity the TPMs that control access to the work, the method of circumvention of those TPMs, whether their presence is adversely affecting noninfringing uses, and whether eligible users may engage in the proposed use through alternate means that do not require circumvention. In general, the Office seeks comment on whether these proposed exemptions should be adopted, including any proposed regulatory language.
Commenters' legal analysis should explain why the proposal meets or fails to meet the criteria for an exemption under section 1201(a)(1), including why the uses sought are or are not noninfringing as a matter of law. The legal analysis should also discuss statutory or other legal provisions that could impact the necessity for or scope of the proposed exemption. Legal assertions should be supported by statutory citations, relevant case law, and other pertinent authority. In cases where a class proposes to expand an existing exemption, participants should focus their comments on the legal and evidentiary bases for modifying the exemption, rather than the underlying exemption. As discussed above, the Register intends to recommend all but one current temporary exemption for renewal, which was meaningfully opposed. That petition will be subject to three rounds of public comment.
2. Comment Submission Instructions and Three Rounds of Written Public Comment
To ensure a clear and definite record for each of the proposals, separate submissions must be submitted for each proposed class and not combined. Accordingly, the same party may submit multiple written comments on different proposals. The Office acknowledges that the requirement of separate submissions may require commenters to repeat certain information across multiple submissions, but concludes that the administrative benefits of creating a self-contained, separate record for each proposal justify the modest added effort.
The first round of public comment is limited to submissions from proponents (
e.g.,
those who proposed new exemptions during the petition phase or provide the legal and evidentiary basis for them during the public comment phase) and other members of the public who support the adoption of a proposed exemption. Those who neither support nor oppose an exemption may also comment with pertinent information. Proponents should present their complete affirmative case for an exemption during the initial round of public comment, including complete legal and evidentiary support.
The second round of public comment seeks comments from those who oppose a proposed exemption; these commenters should present the full basis for their opposition, including complete legal and evidentiary support. The third round of public comment is limited to reply comments from those permitted to comment in the first round, addressing arguments and evidence presented by others during prior rounds. Reply comments should not raise new issues or evidence.
[
299
]
3. Comment Page Limit
In this proceeding, the Office is establishing a page limit for each of the three rounds of written public comments per class. Each commenter may submit a maximum of twenty-five (25) pages, in at least 12-point type, per class per round of comments, except for Proposed Class 8: Computer Programs—Repair, where comments submitted for each subclass should total twenty-five (25) pages or less.
[
300
]
The limitation applies to all comments, including jointly submitted comments.
[
301
]
This page limit does not apply to documentary evidence; specifically, those containing material authored by persons other than the comment submitters (
e.g.,
affidavits, exhibits, letters).
Commenters wishing to exceed the page limit must contact the Office, using the contact information contained within the
For Further Information Contact
section of this NPRM, prior to submission.
[
302
]
The decision to grant a commenter's request is subject to a showing of good cause and at the Office's discretion.
The Office has determined that the authority to impose this page limit is within section 1201(a)(1) and is further supported by its accompanying legislative history. As the Office stated in its
Section 1201 of Title 17
study, “section 1201 appears to give the Office considerable flexibility to define and
(
printed page 67808)
tailor the rulemaking process.”
[
303
]
The relevant statutory provisions do not “mandate [the] specific processes that the Register must follow” for conducting the rulemaking,
[
304
]
beyond “report[ing] and comment[ing] on . . . her views in making” recommendations to the Librarian.
[
305
]
Corresponding legislative history also evidences Congress's intent that the specific rulemaking procedures beyond “permit[ting] interested persons an opportunity to participate through the submission of written statements, oral presentations at one or more of the public hearings, and the submission of written responses to the submissions or presentations of others,” lie within the Office's purview.
[
306
]
The Office concludes that the page limit is consistent with its informal rulemaking requirements under the Administrative Procedure Act
[
307
]
and is a needed change to improve the rulemaking process, “while maintaining procedural rules necessary for it to administer the rulemaking efficiently within the statutorily mandated period.”
[
308
]
B. Public Hearings Phase
After the public comment phase, the Office will hold online public hearings in spring 2027. The hearings will focus on unresolved issues material to proposed exemptions that the Office finds unclear or underdeveloped in the written record, and may offer the opportunity to introduce demonstrative evidence. Demonstrative evidence is limited to demonstrations that illustrate uses, technological measures, or methods of circumvention already described in the written record; it is not a vehicle for new factual showings. Participants may not submit additional written evidence during or after the hearings or introduce new evidence or arguments at the hearings. A separate notice providing details about the hearings and how to participate will be published in the
Federal Register
.
1. Post-Hearing Questions
Following the hearings, the Office may direct written questions to specific participants to discuss discrete issues in particular classes, including suggestions regarding regulatory language. Although submission deadlines are provided, responses to these questions are voluntary. Responses will be posted on the Office's website as part of the public record.
2. Ex Parte Communication
As in prior proceedings, the Office will permit
ex parte
communications after the conclusion of the hearings. Participating parties will be required to follow the Office's regulation on
ex parte
communications.
[
309
]
No
ex parte
communications with the Office regarding this proceeding will be permitted before the hearings have concluded or at any time outside of the permitted period. The Office will identify the specific time period it will accept requests for
ex parte
communications in the notice it publishes to initiate the public hearings phase.
C. Register's Recommendation and Librarian's Final Rule
The Office will analyze the complete administrative record, which may include submissions from other parts of the federal government.
[
310
]
Following consultation with the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, the Register will issue her written recommendation to the Librarian as to which exemptions are warranted, including proposed regulatory text for adoption as a final rule. The Librarian, after consideration of the Register's recommendation, will adopt a final rule announcing any exemptions.
[
311
]

Title; Associated Form; and OMB Number:
Standard Form (SF) 87 Fingerprint Charts; SF 87; OMB Control Number 0705-0002.
Needs and Uses:
The SF 87 fingerprint card is utilized to conduct a national criminal history check, which is a component of a background investigation. The SF 87 is completed by applicants who are under consideration for Federal employment; by Federal employees, to determine whether they should be retained in such employment; by individuals being considered to perform work for the Federal Government under a Government contract or to continue such work; and by persons seeking long-term access to Federal facilities and systems. The SF 87 fingerprint chart is used in background investigations to help establish facts required to determine, for example, whether the subject of the investigation should be adjudicated to be eligible for logical and physical access to Government facilities and systems; suitable or fit for Federal employment; fit to perform work on behalf of the Federal Government under a Government contract; eligible to hold a position that is sensitive for national security reasons; or eligible for access to classified information. The SF 87 form is utilized only when a hardcopy fingerprint chart must be obtained, as opposed to the electronic collection of fingerprints.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title; Associated Form; and OMB Number:
NAWCAD STEM Education Outreach Programs; NAWCAD Forms 5726/1, 5726/2, and 5726/4; OMB Control Number 0703-0096.
Needs and Uses:
The mission of the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division's (NAWCAD) Strategic Education Office (SEO) is to provide meaningful opportunities for students in the areas of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) through outreach activities to middle school and high school students. The purpose of the STEM programs is to provide interactive learning experiences for middle school and high school students to create awareness of the additional internship opportunities and naval careers encouraging students to pursue STEM education and career fields. Through the Southern Maryland region partnership agreements between federal agencies and educational institutions providing support and services to public and private school students, the NAWCAD SEO assists in orchestrating of variety of engagement activities to include NAWCAD hosted annual STEM centric summer camp programs, classroom speaking and demonstrations, school field trips, mentorships, and the organizing of volunteer support for all activities. To facilitate annual events, information must be collected from local area educational institutions, community groups, and/or students via three forms: NAWCAD 5726/1, “NAWCAD SEO Program Request,” NAWCAD 5726/2, “NAWCAD SEO Science Fair Mentor Program Student Application,” and NAWCAD 5726/4, “NAWCAD SEO Program Registration.”

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title; Associated Form; and OMB Number:
Navy Insider Threat Report Form; OPNAV 5510/423; OMB Control Number 0703-0092.
Needs and Uses:
The Department of the Navy uses Office of the Chief of Naval Operations (OPNAV) Form 5510/423, Navy Insider Threat Report, to collect standardized information concerning potential insider threats in support of the Navy Insider Threat Program. The collection supports the Navy's implementation of
Executive Order 13587
, which requires executive branch agencies to establish insider threat programs to deter, detect, and mitigate insider threats and unauthorized disclosures of classified national security information.
The form enables the Navy Analytic Hub to receive, assess, integrate, and respond to reports of concerning behavior or other information that may indicate a potential insider threat. Use of a standardized form reduces the need for repeated follow-up communications
(
printed page 67828)
and provides a consistent means to document relevant information, including submitter information, available information about the subject of the report, a narrative description of the concern, and any known mitigation actions or previous reporting.
The form may be completed by individuals reporting observed incidents or information within their knowledge, as well as by Navy personnel gathering information in support of an insider threat inquiry. For purposes of the Paperwork Reduction Act, the collection accounts only for burden imposed on contractor respondents. Respondents provide only the information available to them; they are not expected to provide personal information about a report subject or information concerning mitigation measures when they do not have access to that information. Navy Analytic Hub personnel may supplement incomplete reports using authorized Government sources and coordination with appropriate command personnel.
Information collected through OPNAV Form 5510/423 is used to support the Navy Insider Threat Program's mission to prevent, detect, deter, and mitigate risks posed by malicious or unwitting insiders.

Needs and Uses:
The Navy Chief of Information (CHINFO) requires this recurrent information collection to fulfill its mandate under Office of the Chief of Naval Operations (OPNAV) Instruction 5726.8C, “Outreach: America's Navy,” which requires providing public affairs advice to the Secretary of the Navy and the OPNAV. To provide informed, strategic counsel, CHINFO must continuously assess the public communication environment, track public understanding of the U.S. Navy and its operations, and monitor recent trends that affect public perception. This empirical brand and opinion research is necessary to evaluate current public perceptions, advise senior U.S. Navy leadership on how emerging global issues will be received, and plan strategic communication strategies around the release of information.
CHINFO uses the quantitative data collected quarterly from representative online panels to evaluate public knowledge, favorability, capability perception, and engagement with the Navy. These insights allow CHINFO to adjust its public communication efforts, address areas of low awareness or misunderstanding, and brief senior leaders on national sentiment regarding

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2013-01-05, which applies to certain Airbus Helicopters (Eurocopter France) Model AS350B3 and EC130B4 helicopters. AD 2013-01-05 requires revising the Limitations section of the rotorcraft flight manual (RFM) supplement to reduce the starter generator operating current to 180 amperes (amps) and installing a placard in the instrument panel to indicate the revised limitation. Since the FAA issued AD 2013-01-05, the manufacturer determined the applicability needs to be revised to add helicopters equipped with certain part numbered starter generators and to remove helicopters with certain engines installed. This proposed AD would require revising the Limitations section of the RFM supplement of the existing RFM for the helicopter, to reduce the starter generator operating current to 180 amps and installing a placard in the instrument panel indicating the revised limitation. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

Background
The FAA issued AD 2013-01-05, Amendment 39-17319 (
78 FR 7641
, February 4, 2013) (AD 2013-01-05), for certain Airbus Helicopters (Eurocopter France) Model AS350B3 and EC130B4 helicopters. AD 2013-01-05 was prompted by an MCAI originated by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2006-0337, dated November 7, 2006, (EASA AD 2006-0337) to correct an unsafe condition identified as excessive power consumption of the starter generator, which reduces the engine surge margin and could result in engine failure.
AD 2013-01-05 requires revising the Limitations section of the RFM
(
printed page 67785)
supplement 29 to reduce the maximum current of the starter generator to 180 amps and installing a placard on the instrument panel below the vehicle engine multifunction display indicating the starter generator reduced limitation: “MAXIMUM CONTINUOUS GENERATOR LOAD = 180A” The FAA issued AD 2013-01-05 to prevent the engine surge margin being reduced, which can result in engine failure and loss of control of the helicopter.
Actions Since AD 2013-01-05 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2013-01-05, EASA superseded EASA AD 2006-0337 and issued EASA AD 2026-0089, dated May 7, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0089) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that the manufacturer revised the applicability to add starter generators having part number 200SGL130Q-4 and to remove certain helicopters equipped with an ARRIEL 2D engine.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-11818.

This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the

section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the material referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require revising the Limitations section of the RFM supplement of the existing RFM for the helicopter and installing a placard in the instrument panel to indicate the revised limitation.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

(d) Subject
